statement:
Starting next class, we will use __normalized scientific notation__ to represent both very large and very small numbers. In this notation, any number can be represented by a number (called the "coefficient") greater than $$1.0$$ and less than $$10,$$ multiplied by ten to some power. For example, here are some numbers written in both the ordinary decimal notation and in normalized scientific notation.

The word "normalized" in "normalized scientific notation" means that the coefficient is greater than or equal to $$1$$ and less than $$10.$$ For example, $$42.1 \times 10^5$$ is in scientific notation, but not normalized scientific notation. In normalized scientific notation, we'd write $$4.21 \times 10^6$$ instead. Throughout this class, you should default to using normalized scientific notation. $$\begin{array}{ r | r } \text{decimal notation} & \text{normalized scientific notation} \\ \hline 350 & 3.50 \times 10^2\,\,\; \\ 10{,}005 & 1.0005 \times 10^4\,\,\; \\ 14.3 & 1.43 \times 10^1\,\,\; \\ 578{,}240.92 & 5.7824092 \times 10^5\,\,\;\\ 0.00037 & 3.7 \times 10^{-4} \end{array}$$

If you haven't learned about scientific notation before or would like some extra practice, please go to the "Prep Work" tab and work through the "Scientific Notation" reading. (If you already are comfortable with scientific notation, you can skip this.)

This question is a short practice problem to make sure you are ready to use scientific notation in upcoming classes.

Suppose a student wants to find the moment of mass $$Mx$$ for some lever and measures $$\begin{aligned} M & = 7 \times 10^3 \;\mathrm{g} \\ x & = 3 \times 10^2 \;\mathrm{cm} \end{aligned}$$

What is the moment of mass in normalized scientific notation?

mathjax: $$ Mx = \blank \times 10^{\blank} \;\mathrm{g \cdot cm} $$

name: Part A. In class, we built an equation to help us understand how levers work. In this…
desc: Part A. In class, we built an equation to help us understand how levers work. In this problem (which has several parts), we'll do the same to help us understand how ramps work. Below is an image of the sort of ramp we're talking about. It's used to make it easier to lift heavy…
statement:
Part A. In class, we built an equation to help us understand how levers work. In this problem (which has several parts), we'll do the same to help us understand how ramps work.

Below is an image of the sort of ramp we're talking about. It's used to make it easier to lift heavy loads, in this case into a truck.

__image credit: https://handiramp.com/product/aluminum-walk-ramp-type-a-38in-wide-16ft-long/__

Let's begin with some exploratory research.

Build your own ramp using whatever materials you have around. One easy way to do this is to use a hardcover book (you can simply tilt the cover to different angles to make ramps of different heights). We also found that a tablet with a kickstand and a felt cover worked well (it was easy to adjust how steep the ramp is.) A piece of corrugated cardboard would also make a good ramp. Feel free to use whatever you have around. Below is a picture of our ramp: Once you have a ramp, take a small toy car which rolls freely (i.e. a car on which you can spin the wheels easily) and push it up your ramp. (If you don't have a small toy car, you can try something else that rolls. We used a small cylindrical tube.) Push the car up the ramp with one finger. Take note of how much force you need to use to push the car up the ramp (you should be able to feel this with your finger).

Based on your exploratory research, does it take more force to push something up

a steep ramp

a shallow ramp

It's the total height of the ramp, not how steep or shallow it is, determines how much force you feel with your finger

It's the same force for all ramps.

abc

new lines

Part B. Now that we have done some exploratory research, it's time to define a specific problem we want to solve with our quantitative model.

For the law of the lever, we asked when a lever would be balanced. Let's ask a similar question for a ramp.

We have a ramp with a box on it. We will call that box $$A.$$ Then we tie a rope to that box. The rope goes over a pulley at the end of the ramp and then is attached to a second box, box $$B,$$ which hangs from the rope. This setup is shown below.

Throughout our analysis, we will ignore the mass of the rope (it's very thin and light) and assume there is no friction.

Based on your exploratory research, which of the following is the best description of when such a ramp will be balanced?

When box $$B$$ has the same mass as box $$A.$$

When box $$B$$ is less massive than box $$A.$$

When box $$B$$ is more massive than box $$A.$$

abc

new lines

left align

Part C. Now that we have a precise quantitative problem to solve, we can mathematize the problem.

In class, our first step in creating an equation for a lever was to decide which features of a lever to keep in our equation and which to ignore. Let's use about the same level of detail for the ramp as we did when writing an equation for levers in class.

If you're familiar with the idea of friction, don't include it. In class, we ignored friction in the seesaw. To make a simple model, we leave friction out. More detailed models could account for it, be we will not do that here.

Which **two** of the following features would we **not** account for in our equation for the force needed to push an object up a ramp? Select all that apply.

the slope of the ramp

the material the ramp is made from

the mass of the ramp

the mass of box $$A$$

the mass of box $$B$$

abc

new lines

left align

Part D. To finish mathematizing the ramp, we can introduce variables. Let's use $$\begin{aligned} M_A:& \text{ mass of box } A \\ M_B: & \text{ mass of box } B \\ s: & \text{ slope of ramp} \end{aligned}$$

Next, we would like some different hypotheses to test. Remember that when we studied the law of the lever, we built an equation template for balancing, $$\text{stuff on left side of lever} = \text{stuff on right side of lever}$$

We would like to do something similar for the ramp, since the boxes are balancing each other on the ramp: $$\text{stuff on ramp} = \text{stuff hanging}.$$

This time, $$\text{``stuff''}$$ needs to consist of the masses of the boxes and the slope of the ramp and nothing else, since that's all we've included in our mathematization.

Here are five hypotheses which fit this format: $$ \begin{array}{ c r l } (1) & M_A & = M_B\\ (2) & M_A \cdot s & = M_B \cdot \sqrt{1 + s^2}.\\ (3) & M_A \cdot s & = M_B\\ (4) & M_A & = M_B \cdot s\\ (5) & M_A \cdot \dfrac{s}{\sqrt{1 + s^2}} & = M_B \end{array} $$

Select two hypotheses which are equivalent to each other.

(1)

(2)

(3)

(4)

(5)

Part E. Our hypotheses (with the equivalent hypotheses reduced to just one hypothesis) are $$ \begin{array}{ c r l } (1) & M_A & = M_B\\ (2) & M_A \cdot s & = M_B \cdot \sqrt{1 + s^2}.\\ (3) & M_A \cdot s & = M_B\\ (4) & M_A & = M_B \cdot s\\ \end{array} $$

We would like to test these hypotheses with an experiment. For our experiment, we will set the slope to some specific value, then try different masses for the boxes until we find a pair of masses that balance.

If we want to make just a single measurement, which slope from the choices below would let us choose just one hypothesis that fits the data best, no matter which hypothesis makes an accurate prediction? (We assume at least one hypothesis makes accurate predictions.)

$$s = 0$$

$$s = \dfrac12$$

$$s = 1$$

Part F. Before mathematizing the ramp problem, we made a qualitative analysis based on our exploratory research. That was in part (B) of this question, where you answered whether the box $$B$$ should be more massive, less massive, or have the same mass as box $$A.$$

Remember that our hypotheses are $$ \begin{array}{ c r l } (1) & M_A & = M_B\\ (2) & M_A \cdot s & = M_B \cdot \sqrt{1 + s^2}.\\ (3) & M_A \cdot s & = M_B\\ (4) & M_A & = M_B \cdot s\\ \end{array} $$

Which one of these hypotheses makes predictions which agree with your qualitative analysis for all values of $$s?$$

Your answer here is the best quantitative hypothesis for when the ramp is balanced.

(1)

(4)

Part G. Make sure you solve Part (F) before working on this part. (In general, for any multi-part homework problem, you should work from part (A) forward.)

You should now have one quantitative hypothesis for when a ramp is balanced. This hypothesis uses $$s,$$ the slope, in a way that may not be intuitive, even though experiment would show the hypothesis to be accurate.

The slope is a ratio of side lengths of the ramp, so in order to understand a little better where this hypothesis comes from, let's redraw our diagram and include side lengths of the ramp measurements. If the slope of the ramp is $$s$$ and the horizontal stretch along the bottom is $$x,$$ what is the hypotenuse of the ramp?

For variables, use lowercase letters.

mathjax: \[\text{hypotenuse} = \blank \cdot \sqrt{1 + \blank^{\blank}}\]

allowed: xsh0123456789-

Part H. We've already chosen a single best quantitative hypothesis for when a ramp is balanced. We'd like to go back and understand what this hypothesis means a little better. To do that, we'll turn the equation for the hypothesis into an equation using the side lengths of the ramp.

**Which one of the following is equivalent to our best quantitative hypothesis? ** $$\text{hypotenuse}$$ means the length of the hypotenuse of the ramp. $$\text{height}$$ means the height of the ramp, and $$\text{width}$$ means the length of the horizontal segment at the bottom of the ramp, called $$x$$ in the previous part of the problem.

In the final lesson of the class, we will return to this interpretation of our ramp hypothesis and try to understand it in the same framework as the law of the lever.

$$M_A \cdot \text{width} = M_B \cdot \text{hypotenuse}$$

$$M_A \cdot \text{hypotenuse} = M_B \cdot \text{height}$$

$$\dfrac{M_A}{\text{height}} = \dfrac{M_B}{\text{hypotenuse}}$$

$$\dfrac{M_A}{\text{hypotenuse}} = \dfrac{M_B}{\text{height}}$$

Part I. Most archaeologists believe that the ancient Egyptians used very long ramps while building the pyramids. (It's also likely that ancient Egyptians used levers and ramps in combination.) The ramps had to be long because long ramps are shallow, and the stones the Egyptians assembled into the pyramids were too heavy to lift up steep ramps.

The stones in the upper layers of Khufu's pyramid have a mass of about $$2 \times 10^3 \;\mathrm{kg}$$ $$(2000 \;\mathrm{kg})$$ each.

The pyramids were primarily built by farmers, laboring in the seasons when there was no farm work to do. Let's estimate that a single worker can exert a force big enough to pick a $$60 \;\mathrm{kg}$$ stone straight up. (This means $$60 \;\mathrm{kg}$$ can play the role of "mass B" from our analysis of a ramp.)

What is the steepest slope for the ramp the ancient Egyptians could have used if each block was to be pushed (and pulled with ropes) by a team of 8 workers?

You can neglect friction for this problem. Although there was friction between the ramp and stone blocks during construction of the pyramids, ancient Egyptians put the stones on sleds, likely lubricated with water, to reduce the friction as much as possible.

This is an estimation problem, so your answer only needs to be approximately correct.

In physics, "estimate" does not mean "take a guess at the answer right away". Instead, it means that you can round things off or make approximations as you work through a problem. You should still use the principles of physics, especially the quantitative hypothesis for how ramps work developed in the earlier parts of this question, as you make your estimate. In fact, much of the estimating has been done for you here, since the problem estimates the mass of a farm worker. In future weeks, you might have to estimate that mass yourself as one part of estimating the slope of the ramps.

name: **About writing problems**, In weeks 1, 4, 7, and 10, our homework has one __writing…
desc: **About writing problems** In weeks 1, 4, 7, and 10, our homework has one __writing problem__. This is a problem where you submit your work to AoPS and our graders give you personalized feedback. This week, you will conduct a qualitative experiment on a new type of lever and…
statement:
**About writing problems**

In weeks 1, 4, 7, and 10, our homework has one __writing problem__. This is a problem where you submit your work to AoPS and our graders give you personalized feedback. This week, you will conduct a qualitative experiment on a new type of lever and report your results.

Your goal is to practice making observations and writing them down clearly so that other scientists can understand your work. You will also practice making and testing hypotheses. You can hand-write your lab report on lined notebook paper, graph paper, or blank paper. You are also welcome to type your response. Be sure to keep your work neat and label each part. You are welcome to draw pictures to explain your work.

A style note: In AoPS math courses, students are often encouraged to use "we" in writing problem solutions. E.g. "We will factor this quadratic equation" rather than "I will factor this quadratic equation." That is a norm in mathematics, but not a universal norm in physics. Professional physics style guides allow using either "I" or "we" when writing a scientific report, so feel free to use whichever feels more natural to you when working on writing problems.

**This week's problem**

Below are pictures of a lever with the fulcrum at the end instead of in the middle. The load (the little pot in the pictures) is between the applied force (from the hand) and the fulcrum. This setup is called a __class 2 lever__.

With this type of lever, you can place a load at three different positions, as shown. Then you can lift the lever. Sometimes, it will take more force to lift the lever and sometimes less, depending on which position the load is in.

Make a hypothesis about when it will require more force and when it will require less to lift the lever. Then build a lever and try it out. You do not need to use the same supplies as those shown in the picture; you can build your lever using any supplies you have available.

Write a report on your experiment. The goal of the report is to explain what you did in this experiment, why you did it, and what you found. A report like this is called a __lab report__.

You do not need to use special formatting or sections in your lab report, but it should be clear enough that someone who wasn't part of our class and didn't previously know about levers could still understand it.

Make sure you include: - What you were trying to figure out by doing an experiment. - What your hypothesis was and why you had that hypothesis. - What your result was, and how it related to your hypothesis.

Your report doesn't need to be long. One page is likely enough.

Although we did a quantitative analysis of the law of the lever in class, this experiment is intended to be qualitative. You don't need to include equations in your report.

In most lab reports, you would also include an explanation of how you built your lever, what supplies you used, etc. However, you may omit that this week. This will keep your report from becoming too long.

**note:** In this class, all your submissions to writing problem should stand completely on their own. For example, you shouldn't reference "position 1", "position 2", and "position 3", meaning the positions from the photo in this problem, without explaining what those positions are. Although your grader will understand what you mean because they have access to the problem, they will grade as if they do not understand what you mean. It's your job to explain your thoughts from scratch. We are practicing writing material that can be understood without referencing the problem itself because this is an important skill in communication in science. You can, however, assume that the grader has a basic scientific understanding, can follow algebra steps, knows what technical terms taught in this course mean, etc.

label: I2P01
name: Where Does the Water on a Cold Glass Come From? — If you get a cold drink at a restaurant, you may notice…
desc: If you get a cold drink at a restaurant, you may notice little beads of water forming on the outside of the glass. Those beads are called __condensation__. Noticing them is an __observation__, and many discoveries begin with someone wondering about an observation they've made…
statement:
If you get a cold drink at a restaurant, you may notice little beads of water forming on the outside of the glass. Those beads are called __condensation__. Noticing them is an __observation__, and many discoveries begin with someone wondering about an observation they've made. As a first exploration, we poured ice water into one cup and room-temperature water into another and let them sit side by side:

A scientific guess about how something works is called a __hypothesis__. Three (made-up) scientists each propose a hypothesis for where the condensation water comes from. __Dr. Leakey__: water seeps through the cold glass from the inside. __Professor Slither__: cold water slides over the rim, from the inside of the glass to the outside. __Academician Vapor__: water is already in the air, and it comes out of the air to form droplets on the cold glass. Rather than argue, the scientists run __experiments__ — they set up conditions and make observations. Whatever they record (numbers, photographs, written notes) is their __data__, and before each experiment every scientist writes down a __prediction__ of what will happen.

__(a)__ Based on the photo above, on which cup did condensation form, and what does that observation suggest about the conditions needed for condensation?

__(b)__ Looking closely at the photo, the condensation reaches only a little above the water line inside the cup; the top of the cup stays clear. Dr. Leakey announces that this proves his seeping hypothesis, since the water inside only reaches that high. Professor Slither replies that her hypothesis explains the observation, too. How might she explain it? What does their disagreement show about interpreting an experiment after it is done, and why does writing predictions __before__ an experiment help?

__(c)__ Someone suggests repeating the experiment with a metal cup instead of a glass one. Dr. Leakey predicts condensation (cold water will seep through metal, too); Professor Slither also predicts condensation (cold water will still climb over the rim of a metal cup). Is this a useful experiment for deciding between their hypotheses? Why or why not?

__(d)__ The scientists instead find a cup with a lid. They pour in cold water, seal the lid, and let the cup sit. What does each of the three scientists predict, and why?

__(e)__ Here are their data. Whose predictions were correct, and whose hypothesis is ruled out?

__(f)__ Two hypotheses remain: Dr. Leakey's (water seeps through from inside) and Academician Vapor's (water comes out of the air onto anything cold). Design one more experiment for which these two hypotheses give __different__ predictions. (Hint: one hypothesis needs water inside the cup; the other only needs the cup to be cold.) The photo below shows the result of such an experiment, using an empty cup chilled in a refrigerator and then left out to sit. State each scientist's prediction and the conclusion.

label: I2P01
name: Scientists Who Don't Give Up — In a series of experiments on __condensation__ (the beads of water that form…
desc: In a series of experiments on __condensation__ (the beads of water that form on a cold cup), three hypotheses were tested. __Dr. Leakey__: the water seeps through the cold glass from inside. __Professor Slither__: cold water slides over the rim from inside to outside…
statement:
In a series of experiments on __condensation__ (the beads of water that form on a cold cup), three hypotheses were tested. __Dr. Leakey__: the water seeps through the cold glass from inside. __Professor Slither__: cold water slides over the rim from inside to outside. __Academician Vapor__: the water is already in the air and comes out of the air onto the cold surface. One experiment used a cup of cold water sealed with a lid; condensation still formed on the outside, contradicting Professor Slither's prediction. Another experiment used an empty cup chilled in a refrigerator; condensation formed on it, contradicting Dr. Leakey's prediction and supporting Academician Vapor's hypothesis.

Real scientists often don't give up easily. American physicist Albert Michelson invented a measuring device called an interferometer and used it to try to detect "the aether," a substance he believed filled the entire universe and allowed light to travel. His experiments kept failing to find it, but Michelson kept inventing reasons the experiment wasn't good enough — for example, slight temperature changes could make the interferometer expand or shrink and mess up the results. His experiment eventually inspired Einstein's relativity theory, which says there is no aether at all, but Michelson believed for his whole life that he just needed a slightly better experiment.

Persistence can also pay off. In 1905 Einstein made a prediction about the __photoelectric effect__ (light knocking electrons off a metal). American physicist Robert Millikan thought Einstein must be wrong and spent ten years building an experiment, which required an exceptionally clean metal surface never exposed to the atmosphere. In the end Millikan's experiment confirmed Einstein's prediction, Millikan changed his mind, and he won a Nobel Prize in 1923 — a prize that started with a wrong idea.

__(a)__ How might Professor Slither try to explain the sealed-cup result without giving up her hypothesis, the way Michelson explained away his aether results?

__(b)__ Did the experiments __prove__ that the condensation water comes out of the air? Why or why not?

__(c)__ Could __more than one__ of the hypotheses be correct at the same time? If both Dr. Leakey's and Academician Vapor's hypotheses were correct, would that explain all of the experimental results described above?

__(d)__ Suppose one experimenter works in a dry desert and another in a humid tropical jungle. Each pours water of the same temperature into a glass, in air of the same temperature. Which experiment is more likely to show condensation? When a repeat of an experiment gives a different result than the original, what is it called, and why does it happen so easily?

label: I2P01
name: Theory or Hypothesis? — Water is made of tiny __molecules__. Each water molecule is built from two hydrogen…
desc: Water is made of tiny __molecules__. Each water molecule is built from two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom, so its molecular formula is $$\mathrm{H_2O}.$$ Molecules move and shake around all the time. In liquid water the molecules stay close to one another, but molecules can…
statement:
Water is made of tiny __molecules__. Each water molecule is built from two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom, so its molecular formula is $$\mathrm{H_2O}.$$ Molecules move and shake around all the time. In liquid water the molecules stay close to one another, but molecules can also escape the liquid and float away freely through the air — that escaped water is __water vapor__. The drawing below shows molecules escaping from a liquid:

Glass is made of molecules too, and the colder the glass, the less its molecules jiggle. __Condensation__ is what happens when water vapor molecules come out of the air and form liquid droplets on a surface.

__(a)__ Using this jiggling-molecules picture, explain why a water vapor molecule that hits a __warm__ glass tends to bounce off, while one that hits a __cold__ glass tends to stick — and how that leads to droplets of condensation on a cold cup.

__(b)__ The same jiggling-molecules idea also explains completely different phenomena, such as the law of proportions in chemistry and Brownian motion (the jittery movement of tiny particles suspended in fluid). When one set of related ideas explains many different phenomena like this, what do scientists call that set of ideas? How is it different from a hypothesis?

__(c)__ Classify each description as fitting a __theory__ or a __hypothesis__: (1) a large set of related ideas; (2) a conjecture or guess; (3) connects several or many different phenomena; (4) a proposed explanation for a single phenomenon.

__(d)__ Your friend says, "I have a theory about the scratch marks on the porch: a raccoon did it." In careful scientific language, is your friend's idea a theory or a hypothesis? Separately: if scientists call an idea "just a theory," does that mean the evidence for it is weak?

label: I2P01
name: Mathematizing the Seesaw — A seesaw (or teeter-totter) is a playground toy: a long board balanced on a…
desc: A seesaw (or teeter-totter) is a playground toy: a long board balanced on a central pivot, with a rider on each end. Two children of similar size can easily push each other up and down because the seesaw is nearly balanced. An adult and a child can also balance — but only if the…
statement:
A seesaw (or teeter-totter) is a playground toy: a long board balanced on a central pivot, with a rider on each end.

Two children of similar size can easily push each other up and down because the seesaw is nearly balanced. An adult and a child can also balance — but only if the adult sits closer to the center than the child. We would like to answer: __given the masses of an adult and a child, and where the child sits, how far from the center should the adult sit so the seesaw balances?__

__(a)__ Is this a __quantitative__ problem or a __qualitative__ one? (A problem is quantitative when its answer can be represented by a number, with units.)

__(b)__ To analyze the seesaw mathematically, we first simplify it. What basic features should our simplified seesaw keep, and what features of the seesaw and of the people should we ignore?

__(c)__ Here is a simplified diagram. The board rests on a pivot called the __fulcrum__, and each person is reduced to a dot. We use __variables__: $$M$$ for a mass and $$x$$ for a distance from the fulcrum. Masses are measured in __kilograms__ $$(\mathrm{kg})$$ — a one-liter bottle of water has a mass of about one kilogram — and distances in __meters__ $$(\mathrm{m})$$ — about the height from the floor to a tall adult's hip. Write an equation stating that a person's mass is seventy kilograms.

__(d)__ In the diagram, the variables carry __subscripts__: person 1 has mass $$M_1$$ and sits a distance $$x_1$$ from the fulcrum, while person 2 has mass $$M_2$$ at distance $$x_2.$$ Why do we need the subscripts?

__(e)__ Our writing now contains both $$M$$ (capital, slanted) and $$\mathrm{m}$$ (lowercase, upright). These mean completely different things. What is each one? What is a __unit__?

__(f)__ Turning a real-world situation into diagrams, variables, and measurements is called __mathematizing__ the problem. Summarize the steps we followed to mathematize the seesaw.

label: I2P01
name: Discovering the Law of the Lever — We want a __quantitative hypothesis__ — an equation — describing when a…
desc: We want a __quantitative hypothesis__ — an equation — describing when a seesaw balances. Physicists don't grab equations out of thin air; the equations express understandable ideas, and we can find them by starting with exploratory research. Since we can't bring a seesaw to…
statement:
We want a __quantitative hypothesis__ — an equation — describing when a seesaw balances. Physicists don't grab equations out of thin air; the equations express understandable ideas, and we can find them by starting with exploratory research. Since we can't bring a seesaw to class, we use a simulation: you can experiment with it at https://phet.colorado.edu/sims/html/balancing-act/latest/balancing-act_en.html (select "Balance Lab" and turn on "Rulers" in the middle box on the right). In the simulation, you place bricks on a seesaw held level by pillars, then remove the pillars: if you chose well, nothing moves; otherwise the seesaw tips.

Let $$M_1$$ and $$x_1$$ be the mass of the brick on the left and its distance from the pivot (the __fulcrum__), and let $$M_2$$ and $$x_2$$ be the mass and distance of the brick on the right. We put a $$M_1 = 5\;\mathrm{kg}$$ brick on the left and a $$M_2 = 10\;\mathrm{kg}$$ brick on the right and searched for positions where they balance. Here is one balancing arrangement, with $$x_1 = 1\;\mathrm{m}$$ and $$x_2 = 0.5\;\mathrm{m}$$:

The full set of balancing positions we found is $$\begin{array}{cc} x_1 & x_2 \\ \hline 0.50\;\mathrm{m} & 0.25\;\mathrm{m} \\ 1.0\;\mathrm{m} & 0.50\;\mathrm{m} \\ 1.5\;\mathrm{m} & 0.75\;\mathrm{m} \\ 2.0\;\mathrm{m} & 1.0\;\mathrm{m} \end{array}$$

__(a)__ What is the pattern in the data? Express it as an equation relating $$x_1$$ and $$x_2.$$ (Careful about which variable is bigger!)

__(b)__ Is your equation from part (a) a suitable hypothesis for how to balance a seesaw with __any__ two objects on it? Why or why not?

__(c)__ When a seesaw is balanced, the stuff on the left seems to be just enough to offset the stuff on the right — which feels like the mathematical notion of equality. So we start from the template $$\text{stuff on left} = \text{stuff on right}.$$ Find an equation that fits this template, agrees with all the data in the table, and uses all four variables $$M_1, x_1, M_2, x_2.$$ (Hint: multiplying both sides of your part (a) equation by $$5$$ gives $$5x_1 = 10x_2$$ — does that make the masses' role more obvious?)

__(d)__ In your equation from part (c), the "stuff" being equated is neither a mass nor a distance but the product $$Mx,$$ called the __moment of mass__. State your hypothesis as a sentence about moments of mass.

__(e)__ Use the hypothesis to make a prediction: an $$80\;\mathrm{kg}$$ adult wants to balance a $$40\;\mathrm{kg}$$ child who sits $$1.5\;\mathrm{m}$$ from the fulcrum. How far from the fulcrum should the adult sit?

statement:
Three competing quantitative hypotheses claim to describe when a seesaw is balanced, where $$M_1, x_1$$ are the mass of the object on the left and its distance from the fulcrum, and $$M_2, x_2$$ are the same for the object on the right: __(1)__ $$M_1x_1 = M_2x_2;$$ __(2)__ $$M_1 + 10 \cdot x_1 = M_2 + 10 \cdot x_2;$$ __(3)__ $$\dfrac{M_1}{x_1} = \dfrac{M_2}{x_2}.$$

Experiments with a seesaw simulation established that the seesaw __does balance__ when $$M_1 = 5\;\mathrm{kg},$$ $$M_2 = 10\;\mathrm{kg},$$ $$x_1 = 1.0\;\mathrm{m},$$ $$x_2 = 0.5\;\mathrm{m}.$$ A useful fact about units: when we __multiply__ or __divide__ quantities with different units, we can invent a __compound unit__ for the result, such as the kilogram-meter $$(\mathrm{kg \cdot m})$$ or kilograms per meter $$(\mathrm{kg/m}).$$

__(a)__ Plug the experimental numbers (with their units) into hypothesis (1). Does it correctly say the seesaw balances?

__(b)__ Plug the numbers into hypothesis (3). What does each side equal, and does the hypothesis survive the test?

__(c)__ If you drop the units, hypothesis (2) gives $$5 + 10 \cdot 1.0 = 10 + 10 \cdot 0.5,$$ that is, $$15 = 15$$ — which looks like success. What is wrong with that calculation?

__(d)__ Which hypothesis is the best description of a balanced seesaw, and what is this famous equation called?

name: The Same Hypothesis in Disguise — The __law of the lever__ says a seesaw is balanced when $$M_1x_1 =…
desc: The __law of the lever__ says a seesaw is balanced when $$M_1x_1 = M_2x_2,$$ where $$M_1, x_1$$ are the mass on the left and its distance from the fulcrum, and $$M_2, x_2$$ are the mass and distance on the right. Experiments confirm it: for example, a seesaw balances with $$M_1…
statement:
The __law of the lever__ says a seesaw is balanced when $$M_1x_1 = M_2x_2,$$ where $$M_1, x_1$$ are the mass on the left and its distance from the fulcrum, and $$M_2, x_2$$ are the mass and distance on the right. Experiments confirm it: for example, a seesaw balances with $$M_1 = 5\;\mathrm{kg},$$ $$M_2 = 10\;\mathrm{kg},$$ $$x_1 = 1\;\mathrm{m},$$ $$x_2 = 0.5\;\mathrm{m}.$$ Call this equation hypothesis (1). Now consider two new candidate hypotheses: __(4)__ $$\dfrac{M_1}{M_2} = \dfrac{x_2}{x_1}$$ and __(5)__ $$M_1x_1 = 1.000000000000000000000001 \cdot M_2x_2.$$

__(a)__ Check hypothesis (4) against the balanced arrangement above. What does each side equal, and what units does it carry?

__(b)__ Show, using algebra, that hypothesis (4) can be obtained from hypothesis (1). (Hint: divide both sides of (1) by something.)

__(c)__ Can you design an experiment for which hypotheses (1) and (4) make different predictions? What do scientists say about two hypotheses that always make exactly the same predictions?

__(d)__ Hypothesis (5) is genuinely different from hypothesis (1) — its predictions differ by about one part in $$10^{24}.$$ Could any real experiment tell them apart? Also, what does hypothesis (5) predict about a perfectly symmetric seesaw, with $$M_1 = M_2$$ and $$x_1 = x_2?$$ Given all this, why do scientists still favor hypothesis (1)?

statement:
The goal of this problem is to show you some common measurement devices and get you thinking about how they work. To do that, it introduces a new distinction: the distinction between digital and analog devices.

-----------------------------------------

Measurement devices are either __digital__ or __analog__. A digital device is one that reads out one of a "discrete" means "not smooth" or "discontinuous" set of readings.

An analog device is one that can move smoothly between values. For example, below are pictured an analog thermometer and a digital thermometer. __Analog thermometer. By Doggo19292 - Own work, Attribution, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=102933605__

This is an analog thermometer because the red liquid in the tube can move smoothly to higher or lower values. There are discrete lines on the side of the thermometer, but those are to assist with the reading. The measurement is made by the height of the red column, which advances smoothly.

__Digital thermometer. Popka, product image from Amazon__

This is a digital thermometer because the only readout is one that advances in discrete jumps. In this case, those jumps are $$0.1^\circ \mathrm{C}.$$

Below are images of measuring instruments, along with brief descriptions of what they measure. Categorize each according to whether it is digital or analog.

**a)** This is a multimeter. It is used in electric circuits to measure the voltage, current, or resistance between different parts of the circuit. It reads out voltage, for example, to the nearest thousandth of a volt on its display. __By Binarysequence - Own work, CC BY-SA 3.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=23376138__

**b)** A tape measure used to measure lengths of a few meters. __By User Moriori on en.wikipedia - Photo taken by User:Moriori for Ruler article, Public Domain, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=989462__

**c)** These calipers are used to measure distances to higher accuracy than a ruler. The length is read off from the electronic display, which advances in units of $$0.01 \;\mathrm{mm}.$$ __By Jacek Halicki - Own work, CC BY-SA 4.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=86354986__

**d)** A simple bathroom scale. When the user stands on it, the dial with numbers spins to show the weight. __Sears, https://www.sears.com/taylor-scales-analog-bath-scale-white/p-08311839000P__

**e)** This home radio has a knob you can turn to change the station. As you smoothly turn the knob, the frequency that the radio is tuned to changes. __Tolga Sipahi, Getty Images__

label: I2P02
name: Part A. In this two-part problem, you'll practice figuring out how to find conversion…
desc: Part A. In this two-part problem, you'll practice figuring out how to find conversion factors given some information about units presented in paragraph form. The challenge is to read the information, understand how it can be used to create conversion factors, and then use those…
statement:
Part A. In this two-part problem, you'll practice figuring out how to find conversion factors given some information about units presented in paragraph form. The challenge is to read the information, understand how it can be used to create conversion factors, and then use those conversion factors to answer the question. Part (A) is shorter and you may or may not need a conversion factor for it. In part (B), there will be more conversions to make.

-------------------------------

From 1793 - 1805, France used the "French Republican Calendar" to keep track of time. Under this system, each day was divided into ten hours, each hour was divided into 100 minutes, and each minute into 100 seconds. Because these lengths of time are not the same as ordinary hours, minutes, and seconds, we can call them "FR hours", "FR minutes", and "FR seconds", short for "French Republican hours", etc. So a day was equal to ten FR hours, an FR hour was equal to 100 FR minutes, etc. The length of one day was the same in this system as in the current, modern one.

France no longer uses this calendar. Instead, they use the same definition of hours, minutes, and seconds that people in the US and all other countries around the world do, with 24 hours in a day, 60 minutes in an hour, and 60 seconds in a minute. In this problem we'll imagine France was going to convert back to the French Republican Calendar and figure out the consequences.

Aside from a few highways and roads in cities, most French roads today use the same speed limit, which is currently $$80 \dfrac{\mathrm{km}}{\mathrm{hour}}.$$ (France uses kilometers, not miles to measure distance. This speed limit is approximately 50 mph. France lowered the speed limit to this value in 2018 in a successful attempt to reduce traffic accident deaths. The speed limit is also lower than this when conditions are wet or otherwise dangerous.)

If France were to convert to using FR hours again, how would we write the speed limit in France, assuming drivers should go no faster or slower than before the unit change?

The definition of the kilometer does not change in this scenario.

mathjax: \[80 \dfrac{\text{km}}{\text{hour}} = \blank \dfrac{\text{km}}{\text{FR hour}}\]

Part B. Here, we continue to refer to the French Republican Calendar. You'll need to find multiple conversion factors in this problem.

-----------------------------

Recall that under this system, each day was divided into ten FR hours, each FR hour was divided into 100 FR minutes, and each FR minute was divided into 100 FR seconds. Also, days are the same in the FR system and in our modern system.

Suppose you want to play a few rounds of the South African trivia game "30 Seconds" (in which the rounds all last 30 seconds), but you have a watch that measures FR seconds as defined in the French Republican Calendar, not ordinary seconds. You don't want to change how long a round is, so you'll need to do a unit conversion to figure out the length of a round, as measured in FR seconds.

How many FR seconds are there in 30 ordinary seconds?

Round your answer to the nearest tenth of an FR second.

mathjax: \[30 \;\mathrm{seconds} = \blank \text{ FR seconds}\]

label: I2P02
name: The lesson for this problem is that you don't necessarily need to know where a…
desc: The lesson for this problem is that you don't necessarily need to know where a mathematical expression comes from or what it's an expression for in order to make some sense of it. Here, we'll use dimensions to figure out what type of thing (a length, an area, or a volume)…
statement:
The lesson for this problem is that you don't necessarily need to know where a mathematical expression comes from or what it's an expression for in order to make some sense of it. Here, we'll use dimensions to figure out what type of thing (a length, an area, or a volume) various expressions represent. All the expressions in this problem are real mathematical expressions that you could come across in science or math problems, but you don't need to know what problems they come from in order to figure out what type of thing these expressions represent!

------------------------------------

Each of the following expressions is in terms of some variables. All the variables represent a length of some kind. For example, the variable $$\color{red}{a}\color{black}$$ might be the side length of a rectangle and the variable $$\color{red}{r}\color{black}$$ might be the radius of a circle. In this problem, the exact interpretation of each variable is not important. What matters is that each variable is some length. ($$\pi$$ is not a variable. It is a number with no dimensions. The variables are $$\color{red}{a}\color{black}, \color{red}{b}\color{black}, \color{red}{c}\color{black}, \color{red}{d}\color{black}, \color{red}{\ell}\color{black}, \color{red}{h}\color{black}, \color{red}{r}\color{black}, \color{red}{r_1}\color{black}, \color{red}{r_2}\color{black}$$ and $$\color{red}{R}\color{black}.$$ We've colored them red to help you recognize which symbols are variables.)

Classify each expression according to whether it is for a length, an area, or a volume.

As an example, let's look at $$\sqrt{\color{red}{abc}\color{black}(\color{red}{a}\color{black}+\color{red}{b}\color{black}+\color{red}{c}\color{black})}.$$ First, we look at $$\color{red}{a}\color{black} + \color{red}{b}\color{black} + \color{red}{c}\color{black}.$$ This is the sum of three lengths. When we add any number of lengths, we get another length, so $$\color{red}{a}\color{black} + \color{red}{b}\color{black} + \color{red}{c}\color{black}$$ is a length. That means $$\color{red}{abc}\color{black}(\color{red}{a}\color{black}+\color{red}{b}\color{black}+\color{red}{c}\color{black})$$ is four lengths all multiplied together, so that quantity has dimensions $$\mathrm{L}^4.$$ We are looking at $$\sqrt{\color{red}{abc}\color{black}(\color{red}{a}\color{black}+\color{red}{b}\color{black}+\color{red}{c}\color{black})},$$ which is the square root of something with dimensions of $$\mathrm{L}^4,$$ so its dimensions are $$\sqrt{\mathrm{L^4}} = \mathrm{L^2}.$$ These are the dimensions of area, so $$\sqrt{\color{red}{abc}\color{black}(\color{red}{a}\color{black}+\color{red}{b}\color{black}+\color{red}{c}\color{black})}$$ is an area. We can say this confidently, even though we don't know what area it is.

As another simple example, $$\color{red}{a}\color{black}^3$$ is a volume because if we replace $$\color{red}{a}\color{black}$$ by its dimension $$\mathrm{L},$$ the expression becomes $$\mathrm{L}^3,$$ which is the dimension of a volume. Your job is to classify the remaining expressions.

One of the expressions uses $$\mathrm{ln}.$$ This is the __natural logarithm__. It is okay if you haven't learned about logarithms and don't know what $$\mathrm{ln}$$ means. All you need to know is that $$\mathrm{ln}$$ is not a variable; it is a function. It does not carry any dimensions, so from a dimensions perspective you can ignore the $$\mathrm{ln}.$$

desc: Although this problem doesn't directly test your knowledge of units or unit conversions, it is closely related to the concept of dimensions. Think about the dimensions of the quantities in this problem and use that to help you answer it. ------------------------------ The…
statement:
Although this problem doesn't directly test your knowledge of units or unit conversions, it is closely related to the concept of dimensions. Think about the dimensions of the quantities in this problem and use that to help you answer it. ------------------------------

The __Dictyostelium discoideum__ is an amoeba, a single-celled organism. Under ordinary circumstances, when viewed under a microscope, the amoebas will look like separate individual cells:

__Susan Lee and Rick Firtel, UCSD__

__Dictyostelium discoideum__, however, is a __slime mold__. As part of their lifecycle, the individual amoeba aggregate, forming a film, and then grow into a slug shape. (There are several other shapes that the aggregations take at various stages of the life cycle. Below are several slugs as well as a few other shapes.)

__Queller/Strassmann Lab - Photographed by Usman Bashir__

Scientists wanted to know how many individual amoeba cells go into a slug. To figure this out, they estimated the volume of an individual amoeba and the volume of a slug, then did arithmetic to find the number of amoeba in a slug.

In 1953, two scientists, Bonner and Frascella, estimated the diameter of a single __Dictyostelium discoideum__ to be $$8 \;\mathrm{\mu m}.$$ (Remember that $$1 \;\mathrm{\mu m}$$ is one __micrometer__, or $$10^{-6} \;\mathrm{m}.)$$ They also measured the volume of a __Dictyostelium discoideum__ slug. With these measurements, they estimated there are about $$100{,}000$$ amoeba in a single slug.

In 1998, Bonner returned to the problem and used new methods to estimate the diameter of a single amoeba. This time, he found $$4 \;\mathrm{\mu m}$$ for the average diameter. Bonner did not change his estimate of the volume of a slug between 1953 and 1998. He also didn't change his assumptions about the shape of amoeba, just the overall scale.

Bonner used his updated diameter measurement to re-estimate the number of amoeba in a single slug. What was his new estimate?

(You should enter a number as your answer. To answer this problem, try thinking about the dimensions of the quantities involved; you won't need to use any geometric volume formulas.)

label: I2P02
name: In this problem, you'll practice a different type of unit conversion that we did in…

statement:
In this problem, you'll practice a different type of unit conversion that we did in class. You will not be able to use conversion factors in the form of a fraction equal to one. However, you can solve this problem by setting up linear equations.

-------------------

Converting between temperature scales is a little different than most unit conversions, such as those for length. This is because for temperature scales, the zero can mean different things in different scales. For example, $$0^\circ\mathrm{F} = -\dfrac{160}{9}^\circ\mathrm{C}.$$

There are two common temperature scales that do have the same zero, called __absolute zero__. These are the Kelvin and Rankine scales.

A temperature of $$0^\circ \mathrm{C}$$ corresponds to a temperature $$273.15 \;\mathrm{K}.$$ The Kelvin and Celsius scales are set up so that increasing any temperature by $$1 \;\mathrm{K}$$ also increases that temperature by $$1^\circ \mathrm{C}.$$

Like the Kelvin and Celsius scales, the Fahrenheit and Rankine scales use the same step size between degrees, but have a constant offset from each other. A temperature change of $$1^\circ \mathrm{C}$$ is the same as a temperature increase of $$\dfrac95^\circ$$ in Fahrenheit or Rankine.

The Fahrenheit and Celsius scales have the same numerical value at $$-40^\circ,$$ meaning $$-40^\circ \mathrm{F} = -40^\circ \mathrm{C}.$$

At what numerical value do the Kelvin and Fahrenheit scales have the same temperature?

Do not include units in your answer for this question, since it's asking about two different units simultaneously. Just give the numerical part of the answer. Do not round your answer; the data given above about the temperature scales is exact, so your answer here should be exact and include all the decimal places.

statement:
Physicists using SI measure a quantity called __power__ in __watts__, $$\mathrm{W}.$$ The watt is a derived unit defined as $$1 \;\mathrm{W} = 1 \;\mathrm{kg}\dfrac{\mathrm{m}^2}{\mathrm{s}^3}.$$

The symbol $$``\mathrm{s}"$$ is the SI symbol for "seconds", so one watt is one kilogram square meter per cubic second.

A household microwave will have a power output of approximately $$900 \;\mathrm{W}.$$

We rarely microwave food for one second, but it's common to microwave it for one minute, so let's invent a new unit of power, which we can call the "zap" and denote with the symbol $$\mathrm{z}.$$ We'll define the zap via the equation $$1 \;\mathrm{z} = 1 \;\mathrm{kg} \dfrac{\mathrm{m^2}}{\mathrm{min}^3}.$$

What is the power of a $$900 \;\mathrm{W}$$ microwave when measured in zaps? Enter your answer in scientific notation.

Don't confuse $$\mathrm{m},$$ the symbol for meters, with $$\mathrm{min}$$ for minutes.

statement:
Part A. In this problem, we'll practice identifying dimensions and working with dimensions in mathematical formulas. In the next part, we'll use your result here to figure out something important about planets in around distant stars.

-----------------------

Isaac Newton came up with the following formula for the gravitational force between two objects with masses $$m_1$$ and $$m_2:$$ $$F = \dfrac{Gm_1m_2}{r^2}.$$

(Newton never wrote the formula in quite this way, but he wrote something equivalent, and this is the modern notation.)

Force has dimensions $$\left = \mathrm{M \cdot L \cdot T^{-2}}.$$ $$r$$ is the distance between the two objects.

Given this information, find the dimensions of $$G.$$

mathjax: \[\left = \mathrm{M^\blank L^\blank T^\blank }\]

allowed: -1.023456789

Part B. In this problem, you will use dimensions to answer a question that deals with physics you haven't previously learned. The goal of the problem is to show you how, even if you don't understand everything about a physical scenario or everything about where a formula comes from, you can still often make progress just by thinking about dimensions.

-------------------------------

Using a technique called the __Doppler shift__, astronomers are able to measure how fast distant stars are moving towards or away from Earth.

In 1995, astronomers measuring star Pegasi 51 noticed that the star was coming towards Earth, then moving away, then coming towards Earth again in a regular manner. Their data looked like this:

__image credit: Pearson Education__

Astronomers realized that the reason the star seemed to be shaking back and forth in the sky was that it had a planet orbiting it. Although they couldn't see the planet directly, they knew that the planet's gravity was alternately tugging the star towards and away from Earth, depending on where the planet was in its orbit. It was by examining this graph that astronomers discovered the first known planets around other stars.

Astronomers wanted to know more about the planet orbiting Pegasi 51. One thing they did was draw a horizontal bar beneath all the data points in the plot to indicate the __period__ $$P$$ of the orbit. This is the time it takes the planet to make one complete trip around Pegasi 51. Astronomers also knew that finding the period would help them figure out how far away the planet was from the star, which would help them figure out how hot the planet might be and whether it might support life.

According to the theory of Newtonian mechanics, the distance $$a$$ between a star and a planet is $$a = \left( G (m_1+m_2) \left(\dfrac{P}{2\pi}\right)^2 \right)^n$$ for some number $$n.$$

In this equation, $$G$$ is the gravitational constant from Newton's formula in the previous part of this problem. $$m_1$$ is the mass of the planet and $$m_2$$ is the mass of the star. $$n$$ has no dimensions; it is just a number. What is the exact value of $$n?$$ (Do not use a decimal approximation for this problem.)

statement:
In an online simulation you have a ruler, a spring hanging vertically, and a $$100\;\mathrm{g}$$ cylinder. Your job is to measure how much the spring __stretches__ when you hang the cylinder from its end. You can try the simulation yourself at https://aops-curriculum.github.io/268_Introduction_to_Physics/measure_spring/index.html

__(a)__ When you attach the cylinder and let it go, it bounces up and down — it __oscillates__ — as shown above. Why does this make it hard to measure the stretch, and what is one technique you could use to make the oscillations small enough to measure cleanly?

__(b)__ When a class did this, some students reported the spring stretched about $$60\;\mathrm{cm}$$ to $$70\;\mathrm{cm},$$ while others reported between $$10\;\mathrm{cm}$$ and $$20\;\mathrm{cm}.$$ The two groups were measuring two different things. What were they, and which one is the stretch we actually want?

__(c)__ The class collected everyone's measurements and displayed them in a __histogram__ — a chart with bars, where each bar covers a small range of values and its height shows how many students got a value in that range. If one bar covers the range from $$14.5\;\mathrm{cm}$$ to $$15.0\;\mathrm{cm}$$ and has a height of $$4,$$ what does that tell you?

__(d)__ The class then added two tricks: they turned on guide lines marking the spring's resting position, and they lined the $$10\;\mathrm{cm}$$ mark of the ruler up with the top guide line and subtracted $$10\;\mathrm{cm}$$ from each reading. After these changes, the new histogram was narrower — the bars were clustered into a smaller range of values. In the language of measurement, what improved, and what is the name for the spread in a set of measurements?

label: I2P02
name: Units and Dimensions in the Kitchen — A boy named West is making "pasta sauce" out of jam. His dad asks how…
desc: A boy named West is making "pasta sauce" out of jam. His dad asks how much jam to use, and West answers "ten." __(a)__ Setting aside the unusual choice of jam as a sauce, what is wrong with the instruction to use "ten"? What must always be attached to a measurement to fix this…
statement:
A boy named West is making "pasta sauce" out of jam. His dad asks how much jam to use, and West answers "ten."

__(a)__ Setting aside the unusual choice of jam as a sauce, what is wrong with the instruction to use "ten"? What must always be attached to a measurement to fix this problem?

__(b)__ The fix is to give a __unit__. What is a unit? Explain why a centimeter is a good example of one.

__(c)__ Next West says to add "five inches" of carrot juice. Inches are a perfectly good unit, but they are still the wrong choice here. What is wrong with measuring carrot juice in inches?

__(d)__ A __dimension__ is the category of all units you can convert between, such as the dimension of __length__ (which includes meters, inches, and feet) or the dimension of __volume__. Scientists agree to use the __International System__ of units, abbreviated __SI__. Name two SI units that have the dimension of volume, and name one volume unit people commonly use for cooking.

label: I2P02
name: Feet to Miles: Estimate, Then Compute — There are $$5280\;\mathrm{feet}$$ in a mile. The goal is to find how…
desc: There are $$5280\;\mathrm{feet}$$ in a mile. The goal is to find how many miles there are in $$10{,}000\;\mathrm{feet},$$ working in three stages: first decide whether the answer is large or small, then estimate it, then compute it exactly. __(a)__ You are measuring a distance…
statement:
There are $$5280\;\mathrm{feet}$$ in a mile. The goal is to find how many miles there are in $$10{,}000\;\mathrm{feet},$$ working in three stages: first decide whether the answer is large or small, then estimate it, then compute it exactly.

__(a)__ You are measuring a distance across town. Will the number be bigger if you measure it in feet or in miles? Based on that, to convert a length from feet to miles, should you multiply or divide by $$5280?$$

__(b)__ Estimate the answer by rounding $$5280$$ to $$5000.$$ About how many miles is $$10{,}000\;\mathrm{feet}?$$

__(c)__ Without doing the exact calculation yet, predict whether the true answer is slightly more or slightly less than your estimate from part (b). Explain using the fact that the exact calculation divides by $$5280$$ instead of $$5000.$$

__(d)__ Now compute the exact value of $$\dfrac{10{,}000\;\mathrm{feet}}{5280\;\mathrm{feet/mile}}.$$ The exact answer can also be written as the fraction $$\dfrac{125}{66}\;\mathrm{miles}.$$ For telling someone how far a walk is, which form is more useful, and why is the rough estimate from part (b) often good enough anyway?

label: I2P02
name: Comparing Two Solar Parks — Below are two solar power facilities: the Bhadla Solar Park in Rajasthan, India…
desc: Below are two solar power facilities: the Bhadla Solar Park in Rajasthan, India, and the Copper Mountain Solar Facility in Nevada, USA. We want to compare how much they can produce. A useful number to compare is a park's __capacity__: the maximum rate at which it produces…
statement:
Below are two solar power facilities: the Bhadla Solar Park in Rajasthan, India, and the Copper Mountain Solar Facility in Nevada, USA. We want to compare how much they can produce.

A useful number to compare is a park's __capacity__: the maximum rate at which it produces energy. A rate of energy production has the dimension of __power__, whose SI unit is the __watt__ ($$\mathrm{W}$$). We will use __gigawatts__, $$\mathrm{GW},$$ where the SI prefix "giga" means $$10^9$$ (one billion), so $$1\;\mathrm{GW}=10^9\;\mathrm{W}.$$ Copper Mountain's capacity is about $$0.802\;\mathrm{GW}.$$

__(a)__ Someone proposes comparing the two parks just by counting the number of solar panels in each. Give one reason this is not a great comparison.

__(b)__ The US Department of Energy reports that the average power used by the entire US is about $$101.2\;\dfrac{\mathrm{quad}}{\mathrm{year}}.$$ Why can this number not be compared directly with Copper Mountain's $$0.802\;\mathrm{GW}?$$

__(c)__ Convert $$101.2\;\dfrac{\mathrm{quad}}{\mathrm{year}}$$ into watts using the __factor-label method__ (multiplying by conversion factors that each equal $$1,$$ arranged so unwanted units cancel). Use these facts: $$1\;\mathrm{quad}=1.055\times 10^{18}\;\mathrm{J},$$ $$1\;\mathrm{W}=1\;\mathrm{J/s},$$ and $$1\;\mathrm{year}=3.1536\times 10^{7}\;\mathrm{s}.$$ (The last value comes from $$365\;\mathrm{day}\times 24\;\mathrm{h/day}\times 60\;\mathrm{min/h}\times 60\;\mathrm{s/min}.$$)

__(d)__ Convert your answer from watts to gigawatts, then compare it with Copper Mountain's $$0.8\;\mathrm{GW}.$$ Roughly how many Copper Mountain facilities would it take to supply the average US power demand?

label: I2P02
name: Snow White and the Seven Gardens — Each of the seven dwarfs builds a little circular garden using…
desc: Each of the seven dwarfs builds a little circular garden using $$10\;\mathrm{m}$$ of fencing. Snow White suggests pooling all the fences into one big circular garden. Grumpy objects: "We'd have seven times as much fence, so the garden would be seven times as big. Split seven…
statement:
Each of the seven dwarfs builds a little circular garden using $$10\;\mathrm{m}$$ of fencing. Snow White suggests pooling all the fences into one big circular garden. Grumpy objects: "We'd have seven times as much fence, so the garden would be seven times as big. Split seven ways, we each get the same as before." The figures below show the seven separate gardens and the single big garden made from the same total fence.

__(a)__ Recall the circle formulas $$C=2\pi r$$ (circumference) and $$A=\pi r^2$$ (area). Each little garden has circumference $$10\;\mathrm{m};$$ the big garden uses all the fence, so its circumference is $$70\;\mathrm{m}.$$ Eliminate $$r$$ to show that area can be written $$A=\dfrac{C^2}{4\pi},$$ and use this to find the __exact__ ratio $$\dfrac{A_{\rm large}}{A_{\rm small}}.$$ Was Grumpy right?

__(b)__ Suppose there had been $$n$$ dwarfs instead of seven, each contributing one little garden's worth of fence. How many times the area of one little garden would the single big garden have?

__(c)__ Now suppose the gardens are __heptagons__ (seven-sided figures) rather than circles, and no one knows a formula for a heptagon's area. It turns out the area of a regular heptagon obeys $$A=k\,P^2$$ for some constant $$k$$ (about $$0.074$$), where $$P$$ is the perimeter. Explain why the big heptagonal garden still has exactly $$49$$ times the area of a little one, and why the same conclusion holds for gardens of __any__ single shape, so that $$A\propto \ell^2$$ where $$\ell$$ is any chosen length on the shape.

__(d)__ Grumpy claims a heart-shaped garden instead obeys $$A=1.934\,\ell^{2.07},$$ where $$\ell$$ is a length in meters. Without measuring anything, explain how you can tell at a glance that this formula is wrong. (Hint: what units would the right side have if $$\ell=17\;\mathrm{m}?$$)

__(e)__ We write $$[\,\ell\,]$$ to mean "the dimensions of $$\ell.$$" A length has $$[\,\ell\,]=\mathrm{L}$$ (the symbol $$\mathrm{L}$$ for the length dimension is written upright, unlike a slanted variable). Explain why $$[\,2\ell\,]=\mathrm{L}$$ and why the area of __any__ region has dimensions $$\mathrm{L}^2$$ — including a triangle of area $$A=\tfrac12 b h,$$ where no variable is literally squared.

label: I2P02
name: Gravity, Falling, and the Pendulum — Physics uses three basic dimensions: length $$\mathrm{L},$$ mass…
desc: Physics uses three basic dimensions: length $$\mathrm{L},$$ mass $$\mathrm{M},$$ and time $$\mathrm{T}.$$ The strength of Earth's gravity is described by $$g\approx 9.8\;\mathrm{m/s^2}.$$ A grandfather clock keeps time with a swinging __pendulum__; the __period__ $$P$$ is the…
statement:
Physics uses three basic dimensions: length $$\mathrm{L},$$ mass $$\mathrm{M},$$ and time $$\mathrm{T}.$$ The strength of Earth's gravity is described by $$g\approx 9.8\;\mathrm{m/s^2}.$$ A grandfather clock keeps time with a swinging __pendulum__; the __period__ $$P$$ is the time for one full swing back and forth.

__(a)__ A speed is a length per time, with dimensions $$\mathrm{L}\cdot\mathrm{T}^{-1}.$$ Does $$g$$ have the dimensions of a speed? Find the dimensions of $$g$$ and explain what kind of quantity it is. (Careful: $$\mathrm{m}$$ means meters, a length; $$\mathrm{M}$$ is the mass dimension.)

__(b)__ You drop a rock and it falls for $$t=3.1\;\mathrm{s}.$$ The only quantities available are $$t$$ (with dimensions $$\mathrm{T}$$) and $$g.$$ The speed $$v$$ you want has dimensions $$\mathrm{L}\cdot\mathrm{T}^{-1}.$$ Find the one simple way to combine $$g$$ and $$t$$ to get those dimensions, write the resulting formula, and use it to estimate the rock's speed after $$3.1\;\mathrm{s}.$$

__(c)__ Now the main question: how should the period $$P$$ of a pendulum depend on its length $$\ell?$$ First explain why no power of $$\ell$$ alone can have the dimensions of $$P,$$ given $$[\,\ell\,]=\mathrm{L}$$ and $$[\,P\,]=\mathrm{T}.$$ Then bring in $$g$$ (since gravity drives the swing, $$[\,g\,]=\mathrm{L}\cdot\mathrm{T}^{-2}$$) and find a combination of $$\ell$$ and $$g$$ with the dimension $$\mathrm{T}.$$ This gives the proportionality for $$P.$$

__(d)__ Treating $$g$$ as fixed, your result simplifies to $$P\propto\sqrt{\ell}.$$ By what factor must you change a pendulum's length to __double__ its period?

label: I2P02
name: Temperature Scales and Absolute Zero — Water freezes at $$32^\circ\mathrm{F}$$ on the Fahrenheit scale and at…
desc: Water freezes at $$32^\circ\mathrm{F}$$ on the Fahrenheit scale and at $$0^\circ\mathrm{C}$$ on the Celsius scale. __(a)__ Most unit conversions use a __conversion factor__: a fraction equal to $$1$$ that you multiply by. Explain why no such multiplicative conversion factor can…
statement:
Water freezes at $$32^\circ\mathrm{F}$$ on the Fahrenheit scale and at $$0^\circ\mathrm{C}$$ on the Celsius scale.

__(a)__ Most unit conversions use a __conversion factor__: a fraction equal to $$1$$ that you multiply by. Explain why no such multiplicative conversion factor can convert Celsius to Fahrenheit. (Hint: what happens when you multiply $$0^\circ\mathrm{C}$$ by any factor?)

__(b)__ Scientists plotted the pressure of several dilute gases (in rigid containers) against temperature and found straight lines that all aim toward zero pressure at the same temperature, $$-273.15^\circ\mathrm{C},$$ named __absolute zero__.

Using a constant $$c$$ for the (gas-dependent) slope, write an equation for the gas pressure $$P$$ versus temperature $$T$$ in Celsius that correctly gives $$P=0$$ at absolute zero.

__(c)__ Formulas in the theory of heat kept containing the combination $$\left(T+273.15^\circ\mathrm{C}\right).$$ Scientists fixed this by inventing the __Kelvin__ scale: the same degree size as Celsius, but with its zero placed at absolute zero. Write the conversion from Celsius to Kelvin, and state the Kelvin temperature of $$0^\circ\mathrm{C}.$$

__(d)__ The __Rankine__ scale ($$^\circ\mathrm{R}$$) also places zero at absolute zero, but uses Fahrenheit-sized degrees, with conversion factor $$1=\dfrac{9^\circ\mathrm{R}}{5\;\mathrm{K}}.$$ Convert a body temperature of $$98.6^\circ\mathrm{F}$$ to Rankine. (Plan: Fahrenheit and Rankine, like Celsius and Kelvin, differ only by a constant offset, so find absolute zero in Fahrenheit, then add.)

label: I2P03
name: One of the most important parts of learning is asking questions. Questions are an…
desc: One of the most important parts of learning is asking questions. Questions are an important mode of communication between students and instructors, and from student to student. You can ask questions during class, on the message boards, and when chatting with other students in…
statement:
One of the most important parts of learning is asking questions. Questions are an important mode of communication between students and instructors, and from student to student.

You can ask questions during class, on the message boards, and when chatting with other students in the classroom outside class hours. When you ask them a question, everyone benefits: other students may have had the same question, and instructors learn more about what students are working on.

Below is the AoPS advice on how to ask a good question:

Most often, we ask others questions to get answers. But at AoPS, we won't just tell you what the next step is or what you need to do in order to get a perfect score. Instead, we'll help you understand the material and ask questions that help you develop your own critical thinking skills. This will allow you to solve the problem on your own.

Some students may find this frustrating because the homework is due that day, and they just want to be told what to do. Please understand that you will not learn as much this way, and we will not just give you the answer or solution.

**Moderate Level Question-Asking: Be Specific**

Statements like "Please help" or "I'm stuck" are very hard to answer. After all, there aren't any details there! These statements will generally get a response of "What do you need help with?" or "What are you stuck on?" or "What don't you understand?"

In order to get help, think carefully about what you're are stuck on and try to tell us about it in your question. Some examples are: "I don't understand what the question means when it says ____." "Can someone explain how (some property) applies to this problem?"

**Expert Level Question-Asking: Providing Background**

In addition to asking specific questions, great questions include some background. If we know about what you have already tried or how you're thinking about the problem, it will help us give better, more relevant tips. Expert-level questions look like this:

"I tried (some approach), but now I'm stuck. Can someone give me a hint?" "It seems like we can use (some property) on this problem. I can tell how it applies ____ but I'm stuck on how it works with ____. Any tips?"

Knowing what you are having trouble with is an important skill to develop. To help us assist you in the best way, try to figure out specifically what is stopping you from moving forward. Try to make your question as specific as possible. We are here to help you, but we need some information to directly respond to your inquiry.

**Getting Started**

Regarding homework questions, AoPS has a general policy that students should get the discussion started. If you tell us you have no idea how to start, we will prompt you to come up with an idea to get the ball rolling. It doesn't even have to be a good idea, but looking at a problem and coming up with ideas is an important problem-solving skill that we want you to practice. After you get in the habit of coming up with ideas, then you can sort out the good ones. __source__

Select **three** statements that agree with the handbook's viewpoint on asking questions, as applied to a physics class.

Whoever answers the question should tell you the answer to a problem you're trying to solve.

Asking questions can be part of the process of solving a problem.

'"How do I get started on this problem?" is an expert level question

Questions should communicate what specific part of a problem you are stuck on.

It's often helpful to start your question about a problem by saying what laws of physics you think are relevant.

If you're stuck, it's the instructor's responsibility to tell you the first step on a problem to get you going.

name: In the prereading, we saw that good mathematical notation can make it easier to…
desc: In the prereading, we saw that good mathematical notation can make it easier to communicate ideas via equations. Throughout the course, we will continue to learn new notation to represent ideas we are studying. This new notation can be helpful in communicating with equations…
statement:
In the prereading, we saw that good mathematical notation can make it easier to communicate ideas via equations.

Throughout the course, we will continue to learn new notation to represent ideas we are studying. This new notation can be helpful in communicating with equations, but only if we are able to read and understand the notation fluently. The goal of this problem is to practice interpreting new notation.

Below are several bits of notation which you may or may not be familiar with. There are also definitions for each bit of the notation.

In each example, we add some extra decoration to a variable or set the variable equal to something. We've chosen to use $$q$$ as the variable, but we could modify any other variable in the same way that we modify $$q,$$ and it's this modification you are learning about.

For example, the first bit of notation is $$\bar{q},$$ which means the average of multiple measurements of $$q.$$ Later in the class we might study $$\bar{x},$$ the average of multiple measurements of $$x,$$ or $$\bar{T},$$ the average of multiple measurements of $$T,$$ etc.

Match the notation on the left with the equivalent notation on the right.

\begin{tabular}{c | l} Notation & Meaning \\ \hline $$\bar{q}$$ & the average of several measurements of $$q$$\\ $$q(a+b)$$ & $$q$$ multiplied to the quantity $$a+b$$\\ $$\Delta q$$ & the amount that $$q$$ has changed since its initial value of $$q_0$$ \\ $$q = (a,b)$$ & $$q$$ is a point on a graph with horizontal coordinate $$a$$ and vertical coordinate $$b$$ \\ $$q = a \pm b $$ & $$q$$ is likely between $$a-b$$ and $$a+b$$ \\ $$b \cdot q^a$$ & $$b$$ multiplied by the quantity ($$q$$ multiplied to itself $$a$$ times) \end{tabular}

Column 1

$$\bar{q}$$

$$q(a+b)$$

$$\Delta q$$

$$q = (a,b)$$

$$q = a \pm b$$

$$b \cdot q^a$$

Column 2

$$q\cdot a + q \cdot b$$

$$\dfrac{q_{{}_{{}_1}} + q_{{}_{{}_2}} + \ldots + q_{{}_n}}{n}$$

$$q_{{}_x} = a \text{ and } q_{{}_y} = b$$

$$b \cdot \underbrace{q \cdot q \cdot \ldots \cdot q}_{a \text{ times}}$$

$$\text{it is likely that } \quad a-b < q < a+b$$

$$q - q_{{}_{{}_\tiny{0}}}$$

desc: Part A. Once you have decided __what__ to write (e.g. which details to include in your experimental procedure), you still need to decide __how__ to write it - what words to use, how long your sentences should be, etc. The choices you make about how to write are your __writing…
statement:
Part A. Once you have decided __what__ to write (e.g. which details to include in your experimental procedure), you still need to decide __how__ to write it - what words to use, how long your sentences should be, etc. The choices you make about how to write are your __writing style__.

There is no one writing style that is best for physics communication. However, some scientific organizations have put together style guidelines. We cannot review all these guidelines, so we will practice one particular guideline, taken from the style manual of the American Institute of Physics (AIP). The goal is to practice the skill of reading and understanding style advice.

The period $$T$$ is independent...

The force $$k \Delta x$$ from the spring will be...

But add commas or parentheses if another phrase intervenes:

The period of a pendulum, $$T,$$ is independent...

The force we just found, $$k \Delta x,$$ will be...

In the first example, $$T$$ is a period, so there is no comma when $$T$$ comes directly after "period", but there is a comma when $$T$$ comes after "pendulum". Although $$T$$ is related to a pendulum, $$T$$ isn't a pendulum, so "pendulum" is not the noun that defines $$T.$$

In the second example, the noun that defines $$k\Delta x$$ is "force".

Which of the following snippets of writing does **not** obey this style guideline about commas? Choose one.

The Bohr radius $$a_0$$ is a physical constant...

We should find the volume $$V_H$$ per hydrogen atom...

The ratio of proton mass to electron mass $$\dfrac{m_p}{m_e}$$ is dimensionless.

If you vary the length $$\ell$$ of the pendulum...

The gravitational acceleration on Earth, $$g,$$ is approximately...

Part B. Here is another writing style guideline:

“Bees disperse pollen” is a sentence about bees; “Pollen is dispersed by bees” is a sentence about pollen. If what follows the first sentence is about pollen, or if what follows the second is about bees, readers are certain to be confused. The above quote has been edited, simplifying it for this course, and may not be a complete representation of the authors' intention.

Guidelines like these are not set rules; good writing will sometimes break them. For example, this "topic position" guideline is most useful in the first sentence of a paragraph. The remaining sentences may break it in order to provide some variation in sentence structure, for example.

It is still a useful skill to determine whether or not a piece of writing follows a given guideline. You'll need to understand what a guideline is saying before you can develop a nuanced view on when to break it.

In the following two paragraphs, most sentences obey the guideline, but one does not. To determine which sentence does not obey the guideline, first decide what each paragraph is primarily about. Then, for each sentence, decide whether the topic of the paragraph the sentence is in appears right near the beginning of the sentence.

Select the sentence that does not obey the guideline.

**(a)** People sometimes think the little beads on the outside of a glass of ice water have seeped through the glass, but that's wrong. **(b)** Little beads will form on a cold glass in a warm, wet room, even if the glass is empty. **(c)** The little beads of water are an example of condensation.

**(d)** Water molecules in the air coalesce into little beads of liquid water on a glass. **(e)** When water molecules in the air hit the cold glass, they tend to lose energy until they don't have enough energy to fly off into the air any more. **(f)** Instead, the water molecules stick to the glass, forming the little beads of water you see there.

name: We have thought of writing as a way for one person to take ideas they already understand…
desc: We have thought of writing as a way for one person to take ideas they already understand and communicate those ideas to someone else. Physicist N. David Mermin suggested a different role for writing when he said I'm convinced that you don't understand the real significance of…
statement:
We have thought of writing as a way for one person to take ideas they already understand and communicate those ideas to someone else.

Physicist N. David Mermin suggested a different role for writing when he said I'm convinced that you don't understand the real significance of the research you've been struggling with for the past year, until you begin to write about it.

In computer programming, there is a similar idea called __rubber ducking__. It holds that when you are stuck on a hard problem, you should explain the problem out loud to a rubber duck. As you explain the problem, even if you simply explain why you are stuck and don't know the answer, you may suddenly solve the problem, or at least see a way to make progress on it.

Have you ever found that you understand a physics or math problem better after writing about it on the course message boards, or after talking about it to someone either live or online? If so, what was your experience? Why do you think that explaining a problem you're working on helps you to solve the problem?

Have you ever found that, after you begin writing about a lab or experiment you conducted, you start to understand the purpose or big picture of the experiment better than you did before you began writing? Why do you think that would happen, considering that you had already completed the research and analysis?

This is a discussion problem, so please share your thoughts on the message board, take a look at what your classmates have to say, and respond to them. You don't need to answer every part of this to make a post. Feel free to answer one sub-question or post a related idea.
