desc: During a previous lesson, we used dimensional analysis to determine the period of a pendulum. We found $$T = c\sqrt{\dfrac{\ell}{g}},$$ where $$T$$ is the period of the pendulum, $$\ell$$ is the length of the pendulum, $$g$$ is Earth's gravitational acceleration, and $$c$$ is an…
statement:
During a previous lesson, we used dimensional analysis to determine the period of a pendulum. We found $$T = c\sqrt{\dfrac{\ell}{g}},$$ where $$T$$ is the period of the pendulum, $$\ell$$ is the length of the pendulum, $$g$$ is Earth's gravitational acceleration, and $$c$$ is an unknown constant. We used that model to build two pendulums such that the ratio of their periods was $$2$$.

In this discussion problem, you will design your own experiment with the pendulum, write the methods in an initial post, and review two of your peers' methods.

Have you ever tried to follow someone's exact instructions and it didn't turn out the way you wanted? (https://youtu.be/FN2RM-CHkuI)

As you can see from the video, writing exact instructions can be challenging. Peer feedback is exceptionally helpful for improving the clarity of your writing. Here are a few tips: - Write simple, clear instructions with enough details for accurate replication. - Include which equipment you use. Example: "Use a meter stick to measure the length of your pencil." - Do not include extraneous steps like "measure twice, cut once", “collect all lab equipment” or “sharpen your pencil” or “meditate to clear your mind in preparation for accurate data collection”. - Using bullet points or numbered steps is perfectly acceptable.

For your experiment, you can choose to do this either in real life with a homemade pendulum, or use (https://aops-curriculum.github.io/268_Introduction_to_Physics/pendulum_lab.html).

**Instructions**

**$$1$$) Initial Post**

- Pick a (school appropriate) song. - Write out the name and artist. - Write out your methods to get the pendulum to swing to the beat of this song. Be specific enough that a peer could follow your exact instructions and get the same results. - Post methods and your song title/artist on the discussion board.

**$$2$$) Peer response**

- Read at least two other student posts on the discussion board and replicate their experiment using their exact methods. - Post your results. Were you able to get the pendulum to swing to the beat of the song? - Provide feedback for the methods you followed. Specifically note if any parts of the instructions were confusing.

**Peer Response Tips**

Reviewing another person's work is a valuable way to learn. Providing quality feedback is also a useful skill to master. Here are some tips to help you provide the most helpful, accurate, and consistent feedback possible: - Remember, English isn't everyone's native language. Focus primarily on how well you were able to follow their exact instructions. - When writing critical feedback, use a constructive and polite tone. - Don't forget to write what you liked about their post.

label: I2P03
name: Two Ways to Describe a Diving Eyedropper — The animation below shows someone squeezing a sealed plastic…
desc: The animation below shows someone squeezing a sealed plastic bottle full of water. Inside the bottle floats an eyedropper. When the hand grips the bottle, the eyedropper sinks to the bottom; when the hand lets go, the eyedropper rises and floats again. This phenomenon is called…
statement:
The animation below shows someone squeezing a sealed plastic bottle full of water. Inside the bottle floats an eyedropper. When the hand grips the bottle, the eyedropper sinks to the bottom; when the hand lets go, the eyedropper rises and floats again. This phenomenon is called the __Cartesian diver__.

Here are two different written summaries of what happens in the animation.

__Ms. Y:__ "The eyedropper initially floats with a small fraction above the water. Within a second of when the hand grips the bottle, the eyedropper sinks straight down to the bottom at a roughly constant speed, then hits the bottom and stops. Then, within a second of the hand releasing the bottle, the eyedropper rises at a slightly slower speed to the top and floats again with about the same fraction above the water as before."

__Zak:__ "A hand grips the bottle, which pushes on the water inside, causing the eyedropper to sink. This requires a firm grip to provide sufficient force to overcome the eyedropper's buoyancy. When the hand releases the bottle, the force pushing the eyedropper down is removed and the eyedropper's buoyancy again takes over, causing the eyedropper to rise."

__(a)__ List at least two differences between Ms. Y's description and Zak's. Which one tries to explain __why__ the eyedropper sinks?

__(b)__ Suppose you have just seen the Cartesian diver for the first time, you do not yet know how it works, and you are writing the opening observations of a lab report about it. Whose style is more appropriate, and why?

__(c)__ Describe a situation where Zak's style of communication would work __better__ than Ms. Y's.

__(d)__ The common English name for this phenomenon is "the Cartesian diver" (named after Rene Descartes, though the first person to write about it was probably Raffaelo Maggiotti, a student of Galileo, in 1648). In terms of effective communication, what is an advantage of using the common name instead of inventing your own name, even if you could invent a clearer one?

__(e)__ A lab report about the diver begins with a paragraph of careful observations, followed by this second paragraph: "We were surprised that squeezing a bottle can lead to an eyedropper sinking. Usually when things sink in water, they don't come back up, but the eyedropper did. That makes the Cartesian diver interesting, and we suspect we can learn more about the physics of floating and sinking by studying it. We decided to do an experiment to learn more about how the Cartesian diver works." The second paragraph contains no observations. In broad terms, what does it communicate to the reader?

label: I2P03
name: Exploring the Cartesian Diver — A __Cartesian diver__ is built as follows: fill a flexible two-liter soda…
desc: A __Cartesian diver__ is built as follows: fill a flexible two-liter soda bottle most of the way with ordinary tap water; add some water to an ordinary eyedropper so that it just barely floats (only a small fraction above the surface); place the eyedropper in the bottle, fill…
statement:
A __Cartesian diver__ is built as follows: fill a flexible two-liter soda bottle most of the way with ordinary tap water; add some water to an ordinary eyedropper so that it just barely floats (only a small fraction above the surface); place the eyedropper in the bottle, fill the bottle to the very top with water, and screw the cap on tightly. There are no hidden wires, magnets, or other tricks. When you squeeze the sides of the bottle, the eyedropper sinks; when you let go, it rises and floats again.

__(a)__ __Exploratory research__ means playing with the apparatus and making observations before designing a formal experiment. Here are two write-ups of why exploratory research is valuable. Ms. Y: "Exploratory research is valuable because it lets us generate hypotheses. It makes us more familiar with the equipment we have. If we do some exploratory research first, we will be better able to design a valid and successful experiment." Zak: "If we begin by playing around with the diver, we'll naturally make observations that build our familiarity with the equipment and the phenomena. That familiarity may give us ideas for how the diver works or tests we can perform on it. We can turn those ideas into hypotheses and confirmatory experiments to test the hypotheses." Both write-ups contain essentially the same ideas. In which one do the ideas connect and flow more smoothly from one to the next, and why does that kind of writing make a lab report easier to read?

__(b)__ The animation below is a close-up, slow-motion view of the eyedropper as the bottle is squeezed. Describe, as an objective observation, what happens to the pocket of air inside the eyedropper just before the eyedropper starts to fall.

__(c)__ Here are three more observations from exploratory research. (1) If the cap is left off, squeezing makes water squirt out of the top and the eyedropper never sinks. (2) A sealed ketchup packet, which also contains a bit of air, works as a diver in place of the eyedropper, as the animation below shows. (3) A rigid, sealed metal case that floats because it has air inside does __not__ work as a diver. Based on these observations, what features of the setup appear to be essential for a Cartesian diver to work?

__(d)__ The construction of the diver was communicated above partly with a photograph, and short animated clips (gifs) were used to show the close-up squeeze and the ketchup-packet diver. Why can images, diagrams, and movies make scientific communication more effective than words alone? Do professional scientists ever include movies with their papers?

label: I2P03
name: Reading a Prediction Chart — After exploring the Cartesian diver (a sealed bottle of water in which a…
desc: After exploring the Cartesian diver (a sealed bottle of water in which a barely-floating eyedropper sinks when the bottle is squeezed), a class generated four hypotheses for how it works. __The Air Hypothesis:__ Air makes things float. When you squeeze the bottle, the air pocket…
statement:
After exploring the Cartesian diver (a sealed bottle of water in which a barely-floating eyedropper sinks when the bottle is squeezed), a class generated four hypotheses for how it works.

__The Air Hypothesis:__ Air makes things float. When you squeeze the bottle, the air pocket in the diver gets smaller. That air pocket isn't big enough to hold the diver up any more, so the diver sinks.

__The Current Hypothesis:__ When you squeeze the bottle, you start the water flowing, which is called a __current__. The flowing current pushes the diver down.

__The Force Transmission Hypothesis:__ When you squeeze the bottle, you put a force on the water. The water has nowhere to go, so the force is transmitted to the diver and pushes it down.

__The Density Hypothesis:__ Objects can only float if their density is less than the density of whatever liquid they're in. When we squeeze the bottle, we force more water into the dropper. This increases the mass of the dropper without increasing its volume, so the density of the entire diver goes up. Once the density increases beyond the density of water, the diver sinks.

To organize the relationships between several hypotheses and several possible experiments, scientists can use a __prediction chart__: each row is a hypothesis, each column is an experiment, and each entry is the result that hypothesis predicts for that experiment. Below is an example prediction chart for three hypotheses $$a,$$ $$b,$$ $$c$$ and four proposed experiments $$E1$$ through $$E4,$$ where $$A,$$ $$B,$$ $$C$$ stand for possible experimental results. For example, the first row says: according to Hypothesis $$a,$$ experiment $$E1$$ will give result $$A,$$ experiments $$E2$$ and $$E3$$ will both give result $$B,$$ and experiment $$E4$$ will give result $$C.$$

__(a)__ Of the four experiments in the chart, which one is the __least__ helpful for gathering evidence in favor of one of the three hypotheses? Explain.

__(b)__ Which experiment would help us gather evidence to choose between Hypothesis $$b$$ and Hypothesis $$c?$$

__(c)__ Suppose you only have time for one experiment, as is often the case. Why is it important to write down your hypotheses __before__ designing a confirmatory experiment, rather than just doing whatever experiment comes to mind first?

label: I2P03
name: Two Ways to Define Density — An important part of communicating in science is giving clear definitions of…
desc: An important part of communicating in science is giving clear definitions of technical terms, so readers know exactly what you mean. Here are two written explanations of the term __density__. __Ms. Y:__ "If something is very dense, it has a lot of mass relative to its size. For…
statement:
An important part of communicating in science is giving clear definitions of technical terms, so readers know exactly what you mean. Here are two written explanations of the term __density__.

__Ms. Y:__ "If something is very dense, it has a lot of mass relative to its size. For example, gold is quite dense and stuffed animals are not. If you have a gold bar that is the same size as a stuffed animal, the gold bar will have a lot more mass. That means gold is dense, but we shouldn't say that gold is 'heavy' or 'massive'. You can have a tiny flake of gold that's much less massive than a stuffed animal just because the gold flake is much smaller. That flake would have the same density as a large bar of gold, but much less mass because its volume is so small. That brings us to the mathematical definition of density: the density of an object is its mass divided by its volume. This way, if we have two objects of the same material and one has twice the volume as the other, it will have twice the mass as well, and the density will be the same. Density is a property of materials, not objects."

__Zak:__ "The density $$\rho$$ of an object is defined by $$\rho=\dfrac{m}{V},$$ where $$m$$ is the mass of the object and $$V$$ its volume. For example, if a ball has mass $$m=145\;\mathrm{g}$$ and volume $$V=201\;\mathrm{cm}^3,$$ its density is $$\dfrac{145\;\mathrm{g}}{201\;\mathrm{cm}^3}=0.72\;\dfrac{\mathrm{g}}{\mathrm{cm}^3}.$$ Density is an intensive quantity, not an extensive one."

__(a)__ Check Zak's arithmetic: compute $$\dfrac{145\;\mathrm{g}}{201\;\mathrm{cm}^3}$$ and confirm his answer. Then compute the density of a block with mass $$540\;\mathrm{g}$$ and volume $$200\;\mathrm{cm}^3.$$ Would that block float or sink in water, whose density is $$1.0\;\dfrac{\mathrm{g}}{\mathrm{cm}^3}?$$ (An object floats only if its density is less than the density of the liquid it is in.)

__(b)__ Whose explanation would be more helpful for a reader who did not previously know what density is? Identify at least one strength and one weakness of each explanation.

__(c)__ Ms. Y writes that "density is a property of materials, not objects." Using her gold flake and gold bar example, explain what she means.

label: I2P03
name: Testing the Hypotheses with a Lip Balm Diver — A __Cartesian diver__ is a sealed, flexible bottle filled with…
desc: A __Cartesian diver__ is a sealed, flexible bottle filled with water, containing an eyedropper that just barely floats. Squeeze the bottle and the eyedropper sinks; release it and the eyedropper rises. A close-up view shows that when the bottle is squeezed, water is pushed up…
statement:
A __Cartesian diver__ is a sealed, flexible bottle filled with water, containing an eyedropper that just barely floats. Squeeze the bottle and the eyedropper sinks; release it and the eyedropper rises. A close-up view shows that when the bottle is squeezed, water is pushed up into the eyedropper and the pocket of air inside the eyedropper shrinks; then the eyedropper falls. Two hypotheses for why the diver sinks:

__The Force Transmission Hypothesis:__ When you squeeze the bottle, you put a force on the water. The water has nowhere to go, so the force is transmitted to the diver and pushes it down. (Some people picture the force traveling from the hand, through the water, to the diver, as in the figure below.)

__The Density Hypothesis:__ Objects can only float if their density is less than the density of whatever liquid they're in. When we squeeze the bottle, we force more water into the dropper, raising the density of the diver. Once the density exceeds the density of water, the diver sinks. (We consider the eyedropper plus everything inside it the "object" whose density we are finding.)

__(a)__ According to the density hypothesis, the diver's density $$\rho=\dfrac{m}{V}$$ increases when the bottle is squeezed. Is it the diver's mass or its volume that changes? Consider two reasonable definitions of "the diver": (i) the eyedropper plus everything inside it, including the water that has entered; (ii) the eyedropper plus its air pocket, but not any water inside. Show that the density increases under either definition.

__(b)__ One observation — the shrinking of the air pocket when the bottle is squeezed — is essential to one of these hypotheses but unimportant to the other. Which hypothesis needs it, and why doesn't the other one care?

__(c)__ To tell the hypotheses apart, a second "diver" is added to the bottle: a sealed tube of lip balm, chosen because it just barely floats, like the eyedropper, but is solid and sealed — water cannot get inside it and compress the air within. The photo below shows the bottle with both divers. What does the density hypothesis predict will happen to each diver when the bottle is squeezed? What does the force transmission hypothesis predict?

__(d)__ The experiment is run, with the result shown below: when the bottle is squeezed, the eyedropper sinks but the lip balm keeps floating. Which hypothesis does this result support?

__(e)__ A lab report must include a written __procedure__ — a description of what was done. A good rule for deciding which details to include is: "If a friend were going to replicate this experiment, would they need to know about this?" Apply the rule to two candidate details: (i) the lip balm tube was sealed, never opened; (ii) the temperature of the room when the diver was built. Which belongs in the procedure?

__(f)__ Write one or two sentences explaining why this experiment is __evidence__ for the density hypothesis over the force transmission hypothesis, but does not __prove__ the density hypothesis is the full story.

label: I2P03
name: A Trick Bottle with Two Shapes — In a standard __Cartesian diver__ — a sealed, flexible bottle of liquid…
desc: In a standard __Cartesian diver__ — a sealed, flexible bottle of liquid containing an object that just barely floats — the diver sinks while the bottle is squeezed and rises as soon as the bottle is released. The leading explanation is the __density hypothesis__: squeezing the…
statement:
In a standard __Cartesian diver__ — a sealed, flexible bottle of liquid containing an object that just barely floats — the diver sinks while the bottle is squeezed and rises as soon as the bottle is released. The leading explanation is the __density hypothesis__: squeezing the bottle raises the pressure inside, forcing liquid into the diver and compressing its air pocket; this raises the diver's density $$\rho=\dfrac{m}{V}$$ above the liquid's density, so it sinks, and releasing the bottle reverses everything.

Now watch the diver in the animation below. The hand squeezes; the diver sinks. The hand lets go — and the diver __stays at the bottom__. Only when the hand squeezes a second time does the diver rise back to the top.

Close observation reveals two clues. First, the two squeezes are different: the first squeeze presses the front and back of the bottle, while the second presses the left and right sides, as shown below. Second, the bottle's shape is asymmetric: one side curves inward while the other bulges outward, and the bulge flips when the bottle is squeezed.

__(a)__ Is the diver's behavior — staying down after the hand releases — what the density hypothesis leads us to expect from an ordinary diver? Explain.

__(b)__ Which component of the apparatus do the two clues point to as the source of the unusual behavior: the liquid, the diver itself, the air, or the bottle?

__(c)__ In fact, this bottle has two different stable shapes ("configurations"). It starts in configuration 1; a squeeze flips it to configuration 2; another squeeze flips it back. The diver floats in configuration 1 and sinks in configuration 2. According to the density hypothesis, in which configuration does the bottle hold the larger volume? Explain your reasoning.

__(d)__ The liquid in this bottle is visibly colored — it is not plain water. According to the density hypothesis, does the diver need water in particular to work? What property must the liquid and the floating object have for the trick to work?

name: For digital devices, unless there's a good reason to believe otherwise, we can take the…
desc: For digital devices, unless there's a good reason to believe otherwise, we can take the uncertainty to be half the smallest increment on the device. We can do the same with analog devices. These measurement devices usually have markings on them to indicate different…
statement:
For digital devices, unless there's a good reason to believe otherwise, we can take the uncertainty to be half the smallest increment on the device. We can do the same with analog devices. These measurement devices usually have markings on them to indicate different measurements. Half the increment between markings is a good estimate for the uncertainty.

With that rule in mind, what's the uncertainty $$\sigma$$ when measuring distance with a ruler marked in metric, like the one shown below? The printed numbers indicate centimeters.

mathjax: $$ \sigma = \blank \;\mathrm{mm}$$

label: I2P04
name: We've explored uncertainty in measuring devices. The goal of this problem is to get you…
desc: We've explored uncertainty in measuring devices. The goal of this problem is to get you thinking about uncertainty that may come in due to sources aside from simply the limitations of your measuring device. ---------------------------- There are devices called "micrometers" that…
statement:
We've explored uncertainty in measuring devices. The goal of this problem is to get you thinking about uncertainty that may come in due to sources aside from simply the limitations of your measuring device.

----------------------------

There are devices called "micrometers" that can make much more precise distance measurements than rulers. Micrometers usually have a screw which you can turn to move some metal pieces called "calipers" tiny distances at a time. Eddington and Dyson, the astronomers mentioned in the prereading, used micrometers to measure the positions of stars in their photographs. You saw an older micrometer there. Modern micrometer calipers look like this: By Lucasbosch - Own work, CC BY-SA 3.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=21199504

You have a micrometer that can measure distances down to $$0.001 \;\mathrm{mm},$$ which by our formulation leads to an uncertainty of $$0.0005 \;\mathrm{mm} = 0.5 \mu\mathrm{m}.$$ (The symbol $$\mu \mathrm{m}$$ stands for "micron" or "micrometer". $$1 \mu \mathrm{m} = 0.001 \;\mathrm{mm} = 10^{-6} \;\mathrm{m}.)$$ You are told to use the micrometer to "find how thick normal pennies are." You are given a penny to measure and you decide to use your micrometer to measure its thickness, then report how thick you think normal pennies are.

Choose **two** of the following statements which accurately describe the uncertainty in your report on how thick normal pennies are.

Your uncertainty will be $$0.5 \;\mu\mathrm{m}.$$

Your uncertainty will be larger than $$0.5 \;\mu\mathrm{m}$$ because pennies have different thicknesses at different points.

Your uncertainty will be larger than $$0.5 \;\mu\mathrm{m}$$ because you don't know that your penny is a normal one.

Your uncertainty can be less than $$0.5 \;\mu\mathrm{m}$$ because you can measure the penny many times and take the average.

name: Scientists frequently have to learn new notation for concepts they already know in some…
desc: Scientists frequently have to learn new notation for concepts they already know in some other notation. In this problem, you will first learn a new notation for writing uncertainty, then practice with it. --------------------- We've discussed writing uncertainties using the…
statement:
Scientists frequently have to learn new notation for concepts they already know in some other notation. In this problem, you will first learn a new notation for writing uncertainty, then practice with it.

---------------------

We've discussed writing uncertainties using the $$\pm$$ symbol. In this notation, $$x = 2.2 \pm 0.3 \;\mathrm{m},$$ means the absolute uncertainty in $$x$$ is $$0.3 \;\mathrm{m}.$$

Another way scientists report uncertainties is with a notation that looks like this: $$G = 6.67430(15) \times 10^{-11} \;\mathrm{m^3 \, kg \, s^{-2}}.$$

This is an equation for the __gravitational constant__, a number that's important to both Newton's and Einstein's theories of gravity.

The uncertainty in the last two digits of $$G$$ is represented by the parentheses. In other words, the gravitational constant is approximately $$G \approx 6.67430 \times 10^{-11} \;\mathrm{m^3 \, kg \, s^{-2}},$$ but the last two digits might not be $$30.$$ They are uncertain by $$15,$$ so the last two digits could be anywhere from $$15$$ to $$45$$ and $$G$$ is probably in the range $$6.67415 \times 10^{-11} \;\mathrm{m^3 \, kg \, s^{-2}} < G < 6.67445 \times 10^{-11} \;\mathrm{m^3 \, kg \, s^{-2}}$$

The same equation written in $$\pm$$ notation is $$G = \left(6.67430 \pm 0.00015 \right) \times 10^{-11} \;\mathrm{m^3 \, kg \, s^{-2}}.$$

The absolute uncertainty in $$G$$ is $$\begin{aligned} \sigma_G &= 0.00015 \times 10^{-11} \;\mathrm{m^3 \, kg \, s^{-2}} \\[6pt] &= 1.5 \times 10^{-15} \;\mathrm{m^3 \, kg \, s^{-2}} \end{aligned}$$

----------------

Now we can do a practice problem with this new notation.

According to a group of scientists who worked on the space telescope __Planck__, the age of the universe is $$t_0 = 13.813(38) \times 10^9 \;\mathrm{years}.$$

What is the absolute uncertainty in the age of the universe, in years, according to these scientists?

mathjax: $$ \sigma_{t_0} = \blank \times 10^{\blank} \;\mathrm{years}$$

label: I2P04
name: Error (also called "uncertainty") can be __random__ or __systematic__.
desc: Error (also called "uncertainty") can be __random__ or __systematic__. Random error is error that's different every measurement you make. For example, when weighing items on a scale, you might place them randomly in slightly different positions on the tray, and this could affect…
statement:
Error (also called "uncertainty") can be __random__ or __systematic__.

Random error is error that's different every measurement you make. For example, when weighing items on a scale, you might place them randomly in slightly different positions on the tray, and this could affect the reading.

Systematic error affects every measurement you make in essentially the same way. For example, over time, the spring in a scale might get looser than it originally was. The scale compresses more than it should, resulting in all measurements being too large by about the same percentage. That would be systematic error.

Each of the following describes either random or systematic error. Choose the **one** that is random error.

**a)** In the cold weather, your ruler contracted a bit, and all your length measurements are now too long.

**b)** You can measure the volume of water with a __graduated cylinder__. The surface of the water will not be flat. Instead, it will climb slightly up the sides of the graduated cylinder by the same amount each measurement. To measure the volume, you are supposed to look at the lowest point in the center of the surface, called the __meniscus__, but instead you look at the highest point at the side each time. __image credit: Julie Mallon, https://terpconnect.umd.edu/~jmmallon/Inquiry1.pdf__

**c)** You are conducting an experiment in radioactivity and counting how many radioactive events occur using a device called a Geiger counter. Because radiation is an unpredictable process, sometimes your count is a little higher and sometimes a little lower.

**d)** Your scale has a "tare" button to make sure that zero mass reads out as zero, but you forget to use it. As a result, what the scale should read out as $$0 \;\mathrm{g}$$ it actually reads out as $$-3 \;\mathrm{g},$$ and all your mass measurements are too small by $$3 \;\mathrm{g}.$$

**e)** As you use an oscilloscope to measure electrical voltage, the oscilloscope heats up. This changes its electrical properties, and all your readings are off by a similar amount.

**f)** You're measuring the timing of some events using a video, but you have uncertainty about the frame rate (how many frames per second the video camera took). The camera's frame rate is perfectly steady, but you don't know exactly what that rate is.

(a)

(b)

(c)

(d)

(e)

(f)

statement:
Part A. Some scientists conduct an experiment on the __photoelectric effect__. We mentioned this effect in lesson 1, where we discussed how Albert Einstein made a prediction of the effect and Robert Millikan wound up experimentally confirming Einstein's prediction after a long effort to prove it wrong.

To collect their data, scientists change the __frequency__ of light shining on a metal sheet. They measure the __stopping voltage__ needed to prevent electrons from jumping from the metal sheet to another piece of metal nearby while the light is shining.

The scientists conduct an uncertainty analysis, then plot their data along with error bars representing random error. The scientists also include a straight line representing the predictions of Einstein's theory. Their results are shown below: Which of the following is likely true of the scientists' experiment?

The scientists overestimated their uncertainty.

The scientists underestimated their uncertainty.

The scientists' uncertainty estimates are not a clear underestimate or overestimate.

Part B. Here we continue the analysis of data on the photoelectric effect. The error bars show __absolute error__. This is error expressed in the same units as the measurement itself. This is the type of error we discussed in most of the class session.

Scientists sometimes divide their absolute error by their measurement, getting the __relative error__. For example, in a measurement of $$22.3 \pm 2.0,$$ the absolute error is $$2.0,$$ and the relative error is $$\dfrac{2.0}{22.3} \approx 0.09.$$

Which of the following is true of the scientists' experiment?

name: Scientists can describe good measurements as both __accurate__ and __precise__, but these…
desc: Scientists can describe good measurements as both __accurate__ and __precise__, but these mean different things. (The noun forms are __accuracy__ and __precision__.) In this problem, you will review the difference between accuracy and precision, then decide whether various…
statement:
Scientists can describe good measurements as both __accurate__ and __precise__, but these mean different things. (The noun forms are __accuracy__ and __precision__.) In this problem, you will review the difference between accuracy and precision, then decide whether various measurement procedures have high or low accuracy and high or low precision.

A measurement procedure has high precision when there is very little random error. This means that many repeated independent measurements will return very nearly the same every time. However, that result could still be wrong and be considered "precise". As long as all the results are very similar, the measurement is precise, regardless of how much systematic error there is.

A measurement has high accuracy when there is very little systematic error. This means that a large number of independent measurements is correct on average, with not overall bias to be too high or too low due to systematic error. However, a measurement can have high random error, causing lots of spread in the data, and still be considered accurate as long as the measurements are very close to the best possible value on average.

There are two competing definitions of accuracy. The one we will use in this class is that accuracy refers to how much systematic error there is and ignores random error, as we described above. However, the International Organization for Standardization (ISO) defines "accuracy" as accounting for both random and systematic error. By their definition, a measurement process with high random error and low systematic error would not be accurate, but by our definition it would be.

Below are several histograms. Each summarizes the results from 1000 independent measurements made with the same measurement procedure. There are seven histograms, each representing a different measurement procedure.

All the measurement procedures are measuring the same dimensionless quantity. An eighth measuring procedure is known to be extremely accurate and extremely precise (but perhaps too expensive to use frequently) made the same measurement, coming up with a value of $$5.00.$$

For each histogram, decide whether the measuring procedure associated with it is high or low accuracy and whether it is high or low precision.

For the purposes of this problem, we categorize precision as "high" if the standard deviation of the measurements is below .75 and "low" otherwise. We categorize accuracy as "high" if systematic error is below 1 and "low" otherwise. However, you should not need to perform any calculations; a rough understanding based on the shapes of the histograms should be sufficient.

label: I2P04
name: In this problem, we'll practice the difference between __absolute error__, which we'll…
desc: In this problem, we'll practice the difference between __absolute error__, which we'll call $$\sigma,$$ and __relative error__, which we'll call $$\eta.$$ We'll also see some handy unit conversions that you might use later on. (But you don't need to memorize the unit…
statement:
In this problem, we'll practice the difference between __absolute error__, which we'll call $$\sigma,$$ and __relative error__, which we'll call $$\eta.$$ We'll also see some handy unit conversions that you might use later on. (But you don't need to memorize the unit conversions.)

----------

Many units are defined in terms of one another, and the conversion factors sometimes involve a large number of digits. For example, in class we saw that one pound mass in the Avoirdupois system is defined as $$ 1\;\mathrm{lb} = 0.45359237 \;\mathrm{kg}.$$

Unlike a measurement reported with significant figures and uncertainty, this conversion is exact by definition.

Physical constants also sometimes have exact values as a byproduct of how units are defined. For example, the speed of light is exactly $$ c = 299{,}792{,}458 \;\mathrm{m/s}.$$

The precise speed of light and pound-kilogram conversion factors may be difficult to remember because they have so many digits. Many people instead remember approximate values, such as $$2.2 \;\mathrm{lb} \approx 1 \;\mathrm{kg}$$ or $$c \approx 3 \times 10^8 \;\mathrm{m/s}.$$ Using these approximate values in a calculation will introduce some systematic error, but may be okay if the relative uncertainty in other parts of the calculation is already significantly larger than the relative error introduced by using an approximate unit conversion or physical constant.

Below is a table listing some exact physical constant and unit conversions. Below that are some approximate versions which are draggable. Order the approximate versions from greatest to least relative error.

In some cases, you may have to combine two exact conversions in order to evaluate how much relative error this is in one of the approximate conversions.

Remember that the relative error in a quantity is the absolute error divided by the quantity itself. For example, the absolute error in the speed of light approximation is $$\begin{aligned} \sigma &= 300{,}000{,}000 \;\mathrm{m/s} - 299{,}792{,}458 \;\mathrm{m/s} \\[6pt] &= 207{,}542 \;\mathrm{m/s} \end{aligned}$$

This may seem like a lot of error because $$207{,}542 \;\mathrm{m/s}$$ is a fast speed, but the relative error is $$\begin{aligned} \eta &= \dfrac{207{,}542 \;\mathrm{m/s}}{299{,}792{,}458 \;\mathrm{m/s}} \\[6pt] &\approx 0.00069, \end{aligned}$$ so the relative error is quite small, and $$c \approx 3 \times 10^8 \;\mathrm{m/s}$$ is a good approximation despite the large-seeming absolute error. $$\begin{aligned} {} & \text{\large Conversion or Constant} & \text{\large \,\,\,Exact } & \text{\large \,Equation} \\ \hline {} & \text{pounds to kilograms} \quad\quad\quad & 1 \;\mathrm{lb} & = 0.45359237 \;\mathrm{kg} \\ {} & \text{miles to inches} & 1 \;\mathrm{mile} &= 63{,}360 \;\mathrm{in} \\ {} & \text{inches to centimeters} & 1 \;\mathrm{in} &= 2.54 \;\mathrm{cm} \\ {} & \text{calories to joules} & 1 \;\mathrm{cal} &= 4.184 \;\mathrm{J} \\ {} & \text{speed of light} & c &= 299{,}792{,}458 \;\mathrm{m/s} \\ {} & \text{Planck's constant} & h & = 6.62607015 \times 10^{-34} \;\mathrm{J \cdot s}\\ {} & \text{elementary charge} & e & = 1.602176634 \times 10^{-19} \;\mathrm{C}\\ \end{aligned}$$

draggables

$$1 \;\mathrm{kg}\approx 2.2 \;\mathrm{lb}$$

$$5 \;\mathrm{km} \approx 3.1 \;\mathrm{mile}$$

$$1 \;\mathrm{J} \approx 0.24 \;\mathrm{cal}$$

$$c \approx 3 \times 10^8 \;\mathrm{m/s}$$

$$\dfrac{h}{2\pi} \approx 10^{-34} \;\mathrm{J \cdot s}$$

$$e \approx 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \;\mathrm{C}$$

label: I2P04
name: In this week's writing problem, you'll try two different methods of measuring an area and…
desc: In this week's writing problem, you'll try two different methods of measuring an area and compare them. Cut out a shape from a piece of graph paper. You can cut out any shape you like. Measure its area using the grid on the graph paper itself. You may also use a ruler to help…
statement:
In this week's writing problem, you'll try two different methods of measuring an area and compare them.

Cut out a shape from a piece of graph paper. You can cut out any shape you like.

Measure its area using the grid on the graph paper itself. You may also use a ruler to help you if you like. Briefly explain what you did.

Then, measure the area using a kitchen scale. Briefly explain how you made the measurement.

Part of the challenge of this problem is to figure out how to use a kitchen scale to measure area. If you don't have a kitchen scale, you could borrow one, ask to use a scale from science teacher at school, or come up with another method to measure area, as long as it's independent of the first method you used.

What is your uncertainty in each measurement? Which measurement has greater uncertainty? Explain how you came up with your uncertainties. Before digital methods were common, engineers often measured areas of unusual shapes using a handheld tool called a __planimeter__. (You are welcome to search for and learn how this tool worked, but you don't need to include it in your write up.) Planimeter manufacturers claimed a relative error of about $$0.2\%$$ for their devices. How do your measurements compare to those of a planimeter?

As with the previous writing problem, your writeup should be self-contained so that someone could understand it even without seeing the problem you are responding to.

label: I2P04
name: Galileo's Pendulum Hypothesis — In 1581, a 17-year-old medical student named Galileo Galilei watched a…
desc: In 1581, a 17-year-old medical student named Galileo Galilei watched a chandelier in the cathedral of Pisa swing back and forth — a repeating motion called __oscillation__. Legend says he timed the swings using his own pulse, since pocket watches had only just been invented. A…
statement:
In 1581, a 17-year-old medical student named Galileo Galilei watched a chandelier in the cathedral of Pisa swing back and forth — a repeating motion called __oscillation__. Legend says he timed the swings using his own pulse, since pocket watches had only just been invented. A weight hanging from a cord, free to swing, is called a __pendulum__.

Two quantities describe a swinging pendulum. The pendulum's position at any moment is the angle $$\theta$$ between its cord and vertical. The __amplitude__ $$A$$ is the largest angle $$\theta$$ reaches during the motion, and the __period__ $$T$$ is the time for one full back-and-forth cycle.

__(a)__ Some people expect a pendulum's large swings to take more time than its small swings; others expect the same time, or even less. Give one plausible reason supporting each expectation.

__(b)__ In the animation below, the pendulum swings between the two blue lines, which are separated from each other by an angle of $$18^\circ.$$ What is the amplitude of the oscillation?

__(c)__ The pendulum in the animation completes four full periods — yet it is at its starting position five times, counting the moment of release. When counting oscillations out loud, even careful people often end up with a count that is one too high, a mistake nicknamed __fenceposting__ (a fence with four segments has five posts). Explain why the mistake happens, and give a trick for avoiding it.

__(d)__ Galileo's hypothesis was: __the period of a given pendulum is the same, no matter its amplitude.__ He reasoned that the faster speed of a large swing compensates for the longer distance it covers. Does Galileo's hypothesis imply that all pendulums have the same period? The animation below shows two pendulums of different lengths released together with equal amplitudes — describe what you see, and say whether it is consistent with Galileo's hypothesis.

label: I2P04
name: Timing a Pendulum: Mean, Median, and Outliers — Galileo timed pendulum swings with his pulse — a clock that…
desc: Galileo timed pendulum swings with his pulse — a clock that ticks only about once per second and whose rate can vary. His measurements therefore had a lot of __uncertainty__, also called __error__. You can do better with a stopwatch and a simulated pendulum: open the PhET…
statement:
Galileo timed pendulum swings with his pulse — a clock that ticks only about once per second and whose rate can vary. His measurements therefore had a lot of __uncertainty__, also called __error__. You can do better with a stopwatch and a simulated pendulum: open the PhET Pendulum Lab at https://phet.colorado.edu/sims/html/pendulum-lab/latest/pendulum-lab_en.html, click "Intro", turn on the stopwatch (lower left), leave the controls on the right at their defaults, pull the pendulum back $$5^\circ,$$ release it, and time one full period.

A class of $$30$$ students did exactly this. Every student timed the same simulated pendulum with the same kind of stopwatch, yet their results were all slightly different, spread out between roughly $$1.5\;\mathrm{s}$$ and $$1.8\;\mathrm{s}.$$ To summarize data like this we use __statistics__ — values computed from a data set. Examples: the __range__ (maximum minus minimum), the __mean__ or average (add all the results, divide by how many there are), and the __median__ (a value with half the measurements below it and half above).

__(a)__ Why didn't all the students get the same number?

__(b)__ Suppose one of the $$30$$ students measured $$1.63\;\mathrm{s}$$ but accidentally typed their result in as $$163\;\mathrm{s}.$$ By about how much would this one mistake shift the class mean? Would it shift the median by more, less, or about the same amount?

__(c)__ A wildly wrong data point like that $$163\;\mathrm{s}$$ is called an __outlier__. The class chose to use the mean, and to protect it from outliers they told the computer to ignore any measurement below $$1.45\;\mathrm{s}$$ or above $$1.85\;\mathrm{s}.$$ The result for amplitude $$5^\circ$$ was $$\overline{T}_{5^\circ}\approx 1.63\;\mathrm{s}$$ (the bar over the symbol means "average"). Repeating the whole procedure at amplitude $$10^\circ$$ gave $$\overline{T}_{10^\circ}\approx 1.65\;\mathrm{s}.$$ Galileo hypothesized that a pendulum's period doesn't depend on its amplitude. Do these two numbers confirm his hypothesis? Refute it? Give three genuinely different possible explanations for the $$0.02\;\mathrm{s}$$ difference.

__(d)__ One of those explanations involves __random error__ — chance variation that is different in every measurement. Another involves __systematic error__ — an error that pushes all the measurements in a similar direction. If you repeat an experiment many times and chart the spread in your results, which of these two types of error do you learn about? Why not the other?

label: I2P04
name: Standard Deviation and Plus-Minus Notation — When a measurement is repeated many times, the results spread…
desc: When a measurement is repeated many times, the results spread out. To quantify random uncertainty we use a statistic called the __standard deviation__, written with the Greek letter $$\sigma$$ (sigma). Computing it exactly involves squaring each data point's distance from the…
statement:
When a measurement is repeated many times, the results spread out. To quantify random uncertainty we use a statistic called the __standard deviation__, written with the Greek letter $$\sigma$$ (sigma). Computing it exactly involves squaring each data point's distance from the mean, but for this problem all you need is a visual rule of thumb: __roughly $$70\%$$ of measurements fall within one standard deviation of the mean.__ The histograms below show two simulated data sets; the narrower the histogram, the smaller the standard deviation and the smaller the random uncertainty.

__(a)__ The histogram below shows $$100$$ simulated measurements generated with mean $$5.0\;\mathrm{s}$$ and standard deviation $$1.0\;\mathrm{s}.$$ About how many of the $$100$$ measurements should fall between $$4.0\;\mathrm{s}$$ and $$6.0\;\mathrm{s}?$$

__(b)__ In some data set, the mean is $$100$$ and the standard deviation is $$8.$$ In what interval should about $$70\%$$ of the data fall?

__(c)__ Scientists report a mean and a standard deviation together using $$\pm$$ notation: a mean of $$100$$ with standard deviation $$8$$ is written $$100\pm 8.$$ A class timed one period of a simulated pendulum many times at two amplitudes. At amplitude $$5^\circ$$ the mean was $$1.63\;\mathrm{s}$$ with standard deviation $$0.10\;\mathrm{s};$$ at amplitude $$10^\circ$$ the mean was $$1.65\;\mathrm{s}$$ with standard deviation $$0.08\;\mathrm{s}.$$ Write both results in $$\pm$$ notation.

label: I2P04
name: When Is a Difference Significant? — Two measurements rarely come out exactly equal — the important question…
desc: Two measurements rarely come out exactly equal — the important question is whether their difference means anything. Scientists call a difference between measurements __significant__ when it is large enough that random error alone would be unlikely to cause it. __(a)__ You hold a…
statement:
Two measurements rarely come out exactly equal — the important question is whether their difference means anything. Scientists call a difference between measurements __significant__ when it is large enough that random error alone would be unlikely to cause it.

__(a)__ You hold a heavy bowling ball $$1\;\mathrm{m}$$ above the ground with one hand and use a stopwatch in your other hand to time its fall. Then you repeat the measurement inside a tube with the air pumped out, eliminating air resistance. The two results come out different. Do you expect the difference to be significant? Explain.

__(b)__ Which of these changes would increase the likelihood of finding a significant difference between the with-air and without-air drops? (You may choose more than one.) (i) Drop the ball from higher up. (ii) Use better timing equipment. (iii) Use better equipment for measuring the drop height. (iv) Drop a table-tennis ball instead of a bowling ball.

__(c)__ Two quantities are measured with the same uncertainty: $$a = 1.01\pm 0.20$$ and $$b = 1.07\pm 0.20.$$ The figure below draws each value as a dot with a bar covering one uncertainty on each side. Even though $$1.07>1.01,$$ should we conclude that $$b$$ is really bigger than $$a?$$ Is the difference significant?

__(d)__ Roughly how small would the shared uncertainty $$\sigma$$ have to become before the difference between $$a$$ and $$b$$ starts to be significant?

__(e)__ A class measured a pendulum's period at two amplitudes and found $$\overline{T}_{5^\circ}=(1.63\pm 0.10)\;\mathrm{s}$$ and $$\overline{T}_{10^\circ}=(1.65\pm 0.08)\;\mathrm{s}.$$ Define $$\Delta T=\overline{T}_{10^\circ}-\overline{T}_{5^\circ}.$$ Is $$\Delta T$$ significant? Galileo hypothesized that the two periods are truly equal — does this result prove him right?

label: I2P04
name: Galileo vs. Legendre: Designing a Better Experiment — Galileo hypothesized in 1581 that a pendulum's period…
desc: Galileo hypothesized in 1581 that a pendulum's period $$T$$ does not depend on its amplitude $$A.$$ About $$300$$ years later, the French mathematician Adrien-Marie Legendre published a competing hypothesis: the period grows slightly as the amplitude increases. The growth is…
statement:
Galileo hypothesized in 1581 that a pendulum's period $$T$$ does not depend on its amplitude $$A.$$ About $$300$$ years later, the French mathematician Adrien-Marie Legendre published a competing hypothesis: the period grows slightly as the amplitude increases. The growth is very slow at small amplitudes — if the period is $$1.65\;\mathrm{s}$$ for tiny swings, Legendre's hypothesis predicts only about $$1.651\;\mathrm{s}$$ at $$A=10^\circ.$$

A class tested the hypotheses using the PhET Pendulum Lab simulation at https://phet.colorado.edu/sims/html/pendulum-lab/latest/pendulum-lab_en.html. Each student used the simulation's stopwatch to time one period, and the class combined their results. They found $$\overline{T}_{5^\circ}=(1.63\pm 0.10)\;\mathrm{s}$$ at amplitude $$5^\circ$$ and $$\overline{T}_{10^\circ}=(1.65\pm 0.08)\;\mathrm{s}$$ at amplitude $$10^\circ$$ (mean $$\pm$$ standard deviation).

__(a)__ Imagine a graph with amplitude $$A$$ on the horizontal axis and period $$T$$ on the vertical axis. What does Galileo's hypothesis look like on this graph? What does Legendre's look like?

__(b)__ When measurements are plotted, each data point gets a vertical bar spanning one uncertainty above and below it, called an __error bar__. If a hypothesis is accurate, its curve should pass through most of the data's error bars. Using the two measurements above, can the class tell whose hypothesis is right?

__(c)__ The class wants to redesign the experiment so it can actually tell the hypotheses apart. There are two general strategies for making a significant result more likely: name them, and say specifically how the class could apply each one here.

__(d)__ Human reaction time is about $$0.1\;\mathrm{s},$$ and that's roughly the timing error whether you time something short or something long. Explain why timing __ten__ oscillations and dividing the total by ten gives a period measurement with only about $$0.01\;\mathrm{s}$$ of uncertainty. (One warning: count carefully! If you mean to time ten periods of this pendulum but get a result near $$1.50\;\mathrm{s}$$ per period, you probably counted only nine — the fenceposting mistake.)

__(e)__ Using the ten-oscillation technique at amplitudes $$5^\circ$$ and $$45^\circ,$$ the class found $$\overline{T}_{5^\circ}=(1.679\pm 0.03)\;\mathrm{s}$$ and $$\overline{T}_{45^\circ}=(1.748\pm 0.03)\;\mathrm{s}.$$ The chart below shows both hypotheses along with the new data and error bars. Whose hypothesis wins? Does the result mean Galileo knew nothing about pendulums?

label: I2P04
name: Too Many Digits: The Cougar Sign and the GPS — A sign at the Como Park Zoo in St. Paul, Minnesota describes a…
desc: A sign at the Como Park Zoo in St. Paul, Minnesota describes a cougar. It lists the cougar's daily "Zoo Diet" as $$1.3608\;\mathrm{kg}$$ of food, its "Average Weight" as $$90.72\;\mathrm{kg},$$ and its "Average Lifespan" as a nice round $$20$$ years. __(a)__ Reporting the diet…
statement:
A sign at the Como Park Zoo in St. Paul, Minnesota describes a cougar. It lists the cougar's daily "Zoo Diet" as $$1.3608\;\mathrm{kg}$$ of food, its "Average Weight" as $$90.72\;\mathrm{kg},$$ and its "Average Lifespan" as a nice round $$20$$ years.

__(a)__ Reporting the diet as $$1.3608\;\mathrm{kg}$$ claims a precision of one ten-thousandth of a kilogram — a tenth of a gram, about three grains of rice. That's strange for a number that surely varies day to day. Here's a clue: this is an American zoo, and Americans usually use pounds. The pound is defined exactly as $$1\;\mathrm{lb} = 0.45359237\;\mathrm{kg}.$$ Convert the diet and the weight into pounds. What do you find, and what probably happened when the sign was made?

__(b)__ The digits of a reported number that convey useful information are called its __significant figures__ (or significant digits). Explain why $$1.3608\;\mathrm{kg}$$ has too many of them.

__(c)__ A phone app uses GPS to report its latitude as $$\phi = 34.731688250423275^\circ,$$ along with an uncertainty of $$\pm 64\;\mathrm{m}.$$ Your __latitude__ is the angle $$\phi$$ measuring how far north or south of the equator you are, shown below; moving $$111\;\mathrm{km}$$ north or south changes your latitude by about $$1^\circ.$$ How many degrees of latitude correspond to $$64\;\mathrm{m}?$$ Use your result to write the latitude in $$\pm$$ notation.

__(d)__ Using the interval of latitudes allowed by the uncertainty, decide which digits of the readout actually convey useful information. How many significant figures should the app report?

label: I2P04
name: Arithmetic with Significant Figures — You want the area of the rectangular face of a stone monolith sticking…
desc: You want the area of the rectangular face of a stone monolith sticking out of the ground. You measure its base carefully: $$7.131\;\mathrm{m},$$ a number with four significant figures. But you can't reach the top and have no ladder, so you have to eyeball the height: about…
statement:
You want the area of the rectangular face of a stone monolith sticking out of the ground. You measure its base carefully: $$7.131\;\mathrm{m},$$ a number with four significant figures. But you can't reach the top and have no ladder, so you have to eyeball the height: about $$9\;\mathrm{m},$$ just one significant figure.

__(a)__ When you multiply to get the area, should you report the result with four significant figures (like the base) or one (like the height)? Explain using the idea of uncertainty.

__(b)__ The general rule for multiplying or dividing: keep as many significant figures as the __least__ precise quantity involved. If you multiply three quantities having two, four, and three significant figures, how many significant figures should the result have?

__(c)__ A measurement reported as "$$10\;\mathrm{m}$$" is ambiguous — it might have one significant figure or two. How does scientific notation resolve the ambiguity?

__(d)__ Addition follows a different rule than multiplication. Consider $$18.2\;\mathrm{m}+0.4\;\mathrm{m},$$ where the first quantity has three significant figures and the second has only one. Someone argues the answer should be rounded to one significant figure, $$2\times 10^1\;\mathrm{m},$$ to match the less precise quantity. What should actually be reported, and why? The rule: when adding, keep the decimal places that are significant in __both__ quantities. Apply the same rule to $$3.42\;\mathrm{kg}+0.1185\;\mathrm{kg}.$$

label: I2P04
name: Weighing a Single Sheet of Paper — You want to know the mass of a single sheet of paper that you just pulled…
desc: You want to know the mass of a single sheet of paper that you just pulled off a large ream of identical sheets. Your kitchen scale reads out mass to the nearest gram. You put the sheet on the scale, and it reads $$5\;\mathrm{g}.$$ Two useful ideas. First, a rule of thumb for…
statement:
You want to know the mass of a single sheet of paper that you just pulled off a large ream of identical sheets. Your kitchen scale reads out mass to the nearest gram. You put the sheet on the scale, and it reads $$5\;\mathrm{g}.$$

Two useful ideas. First, a rule of thumb for digital devices: unless the manufacturer says otherwise, take the __absolute uncertainty__ of a reading to be half the smallest increment the readout can change by — a scale that reads to the nearest gram is uncertain by $$0.5\;\mathrm{g}.$$ Second, besides absolute uncertainty (which carries the same units as the measurement), scientists use __relative uncertainty__: the absolute uncertainty divided by the measured value. For example, a measurement of $$10\pm 2$$ has relative uncertainty $$\dfrac{2}{10}=0.2,$$ or $$20\%$$ — a pure number with no units.

__(a)__ What are the absolute and relative uncertainties in your measurement of the sheet's mass?

__(b)__ Suggest ways to reduce your uncertainty in the mass of one sheet. In particular, explain why weighing a whole stack of sheets at once and dividing by the number of sheets gives a smaller __relative__ uncertainty, even on the same scale.

__(c)__ Suppose you want the relative uncertainty in the mass of a sheet to be less than $$2\%.$$ How many sheets do you need to weigh at once?

__(d)__ Your friend weighs the entire ream of $$500$$ sheets and gets $$2566\;\mathrm{g}.$$ Since the scale's absolute uncertainty is $$0.5\;\mathrm{g},$$ they divide by $$500$$ and claim they now know the mass of the __top sheet__ of the stack to within $$0.5\;\mathrm{g}/500 = 10^{-3}\;\mathrm{g}.$$ Do you trust this as the uncertainty in the top sheet's mass? Why or why not?

__(e)__ A different route to smaller uncertainty is averaging: if you make $$n$$ independent measurements of the same quantity, all with the same uncertainty (and no shared systematic error), the uncertainty of their average is the single-measurement uncertainty divided by $$\sqrt{n}.$$ You have a measurement technique with $$5\%$$ relative uncertainty. How many independent measurements must you average to bring the relative uncertainty down to $$1\%?$$

Below are some symbols, along with a description of the physical quantity each might stand for in an equation $$\begin{array}{c|l} \textbf{Symbol} & \textbf{Quantity} \\ \hline x & \text{the position of an electron moving through a particle accelerator}\\ e & \text{the elementary charge (the charge on any proton in the universe)}\\ c & \text{the speed of light in a vacuum (which is always the same)} \\ m_e & \text{the electron mass (all electrons are identical)}\\ v & \text{the speed of a skydiver}\\ \end{array}$$

Some quantities are __variables__. This means their value can change under different circumstances.

Others are __physical constants__. We can think of these as built into the laws of physics. They are the same in every experiment anywhere in the universe.

Put each quantity in the corresponding category. Categorize them all.

name: Benjamin combs his hair with a plastic comb. In the winter, he notices static electricity…
desc: Benjamin combs his hair with a plastic comb. In the winter, he notices static electricity building up in his hair. Benjamin knows this is because electric charge travels between the comb and his hair. Benjamin also knows electric charge comes in two types: positive or negative…
statement:
Benjamin combs his hair with a plastic comb. In the winter, he notices static electricity building up in his hair. Benjamin knows this is because electric charge travels between the comb and his hair.

Benjamin also knows electric charge comes in two types: positive or negative. He doesn't know which type is in his hair or which type is being transferred in this experiment.

The symbol used to represent an electric charge is $$Q.$$

J.J., a physicist, tells Benjamin that while combing, the charge Benjamin adds to his hair is $$\Delta Q_{\rm hair} = - 5 \;\mathrm{mC}.$$ Then J.J. runs away and is not available to answer more questions.

Pick the one choice that is __not__ a reasonable interpretation for Benjamin to make of the minus sign in this equation.

negative charge moved from the comb onto his hair

positive charge moved from his hair onto the comb

all the electric charge in his hair (including any charge in any atom or subatomic particle in his hair) is negative

label: I2P05
name: In this problem, we'll practice using variables. The problem only requires algebra…
desc: In this problem, we'll practice using variables. The problem only requires algebra skills, especially substitution. It's okay if you don't understand all the physics. The big idea is that it's often useful to define new variables that simplify long expressions or equations…
statement:
In this problem, we'll practice using variables. The problem only requires algebra skills, especially substitution. It's okay if you don't understand all the physics.

The big idea is that it's often useful to define new variables that simplify long expressions or equations.

-------------------------

In 1913, Danish physicist Niels Bohr proposed what became known as the __Bohr model__ of the atom.

__Bohr model image By JabberWok, CC BY-SA 3.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=2639910__

In the Bohr model, an important quantity is the amount of energy needed to completely pull an electron off of a hydrogen atom. This amount of energy is called the __Rydberg,__ $$\mathrm{Ry}.$$ Bohr found this formula for it: $$ 1 \;\mathrm{Ry} = \dfrac{m_e e^4}{8\epsilon_0^2 h^2}.$$

Although you can solve this problem without them, the meanings of the variables are: $$\begin{aligned} m_e: & \text{ mass of an electron} \\ e: & \text{ electric charge of a proton}\\ \epsilon_0: & \text{ permittivity of the vacuum, a physical constant related to electromagnetism}\\ h: & \text{ Planck's constant, a physical constant related to quantum mechanics} \end{aligned}$$ You don't need to know the values of the constants in this problem in order to solve the problem.

Bohr also simplified his formula by introducing the __fine structure constant__ $$\alpha,$$ $$ \alpha = \dfrac{e^2}{2 \epsilon_0 h}.$$

Using algebraic substitution, use $$\alpha$$ to eliminate $$e, h,$$ and $$\epsilon_0$$ from the formula for the Rydberg. Write a new formula for the Rydberg in terms of $$m_e$$ and $$\alpha,$$ with a numerical coefficient in front.

Enter your answer below.

label: I2P05
name: The goal of this problem is to explore the relationship between how units are defined and…
desc: The goal of this problem is to explore the relationship between how units are defined and the values of constants. For example, the speed of light is approximately $$c \approx 3 \times 10^8 \;\mathrm{m/s}.$$ Imagine we doubled how long the meter is. That wouldn't change how long…
statement:
The goal of this problem is to explore the relationship between how units are defined and the values of constants. For example, the speed of light is approximately $$c \approx 3 \times 10^8 \;\mathrm{m/s}.$$ Imagine we doubled how long the meter is. That wouldn't change how long it takes light to get from place to place. For example, if we shine light from one mountaintop to the next and it used to take $$10^{-4}$$ seconds to go from mountaintop to mountaintop, it still would take $$10^{-4}$$ seconds after the meter redefinition.

However, if we doubled the length of the meter, we'd cut the number of meters between the mountaintops in half. If it used to be about $$3\times 10^5 \;\mathrm{m}$$ between mountaintops, with the new, longer meter, we'd only need $$1.5 \times 10^5 \;\mathrm{m}$$ to span the same distance. That means light would now travel only $$1.5 \times 10^5 \;\mathrm{m}$$ in $$10^{-4} \;\mathrm{s},$$ so the speed of light would be $$c \approx 1.5 \times 10^8 \;\mathrm{m/s}$$ after we doubled the length of a meter. Light would still go just as fast, but with the new unit system we'd refer to that speed with a different number.

Notice that $$\mathrm{m}$$ appears in the numerator of $$\mathrm{m/s},$$ and when we double the length of a meter, we cut the speed of light in half. If we were to double the how long a second is, that would give light twice as much time to travel in what we call "one second", and the speed of light would double. $$\mathrm{s}$$ are in the denominator of $$\mathrm{m/s},$$ and doubling the duration of a second doubles the speed of light.

Your job in this problem is to extend this reasoning to the gravitational constant. As you think about this problem, remember that in the gravitational constant, the dimensions are not all to the first power or negative first power, like they are in the speed of light.

----------

We saw in the prereading that Newton's gravitational constant is $$G \approx 6.674 \times 10^{-11} \dfrac{\mathrm{m}^3}{\mathrm{kg} \cdot \mathrm{s}^2}.$$

Suppose we want to redefine some units to change the numerical part of Newton's gravitational constant so that instead of $$6.67 \times 10^{-11},$$ it becomes $$10^{-10},$$ which is a bit larger. That is, we want to make a unit redefinition so that $$G_{\rm after \; redefinition} = 1\times 10^{-10} \dfrac{\mathrm{m}^3}{\mathrm{kg} \cdot \mathrm{s}^2} $$

In this equation, at least one of the meter, second, or kilogram would have to change to a new value.

For example, if we doubled the mass of the kilogram to define a new kilogram, $$G$$ would also double. This would not solve the problem, because then $$G \approx 1.3348 \times 10^{-10} \dfrac{\mathrm{m}^3}{\mathrm{kg} \cdot \mathrm{s}^2},$$ but instead of doubling the kilogram, we could multiply it by some number a bit less than two such that the numerical part of $$G$$ came out exactly to $$10^{-10}.$$

Find the number we would need to multiply the kilogram by to change $$G$$ in this way. Then find the number we would need to multiply the second by to change $$G$$ in the same way, assuming we don't change the kilogram and only change the second. Finally, find the number we would need to multiply the meter by to change the numerical part of $$G$$ to $$10^{-10}.$$

name: Suppose there is a box connected to a spring sitting on the ground. There is also wind…
desc: Suppose there is a box connected to a spring sitting on the ground. There is also wind blowing on the box. The wind exerts a force on the box that compresses the spring a bit to some new equilibrium length. The distance between where the box sits at equilibrium without wind and…
statement:
Suppose there is a box connected to a spring sitting on the ground. There is also wind blowing on the box. The wind exerts a force on the box that compresses the spring a bit to some new equilibrium length.

The distance between where the box sits at equilibrium without wind and where it sits with wind is called $$\Delta x.$$ In this problem, we will focus on magnitudes, and you can assume $$\Delta x$$ is positive.

Remember that in class, we found that the size of the force from the spring is $$|F_{\rm spring}| = k \Delta x,$$ and the size of the force from wind is $$|F_{\rm wind}| = \dfrac12 C_D \rho A v^2.$$

We can assume there is no friction with the ground, and the only forces we need to worry about are the force from the wind on the box and the force from the spring on the box.

Find an equation for $$\Delta x$$ in terms of the other variables.

name: Part A. Suppose you pull the drain on a bathtub. The water will not flow out at a…
desc: Part A. Suppose you pull the drain on a bathtub. The water will not flow out at a constant rate. Instead, when the tub is very full, the weight of the water pushes water out the drain faster. As the tub empties, the rate that water flows out slows down. A simple theory says that…
statement:
Part A. Suppose you pull the drain on a bathtub. The water will not flow out at a constant rate. Instead, when the tub is very full, the weight of the water pushes water out the drain faster. As the tub empties, the rate that water flows out slows down.

A simple theory says that the speed $$v$$ of water, as it leaves the bathtub, depends only on the height $$h$$ of the water level above the bottom of the tub and on the gravitational acceleration $$g.$$

The dimensions of these quantities are $$\begin{aligned} \left[ v\right] & = \mathrm{L\cdot T^{-1}}\\ \left & = \mathrm{L\cdot T^{-2}} \\ \left[ h \right] &= \mathrm{L} \end{aligned}$$

When the bathtub is full, water leaves the bath tub at $$2.9 \;\mathrm{m/s}$$ through the drain.

At what speed does water leave the bathtub when it is half full?

Aside from a constant coefficient (whose value doesn't matter in this problem), there is only one possible formula for $$v$$ in terms of $$g$$ and $$h.$$ Use the dimensions of each quantity to find that formula, then use the formula to answer the question.

mathjax: \

width: 5

Part B. In the previous problem, we imagined a bathtub draining. Water would leave the tub with a speed of $$2.9 \;\mathrm{m/s}$$ when the tub is full.

Suppose the cross sectional area of the drain is $$8.0 \;\mathrm{cm}^2.$$ You may assume that all water leaving the bathtub through the drain exits through the drain with the same speed, and that speed follows the theory mentioned in part (A).

Also suppose that we pour $$1.0 \; \mathrm{L/s}$$ of water into the bathtub. $$1 \;\mathrm{L}$$ stands for "one liter", it is defined as $$1 \;\mathrm{L} = 10^3 \;\mathrm{cm}^3.$$

Then after some time, the water in the tub will come to a constant height as we continuously pour water in and it continuously leaves. We can call this the "steady state". What percentage of the tub will be full of water in the steady state?

name: Part A. In this multi-part problem, we will study a collision. It's possible to…
desc: Part A. In this multi-part problem, we will study a collision. It's possible to understand collisions using concepts such as __momentum, energy,__ and __reference frames__. We haven't studied those concepts yet, though. Our goal here is to demonstrate how much we can figure out…
statement:
Part A. In this multi-part problem, we will study a collision. It's possible to understand collisions using concepts such as __momentum, energy,__ and __reference frames__. We haven't studied those concepts yet, though. Our goal here is to demonstrate how much we can figure out not by applying formal theories of physics, but by combining mathematical and logical reasoning in a way similar to how we did in class. This problem is a new context, but you can figure it out in stages by thinking about what the symbols mean and using some basic intuition.

---------------

A ball of mass $$m$$ moving at velocity $$v$$ approaches a ball of mass $$M$$ that is sitting stationary. $$v$$ is positive for motion to the right and negative for motion to the left.

Here's a picture of the situation:

We have drawn the ball of mass $$m$$ smaller than the ball of mass $$M,$$ but we imagine that either ball could be the more massive one, depending on the values of $$m$$ and $$M.$$

The balls collide and bounce off each other. The ball on the right winds up moving to the right at a velocity $$v_M$$ and the ball on the left will, in this example, bounce off to the left, moving with some velocity $$v_m.$$

Over the rest of this problem (which has several parts), we'll find a formula for $$v_m.$$

To begin, we note that $$v_m$$ needs to be a function of only the variables that go into the problem: $$v, m,$$ and $$M.$$

With that in mind, what is the proportionality between $$v_m$$ and $$v?$$

mathjax: \[ v_m \propto v^{\blank}.\]

width: 3

Part B. To continue analyzing the collision problem, we introduce a __special case__. Although the entire problem is hard to tackle head on, it becomes easier if we make a simplifying assumption. That simplifying assumption is the "special case".

Let's take the special case that the ball on the left is very small and has very little mass. (Think of a tiny ball bearing just a millimeter across bouncing off a giant ball the size of a whale.) The little ball comes in for a collision and bounces off. No energy is lost in the collision.

We can write the masses in this special case as $$m \ll M,$$ meaning "$$m$$ is much less than $$M".$$

Using intuition, we can guess what will happen here. As far as the tiny ball is concerned, the large ball is almost impossible to move, like a hard wall. The tiny ball will bounce back with nearly the same speed it had coming into the collision, but it will reverse direction.

The large ball will hardly be affected, but there will be at least a tiny bit of motion because the tiny ball does impart at least a very small influence on the large ball when it bounces off.

Since the large ball has a tiny bit of Kinetic energy is energy due to motion after the collision, there's a little bit less energy left over for the small ball, so although its rebound speed will be close to the speed it initially had in its approach, the rebound will be a tiny bit slower.

To practice translating this intuition into mathematical statements, select all four statements from below that are true in this special case.

Remember that quantities like $$v, v_m,$$ and $$v_M$$ can be positive or negative depending on the direction of motion. The notation $$|v_m|$$ means the magnitude (like the absolute value) of $$v_m.$$ It is never negative. If $$v_m < 0,$$ then $$|v_m| = -v_m.$$ Also keep in mind that motion to the right is positive and motion to the left is negative.

Also, remember that $$\ll$$ is different than $$<.$$ The notation $$a \ll b$$ means $$``a$$ is much less than $$b''\,.$$

Part C. Another special case is $$m \gg M.$$

First, draw a picture to illustrate this case. Then use your intuition to guess what happens to the ball of mass $$m.$$ Based on your intuition, which choice below is true in this special case?

$$v_m = -v$$

$$v_m \approx -v$$

$$v_m = 0$$

Part D. There is one final special case that is important: $$m = M.$$

This special case corresponds to what we would see in a game of billiards.

Here is an illustration of what happens: The incoming ball stops perfectly.

(In real life, there is some spinning and the collision may lose a tiny bit of energy, and the collision isn't perfectly head on. All these influences make it so the incoming ball doesn't quite perfectly stop. However, the ideal mathematical solution is $$v_m = 0$$ in this case.)

We now know: - the proportionality between $$v_m$$ and $$v$$ - how $$v_m$$ behaves when $$m \ll M$$ - how $$v_m$$ behaves when $$m \gg M$$ - how $$v_m$$ behaves when $$m = M$$

Combine these four bits of knowledge to determine a formula for $$v_m$$ that works in every case.
