name: A Ball Built from Three Pieces — Watch a golf ball closely during its impact with a club, as in the…
desc: Watch a golf ball closely during its impact with a club, as in the slow-motion clip below. The ball __compresses__ — gets squashed a bit — during the impact, then bounces back to its original shape, just like a spring. Golf balls and springs are similar enough that sometimes we…
statement:
Watch a golf ball closely during its impact with a club, as in the slow-motion clip below. The ball __compresses__ — gets squashed a bit — during the impact, then bounces back to its original shape, just like a spring. Golf balls and springs are similar enough that sometimes we can use the same equations for each; in fact, lots of things act like springs even when they aren't literally springs.

In a research paper titled "A mass-spring-damper model of a bouncing ball," physicists Mark Nagurka and Shuguang Huang built a simplified stand-in — a __model__ — for a real bouncing ball. Their diagram of a "ball" is shown below. It has a box at the top carrying the entire __mass__ $$m$$ of the ball, a spring with variable $$k$$ supplying the __elasticity__ (bounciness), and a device called a __damper__, all above a flat plate representing the floor (the plate wasn't important to the mathematical analysis). The picture does not look like a ball, but the pieces together perform mathematically much like a real ball bouncing.

__(a)__ Real balls don't bounce back up to the height they were dropped from. Which of the three elements of the model accounts for that, and what does it represent physically?

__(b)__ Nagurka and Huang set the mass __of the spring__ equal to zero, even though real springs do have mass. Why is this simplification useful?

__(c)__ The figure below shows five stages of the model ball during a bounce. In which stage is the spring the most compressed?

__(d)__ To explain how balls bounce, the authors needed equations beyond the ones for springs and dampers. Name two other kinds of equations they needed, and explain why they did __not__ need a separate equation for air drag.

label: I2P05
name: What Does the Spring Constant Measure? — Physicists describe a spring with a single variable $$k,$$ called…
desc: Physicists describe a spring with a single variable $$k,$$ called the __spring constant__. In diagrams of a ball bouncing modeled as a mass on a spring, the same symbol $$k$$ is written next to the spring at every stage of the bounce — even as the spring squashes down and…
statement:
Physicists describe a spring with a single variable $$k,$$ called the __spring constant__. In diagrams of a ball bouncing modeled as a mass on a spring, the same symbol $$k$$ is written next to the spring at every stage of the bounce — even as the spring squashes down and rebounds. The length of the spring changes during the bounce, but $$k$$ does not; that's why it's a spring __constant__. Each spring has its own value of $$k$$: it's a property of the spring.

So $$k$$ should describe the __most important__ aspect of a spring, it should __not__ change as the spring is compressed, and it __can__ be different for different springs.

__(a)__ Which of the following could $$k$$ represent: (i) how stiff the spring is, (ii) how much mass the spring has, (iii) how long the spring is, (iv) the force the spring exerts? Use the three requirements above to rule out the wrong choices. (In the mass-spring model of a ball, the spring is taken to be massless.)

__(b)__ The photo below shows two springs, (a) and (b). Which one has the higher spring constant, and why?

__(c)__ Golf balls and tennis balls both squash like springs when struck. Which has the higher spring constant?

label: I2P05
name: Reading Hooke's Law Symbol by Symbol — The most common equation for a spring is __Hooke's law__, $$F =…
desc: The most common equation for a spring is __Hooke's law__, $$F = -k\,\Delta x.$$ Physics problems often involve a lot of algebra — moving variables around, squaring things — and while doing that it's easy (and often okay) to temporarily forget what an equation means. Before any…
statement:
The most common equation for a spring is __Hooke's law__, $$F = -k\,\Delta x.$$ Physics problems often involve a lot of algebra — moving variables around, squaring things — and while doing that it's easy (and often okay) to temporarily forget what an equation means. Before any algebra, though, it pays to understand how each part of this equation relates to a real spring. The symbol $$k$$ is the __spring constant__, measuring the spring's stiffness. To explore the rest, picture a spring attached to a wall on its left, with its free end on the right; you can experiment with exactly this setup in the simulation at https://phet.colorado.edu/sims/html/hookes-law/latest/hookes-law_en.html (click "Intro", then turn on the checkboxes for "Spring Force", "Displacement", and "Equilibrium Position").

__(a)__ $$F$$ stands for "force", measured in SI in __newtons__ $$(\mathrm{N}).$$ There are two possible interpretations: (1) the force that other objects exert __on the spring__, or (2) the force that the spring exerts __on other objects__. Imagine a spring poking straight up out of a desk, and you push down hard on it, compressing it. Identify the two forces in this situation. Do they point in the same direction or opposite directions? (In Hooke's law we use interpretation (2): $$F$$ is the __spring force__ the spring exerts on other objects.)

__(b)__ The free end of the spring naturally rests at a location called the __equilibrium position__ (the dotted line below). The symbol $$\Delta$$ means "change in." If $$x$$ is the position of the free end of the spring, what does $$\Delta x$$ represent? Is $$\Delta x$$ positive or negative when the spring is stretched? When it is compressed?

__(c)__ Multiplying a force by $$-1$$ makes it point the opposite way — a stick figure pushing a box to the right would, after multiplying its force by $$-1,$$ push the box to the left. So the minus sign in Hooke's law is somehow related to direction. Which of the three quantities $$F,$$ $$k,$$ and $$\Delta x$$ have a direction associated with them (can be positive or negative), and which do not?

__(d)__ In the simulation, the spring-force arrow and the displacement arrow always point in opposite directions, as in the animation below. What does the minus sign in $$F = -k\,\Delta x$$ indicate physically? The spring force is called a __restoring force__ — explain why that name fits.

label: I2P05
name: How Far Does a Hanging Spring Stretch? — A spring hangs from a ceiling, and we attach an orange box of mass…
desc: A spring hangs from a ceiling, and we attach an orange box of mass $$m$$ to its lower end. The box pulls down on the spring, stretching it; the box and spring oscillate for a bit, then settle down to a new __equilibrium__. "Equilibrium" is when there are no unbalanced forces…
statement:
A spring hangs from a ceiling, and we attach an orange box of mass $$m$$ to its lower end. The box pulls down on the spring, stretching it; the box and spring oscillate for a bit, then settle down to a new __equilibrium__. "Equilibrium" is when there are no unbalanced forces causing acceleration in a system, and everything remains constant and unchanging.

Call the upward direction positive and downward negative. The spring obeys Hooke's law: the force the spring exerts is $$F_{\rm spring} = -k\,\Delta x,$$ where $$k$$ is the spring constant and $$\Delta x$$ is the displacement of the spring's end from its natural, unstretched position. Since the box stretches the spring downward, $$\Delta x < 0$$ here. Gravity pulls down on the box with force $$F_{\rm gravity} = -mg,$$ where $$g$$ measures the strength of gravity; the minus sign means the gravitational force points down. We want to find $$\Delta x_{\rm eq},$$ the value of $$\Delta x$$ once everything settles at the new equilibrium.

__(a)__ At the new equilibrium, which force is bigger: gravity pulling the box down, or the spring force holding it up? When two things balance, an equation for them fits the template $$\square = \square.$$ Write an equation relating $$F_{\rm spring}$$ and $$F_{\rm gravity},$$ including whatever sign is needed to account for the forces pointing in opposite directions.

__(b)__ Combine your equation from part (a) with $$F_{\rm spring} = -k\,\Delta x_{\rm eq}$$ and $$F_{\rm gravity} = -mg$$ to build an equation for $$\Delta x_{\rm eq}$$ in terms of $$g,$$ $$k,$$ and $$m$$ alone.

__(c)__ Now use the equation to make a prediction. Suppose that while the box hangs there, we magically stiffen the spring, increasing its spring constant $$k$$ (leaving $$m$$ and $$g$$ unchanged). Focusing on just the two relevant variables, write the proportionality between $$\Delta x_{\rm eq}$$ and $$k.$$ As $$k$$ increases, does the box rise, fall, or stay put?

label: I2P05
name: Building an Equation for Air Drag — and Terminal Velocity — When a skydiver jumps out of a plane, they fall…
desc: When a skydiver jumps out of a plane, they fall faster and faster at first. As they fall faster, they feel more and more wind. Eventually the wind is so strong that the skydiver doesn't fall any faster: they fall at a constant speed, called __terminal velocity__, until opening…
statement:
When a skydiver jumps out of a plane, they fall faster and faster at first. As they fall faster, they feel more and more wind. Eventually the wind is so strong that the skydiver doesn't fall any faster: they fall at a constant speed, called __terminal velocity__, until opening their parachute — about $$50\;\mathrm{m/s}$$ for a typical skydiver. The upward force from the wind even makes indoor skydiving possible: a big fan blows air upward at about that speed, and you can float on it inside a big tube. The force from the wind is called __air drag__, $$F_{\rm drag},$$ and for a falling object it points upward, opposing the motion. In this problem we will build an equation for air drag, then use it to find a formula for terminal velocity.

__(a)__ Air drag increases as a falling object speeds up — but that does __not__ necessarily mean doubling the speed doubles the drag. Suppose $$F_{\rm drag} \propto v^{\alpha},$$ where $$v$$ is the falling speed. Which of these exponents are consistent with drag increasing as speed increases: $$\alpha = -2,$$ $$-1,$$ $$-\tfrac12,$$ $$\tfrac12,$$ $$1,$$ $$2$$? What is the most we can conclude about $$\alpha$$ from this fact alone?

__(b)__ To pin down the exponent, picture the falling object as a ball smashing its way through a crowd of tiny dots — air molecules — as in the animations below (one slow ball, one fast ball). Every collision pushes backward on the ball a little. Suppose the slow ball averages $$20$$ collisions per second, and the fast ball moves three times as fast. How many collisions per second does the fast ball average? Write the proportionality between collisions-per-second and $$v.$$

__(c)__ A faster ball not only has more collisions per second — each collision is also more violent. Newtonian mechanics suggests the __force per collision__ is also proportional to $$v.$$ The total drag combines the two effects: $$F_{\rm drag} \propto (\text{force from a collision}) \cdot (\text{collisions per second}).$$ What is the proportionality between $$F_{\rm drag}$$ and $$v$$?

__(d)__ Speed isn't the only thing that matters. A larger object hits more air, so we guess drag is proportional to the object's __cross-sectional area__ $$A$$ — the area of the surface you'd create by slicing the object open across its direction of motion (see figure below). A sleek, aerodynamic shape cuts through wind better than a boxy one; this is captured by the __drag coefficient__ $$C_D,$$ defined so that $$F_{\rm drag} \propto C_D.$$ Finally, the __density__ $$\rho$$ (Greek "rho") of the air matters, with $$F_{\rm drag} \propto \rho.$$ (In 2012, Austrian skydiver Felix Baumgartner jumped from a balloon $$39\;\mathrm{km}$$ up, in the stratosphere, where the air is so thin he needed a spacesuit — with so little drag, he reached about $$375\;\mathrm{m/s},$$ faster than the speed of sound!) Combine all the proportionalities into a single proportionality for $$F_{\rm drag}.$$

__(e)__ The standard equation adds a conventional factor of one half: $$|F_{\rm drag}| = \tfrac12 C_D \rho A v^2$$ (the absolute value lets us set aside minus signs, since $$v^2$$ is always positive; the $$\tfrac12$$ is just a convention so the equation matches what you'd look up in books). At terminal velocity the drag force balances the gravitational force, whose size is $$|F_{\rm gravity}| = mg,$$ as in the diagram below — zero net force here doesn't mean the skydiver is stationary, only that they are no longer speeding up. Set the two forces equal and solve for the terminal velocity $$v_{\rm terminal}.$$

label: I2P05
name: Checking the Formula: Estimating Terminal Velocity — The terminal velocity of a falling object — the constant…
desc: The terminal velocity of a falling object — the constant speed it reaches when air drag balances gravity — is $$v_{\rm terminal} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2mg}{C_D \rho A}},$$ where $$m$$ is the object's mass, $$g$$ is the strength of gravity, $$C_D$$ is the drag coefficient (a number…
statement:
The terminal velocity of a falling object — the constant speed it reaches when air drag balances gravity — is $$v_{\rm terminal} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2mg}{C_D \rho A}},$$ where $$m$$ is the object's mass, $$g$$ is the strength of gravity, $$C_D$$ is the drag coefficient (a number describing how aerodynamic the shape is), $$\rho$$ is the density of the air, and $$A$$ is the object's cross-sectional area. One way to check that a formula works is to estimate each value, plug them all in, and make sure the quantity that pops out is approximately right. Real skydivers fall at about $$50\;\mathrm{m/s}.$$

__(a)__ Estimate the cross-sectional area $$A$$ of the belly-down skydiver in the photo above. (One meter is a bit more than three feet. Estimate the height, then the width, and multiply — but don't use the arm span as the width, since most of the skydiver's cross section is much narrower than that.)

__(b)__ Density is mass per unit volume. In SI units — combinations of kilograms, meters, and seconds — what units is density measured in? The density of air at low altitudes is about $$1.2$$ in those units.

__(c)__ Use $$m = 80\;\mathrm{kg},$$ $$g \approx 10\;\mathrm{m/s^2},$$ $$C_D \approx 1,$$ $$\rho = 1.2\;\mathrm{kg/m^3},$$ and $$A = 0.5\;\mathrm{m^2}.$$ Compute $$v_{\rm terminal},$$ handling the numerical part and the units separately. Before you even work out the number, why is the unit you get an encouraging sign? How does the result compare with real skydivers?

__(d)__ Now suppose the skydiver falls head first, as in the photo below, reducing their cross-sectional area to $$A = 0.25\;\mathrm{m^2}$$ with all the other variables unchanged. Without plugging in all the numbers again, use the proportionality between $$v_{\rm terminal}$$ and $$A$$ to modify your answer from part (c). Do they fall faster or slower, and at what speed?

label: I2P05
name: The Up/Down Game: Heating Water in a Steel Pot — Water, like any substance, increases its temperature when…
desc: Water, like any substance, increases its temperature when you add heat to it. Water has a __specific heat capacity__ of $$c_{\rm water} = 4.18\;\mathrm{J/(K \cdot g)}$$: one gram of water increases its temperature by one kelvin for every $$4.18$$ joules of heat added. We want an…
statement:
Water, like any substance, increases its temperature when you add heat to it. Water has a __specific heat capacity__ of $$c_{\rm water} = 4.18\;\mathrm{J/(K \cdot g)}$$: one gram of water increases its temperature by one kelvin for every $$4.18$$ joules of heat added. We want an equation for the temperature $$T$$ of a quantity of water of mass $$m$$ that begins at temperature $$T_0$$ and has heat $$Q$$ added to it.

__(a)__ Start with a simple case: suppose $$Q = 0.$$ What should $$T$$ equal then, and why does that suggest building the equation from the template $$T = T_0 + \Delta T,$$ where $$\Delta T$$ is the temperature increase caused by the added heat?

__(b)__ Suppose you have a fixed amount of heat to add — say just $$1\;\mathrm{J}.$$ Which heats up more: a small quantity of water or a huge one? In an equation for $$\Delta T$$ written as a fraction, should the mass $$m$$ go in the numerator or the denominator?

__(c)__ Play the same "up/down game" with the remaining quantities — for each variable, decide whether increasing it pushes $$\Delta T$$ up (numerator) or down (denominator) — to place $$Q$$ and $$c_{\rm water},$$ and write the complete equations for $$\Delta T$$ and for $$T.$$ (Two ways to think about $$c_{\rm water}$$: check where the temperature units sit in $$\mathrm{J/(K \cdot g)},$$ or imagine the heat capacity were a trillion joules per kelvin per gram and ask what would happen to the temperature.)

__(d)__ Now apply the equation. Steel has a specific heat capacity of $$c_{\rm steel} = 0.466\;\mathrm{J/(K \cdot g)}.$$ A steel pot with a mass of $$1.5\;\mathrm{kg}$$ is heated to $$400\;\mathrm{K},$$ and then $$10\;\mathrm{kg}$$ of water at $$300\;\mathrm{K}$$ is added. No other heat enters or leaves the system. Which way does heat flow, and what happens to each temperature? Will the final shared temperature be close to $$300\;\mathrm{K},$$ close to $$400\;\mathrm{K},$$ or roughly halfway between? Explain using the masses and heat capacities.

__(e)__ Finding the exact answer requires a system of equations and a lot of number crunching. Instead, use an __approximation__ — a method that is slightly wrong but very close to correct and much easier: take the pot's temperature change to be $$\Delta T_{\rm pot} \approx -100\;\mathrm{K}.$$ Compute the heat the pot gives up, then how much that heat warms the water, and so the final temperature. (Careful: the heat capacities use grams, while the masses are given in kilograms.) Finally, did this approximation overestimate or underestimate the water's temperature rise?

label: I2P06
name: Recall that, in the prereading, we learned about several different models for DNA. These…
desc: Recall that, in the prereading, we learned about several different models for DNA. These are summarized in the image below: __Phillips, Rob, et al. Physical biology of the cell. Garland Science, 2012.__ Each model is applicable to solving different scientific problems. **Connect…
statement:
Recall that, in the prereading, we learned about several different models for DNA. These are summarized in the image below:

__Phillips, Rob, et al. Physical biology of the cell. Garland Science, 2012.__

Each model is applicable to solving different scientific problems. **Connect each problem to the single most relevant model.**

The connections are one-to-one.

**Scientific Problems:**

**(A)** If a strand of DNA sits on its own in water, it will uncoil. It doesn't become straight. Instead, the random motion of the molecules in the water leads the DNA to have a winding, random shape. How does the shape change as we change the temperature of the water?

__Phillips, Rob, et al. Physical biology of the cell. Garland Science, 2012.__

**(B)** __RNA polymerase__ is a complicated protein that binds to the DNA and copies a piece of its genetic material. Where will RNA polymerase latch on to the DNA molecule?

**(C)** Cells need to control which genes they are using at any given time. In one example, part of the cell's procedure to control its genes involves bending a short segment of DNA into a loop to bring two parts that are usually separated right next to each other. How much energy does it takes to curve the DNA segment into a circle and form this loop?

**(D)** __Cystic fibrosis__ is a genetic disorder that can cause poor lung function. Where are the genes related to cystic fibrosis located in the human genome? Can we detect cystic fibrosis in a human embryo?

**(E)** When the fluid near DNA is salty, ions (atoms with electric charge) in the water are attracted or repelled from the DNA because of the electric charge on the DNA molecule. How do the charge on DNA and saltiness of the environment affect genetic processes?

**Models**

**sequence model** The sequence model ignores the physical structure of DNA and only reports the human genome as a list of nucleotides. Groups of nucleotides form genes. This model is useful for understanding DNA as genetic information. For example, it could tell us which gene tells the body how to make a certain protein, or which gene is copied incorrectly in a certain genetic disease.

**binding site model** Cells have many complicated proteins in them called __molecular machines__. Some molecular machines attach themselves to the DNA, unwind the DNA, and make copies of it. The binding site model is useful for studying this process of molecular machines attaching to the DNA.

**charged rod model** DNA has negative __electric charge__ because it has more electrons (which have negative charge) than protons (which have positive charge). In the charged rod model, we study how the charge on the DNA interacts with any charged particles in the nearby environment. This model is __not__ concerned with bending of the rod, despite the drawing showing some bending.

**elastic rod model** The elastic rod model views DNA as a series of springs that must be stretched or compressed when the shape of the DNA changes. It is useful for thinking about forces or energy in curved pieces of DNA, especially for short DNA strands.

**random walk model** The random walk model thinks of longer segments of DNA (about 50 base pairs each) as straight lines, but each straight line goes off in a random direction. This model is useful for studying the behavior of DNA (and many other processes) in a random environment, like when it's immersed in a fluid and molecules strike it randomly from all directions.

desc: In physics classes, it's common to model __projectiles__ - any object that is thrown or hurled in some way. Below are some different types of projectiles and some physical effects that affect projectiles. **Connect each projectile to the effects critically important for…
statement:
In physics classes, it's common to model __projectiles__ - any object that is thrown or hurled in some way. Below are some different types of projectiles and some physical effects that affect projectiles. **Connect each projectile to the effects critically important for understanding its motion.**

By "critically important", we mean any model that leaves out the effect would be very unlikely to be useful for any meaningful prediction, even for an order of magnitude estimate.

There are no limits on how many connections you are allowed to make.

**Projectiles**

**comet**: Comets are icy objects orbiting the sun. They usually have very elliptical orbits, meaning they're much closer to the sun at some times than at others. They orbit in deep outer space, where there is no atmosphere.

**paper airplane**: Imagine a student tossing a small, hand-folded paper airplane and hoping to make it fly across a classroom, much further than a rock would go if tossed with the same initial speed.

**long jumper**: A long jumper is an athlete in track and field. Top long jumpers travel about $$8 \;\mathrm{m}$$ in the air, so the total mass of air they interact with is much less than their own mass.

**dust speck**: A small speck of dust, when released into the air, is so light that moves along with the air next to it. If it has some initial motion relative to the air around it, that motion will be damped out before the speck moves more than a minuscule distance. Small air currents can carry a dust speck around for a long time.

**Effects** $$v_0$$: This is the effect of changing the initial speed of the projectile. In most cases, the faster the initial speed, the further the projectile will go. This effect is important for any sort of projectile motion where if the initial speed is different, the projectile would take a significantly different path.

**Air effects**: a projectile can interact with the air in several ways. The projectile will hit the air, and the air will put a force on the projectile called "air drag". Depending on the shape of the object, the air can also exert an upward force called "lift". These forces are usually only important when the total mass of the air that the projectiles interacts with is at least comparable to the mass of the projectile itself. In other words, heavy things thrown a short distance don't need to worry about the effects of air, but light things do. Heavy things thrown a very long distance will also need to account for air effects, since they move through so much air that the air they move through has as much or more mass than the projectile itself.

**Non-uniform Gravity**: Although we usually model gravity as a uniform force for projectiles, it isn't. The further from the Earth (or sun) a projectile is, the weaker the gravitational pull on it. This effect becomes important when the distance of the projectile from the center of the Earth (or sun) changes by a large fraction during its flight. For this effect, you are not choosing whether or not gravity is an important influence on the projectile. Instead, you're imagining a default model where gravity is uniform - the same over the entire path the projectile follow. Then you're deciding whether the correction of __non-uniform__ gravity is a vital correction for modeling the projectile.

The goal of this problem is to show you that although we made the computer execute the Nagel-Schreckenberg model, you can do it by hand if you want to. The problem should also help you understand how the cars make their decisions in the Nagel-Schreckenberg model.

-------------------------

We can simplify the Nagel-Schreckenberg model by setting $$p = 0,$$ so cars never slow down randomly. Suppose a roadway looks like what's below with cars moving in the counter-clockwise direction. In this model, during each timestep:

- (1) Each car will increase its speed by 1 if it was going below the speed limit. - (2) Each car will reduce its speed if the way is not clear. For example, if there are only three blank cells in front of a car and its speed is greater than 3 cells/timestep, its speed will be reduced to 3 cells/timestep. - (3) Each car will move forward a number of cells corresponding to its speed.

Remember that first we do step (1) for every car. Then we do step (2) for every car. Then we do step (3) for every car. This is a little different than doing steps (1), (2), and (3) in order for the first car, then moving on to the next car and repeating them.

__Iannini, M. L. L., and Ronald Dickman. "Kinetic theory of vehicular traffic." American Journal of Physics 84.2 (2016): 135-145.__

Their paper includes the following figure: $$\bar{v}$$ is the average speed of the cars.

In this model, the cars do not all have the same maximum speed. Instead, some cars want to go a bit faster than average and some want to go a bit slower than average. $$v_0$$ is the average speed that the cars want to go (although they may be slowed down by other cars in their way). $$v_a$$ is the spread in how fast the cars want to go. For example, if $$v_0 = 50 \;\mathrm{mph}$$ and $$v_a = 5 \;\mathrm{mph},$$ then cars want to go anywhere from $$45 \;\mathrm{mph}$$ to $$55 \;\mathrm{mph}.$$ $$\gamma$$ is a parameter of the model that can tell us how crowded the road is.

The axes on the plot from the Iannini-Dickman model are both dimensionless. For example, the vertical axis plots $$\dfrac{\bar{v}}{v_0}.$$ Since the numerator and denominator are both velocities, they both have dimensions of $$\mathrm{L T^{-1}}.$$ These dimensions cancel out, and the fraction is dimensionless. The horizontal axis is also dimensionless.

statement:
Part A. For this problem, you will need a little background information on __protein translation__, the process by which living cells create proteins.

**Background on protein translation**

When cells need to build new proteins, they do this using __RNA__ and __ribosomes__. The RNA molecules are copies of bits of DNA in the cell. They look like long strings. A ribosome is a molecule machine that latches onto an RNA on one side and moves steadily down the RNA. As the ribosome moves, it reads the sequence of the RNA and uses it to determine what protein to build from raw materials in the cell. This process is called __protein translation__.

Many ribosomes can latch onto an RNA molecule at the same time, and they all move down the RNA building new proteins. One ribosome cannot pass by another ribosome from behind. Instead a faster-moving ribosome will have to wait behind the ribosome in front of it. In this way, ribosomes on an RNA have some similarity to cars in traffic. If too many ribosome latch onto the same RNA molecule, there will be crowding that slows things down.

Scientists want to know how quickly new proteins can be made with this system. We will examine a simple model for ribosomes moving down an RNA molecule to study the rate at which proteins are made.

**TASEP** One model used to study protein translation is TASEP, which stands for __Totally Asymmetric Stochastic Exclusion Process__. "Totally asymmetric" means that the objects in the model can only move in one direction. "Stochastic" means that there is some randomness in the model. "Exclusion" means that the objects cannot pass through or by each other.

You can use an implementation of the TASEP model at this link (Open this in a new tab.)

You will see a line of gray squares representing an RNA molecule. You'll also see black dots moving through the gray squares from left to right. These represent ribosomes moving down the RNA. When a ribosome gets to the end of the RNA molecule, it can disappear from the model, representing finishing its protein and detaching from the RNA. New ribosomes appear at the beginning of the RNA molecule.

The simulation counts how many proteins are completed per unit time. This is called the flux. The long term average flux is equal to the number of ribosomes that have left the end of the mRNA molecule divided by number of timesteps the simulation has run.

name: Physical Models and Conceptual Models — Building, testing, and exploring __models__ is a central part of what…
desc: Building, testing, and exploring __models__ is a central part of what physicists do. There are two big families. A __physical model__ is a copy of an object, usually larger or smaller than the real thing, that reproduces only some of its essential features. A __conceptual…
statement:
Building, testing, and exploring __models__ is a central part of what physicists do. There are two big families. A __physical model__ is a copy of an object, usually larger or smaller than the real thing, that reproduces only some of its essential features. A __conceptual model__ is an abstract idealization of a system — a collection of diagrams, variables, equations, rules, and conclusions used to understand a real phenomenon.

The photograph below shows a model airplane in a __wind tunnel__ (a tube with a giant fan that blows air past the model). This model plane has a wingspan of $$2\;\mathrm{m},$$ while the real passenger jet it represents has a wingspan of $$50\;\mathrm{m}.$$ Aeronautical engineers study how air flows around the small model to learn about air flow around the full-size plane.

__(a)__ The wind-tunnel airplane is a physical model. Name a feature of a real passenger jet that almost certainly is __not__ included in this model, and explain why physical models leave such features out.

__(b)__ Earlier in the course we found the __law of the lever__: a seesaw balances when $$M_1 x_1 = M_2 x_2,$$ where each person's mass is $$M$$ and their distance from the central pivot (the __fulcrum__) is $$x.$$ The diagram below is the conceptual model we used. Working from the real seesaw to this diagram, we made several simplifications. List as many of these modeling steps and simplifications as you can.

__(c)__ When we speak of "the model" of the seesaw, which pieces are we including — just the equation, or something more? And does every conceptual model have to contain an equation?

label: I2P06
name: The Nagel-Schreckenberg Traffic Model — The __Nagel-Schreckenberg model__ is a conceptual model of cars on a…
desc: The __Nagel-Schreckenberg model__ is a conceptual model of cars on a road. Cars are represented by colored circles, and the road is a circular loop of gray squares called __cells__. All cars travel counterclockwise in a single lane; there are no stoplights and no intersections…
statement:
The __Nagel-Schreckenberg model__ is a conceptual model of cars on a road. Cars are represented by colored circles, and the road is a circular loop of gray squares called __cells__. All cars travel counterclockwise in a single lane; there are no stoplights and no intersections. The model advances in __timesteps__ (discrete jumps forward in time). In each timestep, every car moves forward and may change color. The color of a car tells you its __speed__: a red car has speed $$0$$ (it does not move), while a dark-blue car is the fastest, moving five cells in a single timestep. When a car's color changes, it has sped up or slowed down.

Two rules govern the cars. First, a car always slows down enough to avoid colliding with the car in front of it. Second, Nagel and Schreckenberg added randomness: in any given timestep, each car has a probability $$p$$ of being randomly slowed by $$1\;\dfrac{\mathrm{cell}}{\mathrm{timestep}}.$$ The value of $$p$$ can be changed in the code. You can experiment with the model at https://glowscript.org/#/user/mark.d.eichenlaub/folder/AoPS/program/traffic .

__(a)__ In this model, what does the color of a car represent? What does it mean when a car suddenly changes color?

__(b)__ The image below runs the same model with more cells. Rather than following one car, watch the red patches — regions where cars are stopped and bunched up. These red patches are __traffic jams__. Which direction does a traffic jam tend to move: the same way as the cars, or the opposite way? Explain why a jam moves that way.

__(c)__ In a model, a __variable__ changes on its own while the simulation runs (with no user input); a __parameter__ stays fixed during a run but can be changed between runs (the model resets when it changes); and a __constant__ is never allowed to change at all. The simulation has slider bars for the number of cars, the number of cells, and the value of $$p.$$ Are these sliders variables, parameters, or constants? Give an example of something in the model that is a variable instead.

label: I2P06
name: Traffic Jams, Phase Transitions, and a Parameter Space — We continue with the __Nagel-Schreckenberg__ traffic…
desc: We continue with the __Nagel-Schreckenberg__ traffic model: cars are colored circles on a loop of cells, color shows speed, cars slow to avoid collisions, and each car has probability $$p$$ of a random slowdown each timestep. Imagine you are a driver who cares how long the…
statement:
We continue with the __Nagel-Schreckenberg__ traffic model: cars are colored circles on a loop of cells, color shows speed, cars slow to avoid collisions, and each car has probability $$p$$ of a random slowdown each timestep. Imagine you are a driver who cares how long the commute will take. The phrase "traffic jam" has no precise definition, but a clearly computable quantity that addresses your concern is the __average speed of all the cars__. You can explore a version that reports it at https://glowscript.org/#/user/mark.d.eichenlaub/folder/AoPS/program/trafficrunningspeed .

__(a)__ If you watch the instantaneous average speed, it keeps jumping around from timestep to timestep, so instead we track the __long-term average speed__. Why is the long-term average a more useful measure of how well traffic is flowing? Suppose we want to plot how the average speed depends on the number of cars: which quantity belongs on the horizontal axis and which on the vertical, and why?

__(b)__ Below is the resulting plot of long-term average speed versus number of cars, with the number of cells fixed at $$100$$ and $$p = 0.1.$$ The curve is nearly flat for a while and then dips downward, with the bend occurring at about $$16$$ cars. What does the flat part of the curve tell you about traffic jams? When changing a parameter suddenly produces a big qualitative change in a model (such as going from no jams to jams), the change is called a __phase transition__. Identify the phase transition in this plot.

__(c)__ The plot above only describes the case of $$100$$ cells with $$p = 0.1.$$ The model actually has three things we can dial: the number of cars, the number of cells, and $$p.$$ We can picture these as three directions of a __three-dimensional parameter space__, and trying out many different parameter values is called __exploring the parameter space__. As $$p$$ is increased (more random slowdowns), do you expect the jam threshold — the number of cars at which jams start — to go up or down? Why? Finally, how could we show the effect of changing __both__ the number of cars and $$p$$ on a single plot?

label: I2P06
name: Bending Beams: Compression, Tension, and the I-Beam — A strand of DNA can be modeled as an __elastic rod__ —…
desc: A strand of DNA can be modeled as an __elastic rod__ — a ladder built from many little springs. The picture below shows such a row of springs. When the rod is bent, the springs must stretch or compress to accommodate the new shape, and Hooke's law (a spring's force is…
statement:
A strand of DNA can be modeled as an __elastic rod__ — a ladder built from many little springs. The picture below shows such a row of springs. When the rod is bent, the springs must stretch or compress to accommodate the new shape, and Hooke's law (a spring's force is proportional to how far it is stretched or compressed) applies to each one.

__(a)__ Suppose we bend the row of springs into a smile shape (curving upward, so the middle dips and the ends rise). Which springs get shorter, and which get longer? A spring that is squeezed shorter is under __compression__; a spring that is stretched longer is under __tension__. Identify which set of springs is under compression and which is under tension.

__(b)__ Now use the same spring picture for a wooden plank, which we want to lay between two supports to make a bridge. We can orient the plank either as a wide, flat __horizontal beam__ or turned on edge as a tall __vertical beam__. A beam is __strong__ if it takes a large downward load to bend it. Imagine bending each plank into the same arc. In which orientation are the springs stretched and compressed more, and therefore which orientation pushes back with more force and makes the stronger beam? Explain.

__(c)__ Beams that must support heavy loads are often built in the shape of a capital letter "I" — an __I-beam__, shown below. Using your spring picture, explain why concentrating most of the steel at the very top and very bottom (with only a thin web in the middle) makes a strong beam for a given amount of material.

label: I2P06
name: All Models Are Wrong: From Hooke's Law to the Wormlike Chain — Springs show up everywhere in physics: we…
desc: Springs show up everywhere in physics: we model a bouncing ball, a vehicle's suspension, the bond between two atoms, and the bending of DNA all using springs, with __Hooke's law__ $$|F| = k\,\Delta x$$ (force proportional to stretch). There is a famous saying in science: "all…
statement:
Springs show up everywhere in physics: we model a bouncing ball, a vehicle's suspension, the bond between two atoms, and the bending of DNA all using springs, with __Hooke's law__ $$|F| = k\,\Delta x$$ (force proportional to stretch). There is a famous saying in science: "all models are wrong, but some are useful."

For long strands of DNA, biophysicists often replace Hooke's law with a more sophisticated model called the __wormlike chain__ model. It begins with the elastic rod picture (DNA as a series of springs) and then adds a second force coming from the random jiggling of surrounding molecules. Because this random motion grows stronger at higher temperature, the second force depends on temperature. The plot below compares real measurements (the gray and blue markings are two sets of data) of the force a DNA molecule exerts versus its length against the wormlike-chain prediction (the red curve).

__(a)__ Would Hooke's law hold __exactly__ for a real spring? In light of the saying "all models are wrong, but some are useful," what is the actual purpose of a model — and why don't we try to make it a perfect copy of reality?

__(b)__ The wormlike chain combines two of the simpler models of DNA: the __elastic rod model__ (DNA as springs) and the __random walk model__ (segments of DNA pointing in random directions because molecules in the surrounding fluid strike it from all sides). Which physical effect does the random-walk piece add to the plain spring model, and how does that effect change with temperature? Over what range of distances do the springs dominate, and where does the random motion take over?

__(c)__ Hooke's law alone would predict a straight line on this force-versus-length plot, which fits the data poorly; the red wormlike-chain curve fits well. Yet the wormlike chain is much harder to work with — its formula is $$F \approx \left(\dfrac{z}{L} + \dfrac{1}{4(1 - z/L)^2} - \dfrac14\right)\dfrac{k_B T}{P},$$ where $$L$$ is the molecule's total length, $$z$$ the distance between its ends, $$T$$ the temperature, and $$k_B$$ and $$P$$ are constants. Describe the tradeoff a scientist faces in choosing between Hooke's law and the wormlike chain model.

label: I2P06
name: Estimating the Force of a Golf Club on a Ball — When a club strikes a golf ball, the ball squishes and…
desc: When a club strikes a golf ball, the ball squishes and rebounds much like a spring, so we can __model a golf ball as a spring__ and use Hooke's law, $$F = k\,\Delta x,$$ to estimate the force of the impact. Here $$k$$ is the ball's spring constant and $$\Delta x$$ is how far the…
statement:
When a club strikes a golf ball, the ball squishes and rebounds much like a spring, so we can __model a golf ball as a spring__ and use Hooke's law, $$F = k\,\Delta x,$$ to estimate the force of the impact. Here $$k$$ is the ball's spring constant and $$\Delta x$$ is how far the ball is compressed. By squeezing golf balls in a vise and measuring, scientists find a typical value $$k \approx 1.5\times 10^6\;\mathrm{N/m}.$$

__(a)__ The number $$k \approx 1.5\times 10^6\;\mathrm{N/m}$$ is more than a million newtons per meter — over $$100$$ tons per meter. Does this large spring constant mean the impact force is millions of newtons? Explain why or why not.

__(b)__ To get $$\Delta x$$ we need a real length scale, so we __calibrate__ the impact photo using the ball itself: a golf ball is about $$4\;\mathrm{cm}$$ in diameter. Looking at the most-compressed frame, the ball appears squished by about $$15\%$$ of its diameter. Find $$\Delta x$$ in meters.

__(c)__ Using your $$\Delta x$$ from part (b) and $$k \approx 1.5\times 10^6\;\mathrm{N/m},$$ estimate the force $$F$$ between the club and the ball. Round your answer to a single power of ten, since this is only a rough estimate.

__(d)__ Put your answer in perspective. The weight of an object is $$w = mg$$ with $$g \approx 10\;\mathrm{m/s^2},$$ so a $$1\;\mathrm{kg}$$ object weighs about $$10\;\mathrm{N}.$$ Roughly what mass has a weight equal to the impact force you found? Name an everyday object of about that size.

name: Testing Hooke's Law with a Slinky and Cans of Cat Food — Hooke's law models a spring as $$F = k\,\Delta x,$$…
desc: Hooke's law models a spring as $$F = k\,\Delta x,$$ where $$F$$ is the force the spring exerts, $$\Delta x$$ is how far it is stretched from its rest length, and $$k$$ is the spring constant. To test this model at home, an experimenter hangs a slinky over a staircase and ties a…
statement:
Hooke's law models a spring as $$F = k\,\Delta x,$$ where $$F$$ is the force the spring exerts, $$\Delta x$$ is how far it is stretched from its rest length, and $$k$$ is the spring constant. To test this model at home, an experimenter hangs a slinky over a staircase and ties a plastic bag to the bottom. They add identical cans of cat food to the bag one at a time, and after each can they measure $$h,$$ the distance from the floor up to the bottom of the bag. The data:

$$\begin{array}{cc} \text{cans} & h\,(\mathrm{cm}) \\ \hline 0 & 304 \\ 1 & 252 \\ 2 & 221 \\ 3 & 194 \\ 4 & 173 \\ 5 & 152 \\ 6 & 133 \\ 7 & 114 \\ 8 & 98 \\ 9 & 84 \end{array}$$

__(a)__ Why are identical cans of cat food a better choice for this experiment than, say, books pulled off a shelf? Using a force diagram for the hanging bag (gravity pulling down, the spring pulling up, with zero net force since the bag hangs still), explain why the spring's force is __directly proportional__ to the number of cans. Then explain why this proportionality is enough to test Hooke's law, even though we never measure the weight of a can or the spring constant $$k.$$

__(b)__ Because the force is proportional to the number of cans, we can use the weight of one can as our unit of force, the "__can weight__," so the force column is just $$0,1,2,\dots$$ The quantity $$\Delta x$$ is the stretch from the rest length — the length with __zero__ cans, where $$h = 304\;\mathrm{cm}.$$ So $$\Delta x = 304\;\mathrm{cm} - h.$$ Compute $$\Delta x$$ for the first three loads ($$1,$$ $$2,$$ and $$3$$ can weights).

__(c)__ If you plot force (in can weights) against $$\Delta x,$$ what shape should the graph be if Hooke's law holds exactly? When the experimenter actually does this, the points curve gently upward instead of following a single straight line. What does that curvature tell you about Hooke's law as a model of this slinky?

statement:
Everyone is affected differently by their physical environment. Some people work better in colder rooms, some warmer, some outside, some inside, some with barefeet, some with music, some with silence.

__The real voyage of discovery consists not in seeking new lands but seeing with new eyes. -Proust__

Marcel Proust, a French novelist, had an innovative working environment for his time. He suffered from allergies and he liked to work in quiet environments, but sound-proof rooms were difficult to find in the early 1900s. He constructed his room to be lined with cork, which acted as sound-proofing as well as filtered pollen and dust from the air.

In this discussion board, please respond to the following: -List the characteristics of the most supportive environment possible for problem solving for you. -Does your environment resemble this? If not, why not?

As you read through the discussion board, notice how other people like their environments. If changes to your personal working environment are practical, change it and see if it makes a difference in your productivity this week. It may or may not, but once you make changes, reflect on the outcome.

If you see an idea on the discussion board that you would like to try, be sure to respond to the person's post and let them know that you are going to try it and ask any follow-up questions that could help you.

statement:
Part A. The part of the moon that we see illuminated at a given time is called the __phase__ of the moon.

For example, we sometimes see half the moon brightly illuminated.

credit: NASA

Although half the moon is illuminated, astronomers call this a "quarter moon" because it means we are either one quarter or three quarters of the way through the cycle from new moon to full moon and back again.

In this multi-part problem, our goal is to figure out, just based on what we see when we look up at the moon, whether a half moon is waxing (meaning it's getting larger night after night and will become a full moon in about a week) or waning (getting smaller, will become a new moon in about a week). We also want to know approximately what times of day the quarter moon will be visible.

statement:
For your writing problem this week, you will focus on solving a problem similar to one you've already seen, then explaining your solution clearly.

In class, we found that when an ice cube melts in a cup of water, the level of the water in the cup stays the same. In this problem, we'll add a new twist to the same question.

Imagine two ice cubes. Ice cube A has an air pocket in the center of it.

Ice cube B has a small stone in the center of it. (The stone is more dense than water, but small enough that the entire ice cube still floats.)

If ice cube A is put into a glass of water and melts, what happens to the water level in the cup?

What about ice cube B?

Give complete explanations for what happens to the water level in both scenarios as the ice cubes melt. You can assume that the reader knows about the relationships between floating, displacement, mass, and density, and that when a solid ice cube with no impurities melts, the water level does not change.

name: The Balanced Broom — You hold a broom horizontally and try to balance it on one finger. If you put your…
desc: You hold a broom horizontally and try to balance it on one finger. If you put your finger at the exact middle of the handle, the broom tips. To make it balance, you have to slide your finger much closer to the brush end: Once you find the exact balance point, you saw the broom…
statement:
You hold a broom horizontally and try to balance it on one finger. If you put your finger at the exact middle of the handle, the broom tips. To make it balance, you have to slide your finger much closer to the brush end:

Once you find the exact balance point, you saw the broom in two right there, producing a long piece that is all handle and a short piece carrying the brush.

__(a)__ Why won't the broom balance with your finger at the exact middle of the handle?

__(b)__ The broom is closely related to a problem you may have seen before: a seesaw, where a small child can balance a heavy adult as long as the adult sits close to the pivot. The __law of the lever__ says a seesaw balances when the __moment of mass__ — the mass times the distance from the pivot, $$M \cdot x$$ — is the same on both sides. Match up the two problems: which parts of the broom setup play the roles of the seesaw's fulcrum, the far-away child, and the close-in adult?

__(c)__ Now the key question: which piece of the cut broom weighs more — the long handle piece, the short brush piece, or do they weigh the same since they "balanced"? Explain using the law of the lever.

__(d)__ When asked this question, many students answer that the two pieces must weigh the same. What correct instinct leads them to that answer — and what is the quantity that really __is__ equal on the two sides of your finger?

label: I2P07
name: Chasing the Sunset — In an episode of the TV show __Futurama__, two characters on the Moon run to stay in the…
desc: In an episode of the TV show __Futurama__, two characters on the Moon run to stay in the sunlight, because the line between lunar day and night — called the __terminator__ — is sweeping toward them, and night on the Moon is dangerously cold. Could a person really outrun the…
statement:
In an episode of the TV show __Futurama__, two characters on the Moon run to stay in the sunlight, because the line between lunar day and night — called the __terminator__ — is sweeping toward them, and night on the Moon is dangerously cold.

Could a person really outrun the terminator? That question sounds hard, so we break it into simpler ones — starting with the same question here on Earth. The drawing below shows Earth viewed from far away, looking straight along its rotation axis. Sunlight arrives from the left, so the half of Earth facing the Sun is in daylight and the shaded half is in night. The curved arrow shows the direction Earth rotates in this drawing. A stick figure named Kyra stands on the surface near the terminator. (The drawing is not to scale, which is fine for our purposes.)

__(a)__ What causes day to turn into night on Earth? If you could travel fast enough — say, in a very fast airplane — would it be possible, at least in principle, to escape nighttime entirely?

__(b)__ In the drawing, Earth rotates counterclockwise. Is Kyra about to be carried into the daylight or into the darkness? So what time of day is it for her: morning, high noon, late afternoon/evening, or midnight?

__(c)__ Since we are looking straight along Earth's rotation axis, we must be seeing either the Northern Hemisphere (looking down at the North Pole) or the Southern Hemisphere (looking up at the South Pole). Use the fact that the Sun rises in the east and sets in the west to figure out which hemisphere the drawing shows. (Hint: imagine Kyra facing out of the page, toward you. Which side of her is west?)

__(d)__ Which compass direction should Kyra travel to stay in the sunlight? Is it realistic to outrun the sunset on foot anywhere on Earth? What about in a commercial airliner? (For reference: a five-hour flight from New York, on the US East Coast, to San Francisco, on the West Coast, can take off at noon and land around 2 PM local time.)

label: I2P07
name: Running from the Terminator on the Moon — The __terminator__ is the line between day and night that sweeps…
desc: The __terminator__ is the line between day and night that sweeps across a rotating world. On Earth, near the equator, the terminator moves faster than an airliner — no one outruns the sunset. But could you outrun the terminator on the __Moon__, where night is two weeks of deadly…
statement:
The __terminator__ is the line between day and night that sweeps across a rotating world. On Earth, near the equator, the terminator moves faster than an airliner — no one outruns the sunset. But could you outrun the terminator on the __Moon__, where night is two weeks of deadly cold? To answer, we need two things: how long the Moon's day/night cycle is, and how big the Moon is. Remarkably, we can estimate both using observations available to ancient astronomers.

__(a)__ The Moon orbits Earth once every $$29.5\;\mathrm{days}$$ — close to one month (which is where the word "month" comes from). Because of __tidal locking__, the same side of the Moon always faces Earth: the Moon rotates exactly once per orbit. For an astronaut standing still on the Moon's surface, how long is one full day/night cycle, and about how long does the lunar night last?

__(b)__ To find the Moon's size we first need its distance, and the clue is the __lunar eclipse__: the Moon passing through Earth's shadow, as sketched below. Imagine two possible moons, one orbiting close to Earth and one orbiting far away, each taking exactly one month per orbit. Which moon moves at a faster speed? Which one crosses Earth's shadow in less time? So do __short__ eclipses indicate a close moon or a far one?

__(c)__ Earth's shadow is about as wide as Earth itself: $$12{,}800\;\mathrm{km}$$ across. A lunar eclipse lasts about $$3\;\mathrm{hr}$$ — the time the Moon takes to cross the shadow. About how fast does the Moon move along its orbit?

__(d)__ The Moon takes $$29.5\;\mathrm{days} \approx 708\;\mathrm{hr}$$ to complete one orbit. Use the speed from part (c) to find the circumference of the Moon's orbit, and then the distance from Earth to the Moon. (You may approximate $$2\pi \approx 6.$$)

__(e)__ Looking up at the Moon only tells us its __angular size__ — how big a piece of the sky it covers — not its true size. Held at arm's length, your thumb just barely blocks the Moon, and measuring your thumb and arm shows the Moon's angular size is about $$0.5^\circ.$$ That is $$\dfrac{1}{720}$$ of a full circle, so $$720$$ moons placed side by side would wrap all the way around the Moon's orbit. Estimate the diameter of the Moon.

__(f)__ To escape lunar night, you must circle the whole Moon — a distance of $$\pi D_{\rm Moon}$$ — once every lunar day/night cycle of $$708\;\mathrm{hr}.$$ How fast would you have to go to stay ahead of the terminator? Could a person actually run that fast?

label: I2P07
name: The Melting Ice Cube — An ice cube floats in a glass of water, with part of the cube sticking up above the…
desc: An ice cube floats in a glass of water, with part of the cube sticking up above the surface. As the ice melts, does the water level in the glass rise, fall, or stay the same? Two facts will help: things float when they are less dense than water (ice floats, so ice is less dense…
statement:
An ice cube floats in a glass of water, with part of the cube sticking up above the surface. As the ice melts, does the water level in the glass rise, fall, or stay the same? Two facts will help: things float when they are less dense than water (ice floats, so ice is less dense than liquid water), and when ice melts, its density increases — so the water it becomes takes up __less__ volume than the ice did.

__(a)__ Before analyzing, collect the competing intuitions: give one reason someone might expect the level to __rise__ as the ice melts, and one reason someone might expect it to __fall__.

__(b)__ Imagine doing the melting in three steps that end in the same final state: (1) lift the ice cube out of the water, leaving a "hole" where its underwater part used to be; (2) hold the cube above the glass while it melts; (3) let all the melt water run into the glass. Call the volume of the hole from step 1 — the volume of the cube that was below the waterline — the __displacement__, and call the volume of water the cube turns into the __melt volume__. In terms of these two volumes, when does the final water level end up higher than, lower than, or equal to the starting level?

__(c)__ Now a thought experiment. Invent a plastic block with exactly the same density as water and the same mass as the ice cube. It floats, but perfectly flush with the surface — nothing sticks out. Compare these volumes, explaining each comparison: (i) the block's displacement versus the ice cube's displacement; (ii) the block's volume versus the melt volume; (iii) therefore, the ice cube's displacement versus the melt volume.

__(d)__ So what happens to the water level as the floating ice cube melts? Check your answer against this time-lapse of ice melting in a glass (watch the level against the marked line):

__(e)__ Here is a longer version of the same time-lapse. Watching closely, the water level actually __rises__ during the first part of the video, and only holds steady in the second half. What is happening early in the video that our analysis didn't account for?

label: I2P07
name: Is Air Buoyancy Worth Including? An Estimate — A floating ice cube pokes up out of the water into the air —…
desc: A floating ice cube pokes up out of the water into the air — and air, like water, is a fluid that exerts a __buoyant force__ (that is what makes hot-air and helium balloons float). The buoyant force on an object equals the volume of fluid the object displaces times the density…
statement:
A floating ice cube pokes up out of the water into the air — and air, like water, is a fluid that exerts a __buoyant force__ (that is what makes hot-air and helium balloons float). The buoyant force on an object equals the volume of fluid the object displaces times the density of the fluid. When modeling whether the water level changes as a floating ice cube melts, should we include the buoyancy of the air? Physicists answer questions like this with an __estimate__: not a wild guess, but a quick calculation built from loose arguments, approximate values, and simplifications — sometimes called "ballparking." Whether an effect is worth including depends on how it compares to the precision of the measurement.

__(a)__ To estimate air's buoyancy we need the density of air. Rather than look it up, we estimate it from experience with balloons. Below is a deflated rubber balloon next to a pen for scale. Useful comparisons: a paperclip and a dollar bill each have a mass of about $$1\;\mathrm{g}.$$ Estimate the mass of the balloon.

__(b)__ Here is the same balloon inflated, about as large as it would need to be to float if it were filled with a very light gas. The balloon isn't a perfect sphere, but for an estimate, details of shape are among the first things to ignore: treat it as roughly a cube $$15\;\mathrm{cm}$$ on a side and estimate its volume.

__(c)__ A balloon filled with a very light gas just barely floats in air. That means the balloon's overall density — the rubber plus the nearly weightless gas inside — roughly matches the density of the surrounding air. Use your estimates from (a) and (b) to estimate the density of air in $$\mathrm{g/cm^3}.$$

__(d)__ Your answer to (c) looks like a small number — but any number can look large or small depending on the units. To judge it, compare it to a quantity relevant to the problem: the density of water, about $$1\;\mathrm{g/cm^3}.$$ Given that only about $$\dfrac{1}{10}$$ of a floating ice cube sticks up into the air, decide whether air buoyancy can safely be left out of the melting-ice-cube model.

__(e)__ Tiny isn't zero. Suppose we include air buoyancy in the model anyway. The air pushes up a little on the part of the cube above the waterline, so the water needs to push up a little less, and the cube floats slightly higher: its displacement (volume below the waterline) is slightly __smaller__ than in the no-air model, while the melt volume is unchanged. In this more accurate model, does the water level rise a tiny bit, fall a tiny bit, or stay exactly the same as the cube melts? (Recall: without air, the melt volume exactly equals the displacement and the level doesn't change.)

label: I2P07
name: The Golf Ball and the Detergent — A golf ball floats in a glass of salty water. (The salt is there to raise…
desc: A golf ball floats in a glass of salty water. (The salt is there to raise the water's density above the golf ball's density, so the ball floats.) Now we pour dish detergent on top. The detergent is __less__ dense than the golf ball — dropped straight into pure detergent, the…
statement:
A golf ball floats in a glass of salty water. (The salt is there to raise the water's density above the golf ball's density, so the ball floats.)

Now we pour dish detergent on top. The detergent is __less__ dense than the golf ball — dropped straight into pure detergent, the ball would sink — and the detergent does not mix with the water: it forms a layer floating on top of the water, surrounding the part of the ball that used to be in the air. A useful fact: the buoyant force from a fluid equals the volume displaced times the fluid's density, and even air exerts a (tiny) buoyant force on whatever pokes into it.

__(a)__ When the detergent layer is poured on, does the golf ball rise up a little, get pushed down a little, or stay put? (Hint: before the detergent arrived, what fluid touched the top of the ball, and how does the detergent compare to it?)

__(b)__ A technique called __extreme cases__ (or __special cases__) can make answers like this more intuitive: imagine the problem with some value pushed to its maximum, minimum, or another specially chosen value, and think the simpler problem through. In this problem, what is the largest the detergent's density could possibly be without fundamentally changing the situation — that is, what other density must it stay below?

__(c)__ Now run the extreme case as a __thought experiment__ — an experiment carried out in the imagination. Let the detergent's density be $$0.99999$$ times the ball's density, and let the water be twice the ball's density (so in plain water the ball would float exactly half submerged). Change the order of steps, too: pour the deep detergent layer over the water first, and only then drop in the golf ball. Describe what the ball does, and where it ends up.

__(d)__ Explain why the order of the steps doesn't affect the final position, and conclude what happens in the original experiment. Then check against the video (watch near the bottom of the ball):

label: I2P07
name: Archimedes and the Golden Crown — Archimedes was a Greek mathematician, physicist, engineer, astronomer, and…
desc: Archimedes was a Greek mathematician, physicist, engineer, astronomer, and inventor in the ancient city of Syracuse. According to a famous story, Hiero, the ruler of Syracuse, gave a goldsmith a block of gold to make into a crown. The finished crown had exactly the same mass as…
statement:
Archimedes was a Greek mathematician, physicist, engineer, astronomer, and inventor in the ancient city of Syracuse. According to a famous story, Hiero, the ruler of Syracuse, gave a goldsmith a block of gold to make into a crown. The finished crown had exactly the same mass as the original block — but Hiero suspected the goldsmith had mixed in cheaper silver and kept some of the gold for himself. He hired Archimedes to find out, on the condition that the crown must not be damaged. Useful facts: __density__ is mass per unit volume, and every material has its own density; gold is denser than silver; and the __displacement__ of an object in water is the volume of the part of the object below the surface.

__(a)__ Restating a problem and identifying its parts is the first step of problem solving. What are the givens — the things Hiero and Archimedes already know?

__(b)__ What property of the crown would expose the fraud if it could be measured, and what single missing measurement stands in the way? Why couldn't Archimedes just compute that quantity with a ruler, the way he could for the original block?

__(c)__ Stuck, Archimedes took a break and relaxed in a bath — and noticed that the more his body sank into the water, the more the water level rose. "Eureka!" For a __completely submerged__ object, what does the displacement equal, and how does that give a way to measure the crown's volume without damaging it?

__(d)__ Suppose the goldsmith really did mix silver into the crown while keeping its mass equal to the original block of gold. Would the dishonest crown's displacement, when completely submerged, be greater than, less than, or the same as the displacement of a solid gold crown of the same mass?

label: I2P07
name: How Long Will the World's Largest Iceberg Take to Melt? — In mid-May 2021, a piece of the Filchner-Ronne Ice…
desc: In mid-May 2021, a piece of the Filchner-Ronne Ice Shelf in Antarctica broke off, becoming the world's largest floating iceberg, A-76, with an area of about $$4320\;\mathrm{km^2}$$ — larger than Long Island, New York ($$3564\;\mathrm{km^2}$$). We want to estimate how long A-76…
statement:
In mid-May 2021, a piece of the Filchner-Ronne Ice Shelf in Antarctica broke off, becoming the world's largest floating iceberg, A-76, with an area of about $$4320\;\mathrm{km^2}$$ — larger than Long Island, New York ($$3564\;\mathrm{km^2}$$). We want to estimate how long A-76 would take to melt completely if it stayed in similar conditions.

__(a)__ No one has ever timed an iceberg this size, so we design an experiment with a model: time how long ice cubes of different sizes take to melt in water, under conditions resembling the ocean around the iceberg. Classify each of the following as the __independent variable__ (what the experimenter deliberately changes), the __dependent variable__ (what is measured as the outcome), or a __control variable__ (held the same across trials): ice cube size, time to melt, air temperature, water conditions.

__(b)__ The experiment was run, giving the data below. The graph shows the data with a best-fit line. What kind of relationship does the data show between ice cube length and time to melt? $$\begin{array}{c|c} \text{ice cube length (cm)} & \text{time to melt (min)} \\ \hline 1 & 1.67 \\ 2 & 3.19 \\ 3 & 4.67 \\ 4 & 6.32 \\ 5 & 7.83 \\ 6 & 10.27 \\ 7 & 11.60 \\ 8 & 12.73 \\ 9 & 14.67 \\ 10 & 16.03 \end{array}$$

__(c)__ The slope of the best-fit line is $$1.64\;\dfrac{\mathrm{min}}{\mathrm{cm}}.$$ Convert this slope into units better suited to an iceberg: days per kilometer. (There are $$100{,}000\;\mathrm{cm}$$ in a kilometer.)

__(d)__ The slope relates melting time to a __length__, but for the iceberg we only know its __area__. Physicists often simplify objects into easy shapes — you may have heard jokes about "spherical cows." Treat the iceberg's outline as a square: what is its edge length?

__(e)__ Physicists __extrapolate__ when they take a trend in their data and extend it beyond the range of the data. Extrapolate the melting trend to the iceberg's length to estimate how long A-76 would take to melt. Give the answer in days and in years.

__(f)__ Extrapolating this far beyond the data (from centimeters to tens of kilometers!) is extreme and often inaccurate. Name some places errors could come from in this estimate, and explain why even a careful prediction could be badly wrong.

statement:
Part A. In class, we estimated that while Bob Beamon was long jumping in the Mexico City Olympics, he jumped about $$0.1 \;\mathrm{m}$$ further than he would have at sea level because while he was in the airborne, he experienced less drag force in the thin air of Mexico City.

Remember that a long jump looks like this:

"Men's Long Jump Final | Tokyo Replays", Olympics, YouTube

The high elevation of Mexico City could have affected Beamon's long jump in at least three other ways:

**Thin air and running speed**

Long jumpers begin by running down a runway as fast as they can before they jump. Beamon ran through thin air, which reduced the drag force on him while running and affected his running speed, and therefore his jump distance.

**Tailwind** During Beamon's jump, there was a wind pushing at his back.

**Reduced gravity** Because Mexico City is at high elevation, it is further from the center of the Earth than a city at sea level and the same latitude. This means that the gravitational acceleration in Mexico City is a bit lower that in other places, which allows jumpers to stay in the air longer during their jump.

For each effect, decide whether it likely increased or decreased the distance that Beamon jumped.

It is possible that multiple effects in the left hand column will go to the same place in the right hand column. You should not assume the connections are one-to-one.

Part B. To continue our estimate surrounding Bob Beamon's long jump, we'll need a model for the long jump. Eventually, we will find the total distance the long jumper jumps, and this is the first step. In this part of the problem, we'll introduce a model. Your job is to think about the vertical motion of the long jumper in the model.

----------------

A simple model for the long jump is that first, an athlete runs as fast as they can down the runway, attaining a top speed of $$v_r.$$ This stage is called the "run up".

Next, at the end of the runway, the athlete leaps into the air. This stage is called the "takeoff". During the takeoff, the athlete's goal is to jump up as high as possible. They have already attained their top horizontal speed and can't run any faster, so they don't think about adding horizontal speed during the takeoff. Instead, they maintain the same horizontal speed while adding as much vertical speed as they can. We will assume that during takeoff, the athlete jumps upward with a speed $$v_j.$$

In this model, when the athlete jumps into the air, they are moving diagonally upward and forward. They still have a forward speed $$v_r$$ from their run, and they have an upward speed $$v_j$$ from their jump.

During the jump, we can analyze the athlete's horizontal and vertical motions separately. While in the air, the athlete moves forward with constant speed $$v_r.$$ In the vertical direction, the athlete begins with upward speed $$v_j,$$ but gravity pulls downward on the athlete, reducing their vertical speed down to zero at the height of the jump, and then down to $$-v_j$$ when the athlete hits the ground.

To find the total distance of the jump, we can consider how fast the athlete moved forward and how long they were in the air.

Part E. Now that we have a model of the long jump, we can estimate how much the conditions in Mexico City affected Beamon's jump.

In Mexico City, $$g \approx 9.78 \;\mathrm{m/s^2},$$ but at most sea level cities, $$g \approx 9.81 \;\mathrm{m/s^2}.$$ As we mentioned earlier, the lower value of $$g$$ allowed Beamon to stay in the air longer.

We will ignore any possible influence of $$g$$ on Beamon's running speed. Remember that Beamon jumped $$8.90 \;\mathrm{m}.$$

With that assumption, how much extra distance did Beamon jump due to the lower value of $$g$$ in Mexico City?

Part F. In this part, we'll estimate how the thin air and tailwind affected Beamon's running speed, and therefore his jump distance.

It is difficult to estimate how much faster an athlete can run due to reduced air drag or a tailwind because the forces involved in running are quite complicated. By studying data from sprinting competitions, scientists have found that running $$100 \;\mathrm{m}$$ in $$10.0 \;\mathrm{s}$$ at the altitude of Mexico City with a $$2.0 \;\mathrm{m/s}$$ tailwind is equivalent to running $$100 \;\mathrm{m}$$ in $$10.15 \;\mathrm{s}$$ at sea level with no tailwind.

Assuming this is correct and that Beamon was running at a speed of about $$10 \;\mathrm{m/s},$$ how much did the conditions of his long jump increase his jump distance due to increasing his running speed, compared to what he could have done if jumping at sea level and without a tailwind?

name: We saw in the reading that stars like the sun cannot run on chemical energy. If they did…
desc: We saw in the reading that stars like the sun cannot run on chemical energy. If they did, we estimated that they would burn through all their fuel within a few thousand years. Stars run on nuclear energy. In the sun, this is almost entirely the energy given off when hydrogen…
statement:
We saw in the reading that stars like the sun cannot run on chemical energy. If they did, we estimated that they would burn through all their fuel within a few thousand years.

Stars run on nuclear energy. In the sun, this is almost entirely the energy given off when hydrogen fuses together to form helium.

By measuring its gravity, we know that the mass of the sun is approximately, $$m_{\rm sun} \approx 2 \times 10^{30} \;\mathrm{kg}.$$

The mass of a single hydrogen atom is $$m_{\rm H} \approx 1.7 \times 10^{-27} \;\mathrm{kg},$$ and every time two hydrogen atoms fuse to make one helium atom, they give off about $$2.3 \times 10^{-13} \;\mathrm{J}$$ of energy.

In the prereading, we saw that the rate that the sun gives off energy, called the sun's __power__, is about $$3.6 \times 10^{26} \;\mathrm{J/s}.$$

Estimate the lifetime of the sun based on this information, assuming it will burn all its hydrogen into helium and then die, and assuming that it will continue shining at the same brightness that it does now for its entire life. You can assume that the sun began as pure hydrogen.

mathjax: $$ \blank \times 10^{\blank} \;\mathrm{year} $$

label: I2P08
name: Part A. We've already studied the question: "What is the terminal velocity of an object…
desc: Part A. We've already studied the question: "What is the terminal velocity of an object falling through air?" If we wanted to measure terminal velocity, we could see how far something falls, measure how long that takes, and divide to get the terminal velocity. On the other hand…
statement:
Part A. We've already studied the question: "What is the terminal velocity of an object falling through air?"

If we wanted to measure terminal velocity, we could see how far something falls, measure how long that takes, and divide to get the terminal velocity.

On the other hand, that method would fail if the object were still accelerating up to its terminal velocity when we took the measurement. To measure terminal velocity, we want to drop something, let it fall until it reaches its terminal velocity (or gets very close to it), and only then begin measuring distance and time for the rest of the fall.

To help with this, in this problem we'll address a different question:

"How far does an object have to fall through the air before it reaches its terminal velocity?"

We know that when we let something go, gravity pulls it to the ground. The speed of the object gets faster and faster as it falls. The rate that the speed increases is the object's __acceleration__. As we've seen, the acceleration of objects dropped near the surface of Earth (ignoring any wind drag) is $$g \approx 10 \;\mathrm{m/s^2}.$$

Assuming there is no air drag, the speed is $$|v| = gt,$$ where $$t$$ is the time the object has been falling.

We've already estimated the terminal velocity to be $$|v_{\rm terminal}| \approx \sqrt{\dfrac{2 mg}{\rho A}}.$$

(We have left $$C_D$$ out of this equation because we estimated that it was close to $$1,$$ and so doesn't have much effect.)

As a simple model, assume that an object that has dropped follows the equation $$|v| = gt$$ until it reaches terminal velocity. This is not completely accurate, but okay for our estimation. Combine $$|v| = gt$$ and $$v_{\rm terminal} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2 mg}{\rho A}}$$ to estimate the time it takes a falling object to reach terminal velocity.

Next, multiply the terminal velocity by the time you just found. This gives an estimate for the distance $$d$$ something needs to fall before reaching a speed close to its terminal velocity. You should get an equation for $$d$$ in terms of $$m, \rho, A, C_D,$$ and $$g.$$

Find this equation, then use it to estimate how far a piece of notebook paper needs to fall through air before approximately reaching its terminal velocity.

mathjax: $$ \blank \;\mathrm{cm} $$

Part B. One common byproduct of doing an estimate is that you learn something new about physics. This could happen when, during an estimate, you derive a new equation. Then you could try to make sense of what the equation says, and in that way, understand the situation you were estimating in a new way.

For example, in part (A), we estimated the distance $$d$$ something needs to fall before its speed is close to terminal velocity. Imagine a student is working on that problem and finds the equation $$d \rho A \approx m.$$

As a reminder, $$A$$ is the cross sectional area of the object and $$\rho$$ is the density of air.

On the right hand side of the equation, $$m$$ is the mass of the object.

The student could plug in numbers to this equation to get an estimate for $$d,$$ but they could also pause, examine the equation, and come up with an interpretation for it.

Which one of the following is a reasonable interpretation of this equation?

$$\mathbf{(a)}$$ An object needs to fall until the total mass of air it has fallen through is similar to its own mass before it is close to terminal velocity.

$$\mathbf{(b)}$$ Increasing air density in an experiment will increase the mass of objects you use in that experiment.

$$\mathbf{(c)}$$ Objects fall faster and faster until gravity stops pulling on them.

$$\mathbf{(d)}$$ Air drag is not significant if the density of an object is high.
