label: I2P08
name: Dividing Up Earth's Land — A 2022 report from the United Nations projected that the world population could…
desc: A 2022 report from the United Nations projected that the world population could grow about $$50\%,$$ from around $$8$$ billion people in 2022 to about $$12$$ billion by 2090. Feeding, housing, and supplying resources to that many people is a major challenge, and it leads to a…
statement:
A 2022 report from the United Nations projected that the world population could grow about $$50\%,$$ from around $$8$$ billion people in 2022 to about $$12$$ billion by 2090. Feeding, housing, and supplying resources to that many people is a major challenge, and it leads to a natural question: if we took all the land on Earth and divided it up evenly between all the people, how much land would each person get? That's hard to guess off the top of your head, so we break the problem into pieces: first estimate the total land area of Earth, then the number of people, then divide.

Useful facts: the radius of Earth is about $$R_{\rm Earth} \approx 6{,}000\;\mathrm{km}.$$ The surface area of a sphere of radius $$R$$ is $$A = 4\pi R^2.$$ Only about $$30\%$$ of Earth's surface is land — the rest is water. The current population of Earth is about $$N_{\rm Earth} \approx 8 \times 10^9$$ people.

__(a)__ The formula $$A = 4\pi R^2$$ gives the total surface area of Earth. Will using it directly overestimate or underestimate the __land__ area? Estimate the land area $$A_{\rm land}$$ of Earth, rounding numbers as you go to keep the arithmetic easy (for example, take $$\pi \approx 3$$).

__(b)__ If all the land on Earth were divided evenly among all the people alive today, how much land would each person get? Give your answer in $$\mathrm{km}^2$$ per person.

__(c)__ An answer written in powers of ten can be hard to picture. Useful comparisons: $$2 \times 10^{-2}\;\mathrm{km}^2$$ is about $$5$$ acres, a square about $$140\;\mathrm{m}$$ on a side, or roughly twice the size of a major league baseball field. Is each person's share more or less land than you expected? Name some things besides growing food that this land has to provide for each person.

__(d)__ Land suitable for growing crops is called __arable land__, and only about $$10\%$$ of the world's land is arable. Estimate how much arable land there would be per person if the population grows to $$12$$ billion.

label: I2P08
name: Benjamin Franklin Measures a Molecule — Today scientists can measure the position of every atom in a molecule…
desc: Today scientists can measure the position of every atom in a molecule using electron microscopes and x-ray diffractometers. But in 1774, Benjamin Franklin estimated the size of molecules with no modern equipment at all. He poured one teaspoon of olive oil onto the surface of a…
statement:
Today scientists can measure the position of every atom in a molecule using electron microscopes and x-ray diffractometers. But in 1774, Benjamin Franklin estimated the size of molecules with no modern equipment at all. He poured one teaspoon of olive oil onto the surface of a large pond in Clapham, London. Oil doesn't mix with water and is less dense than water, so the oil spread out into a thin patch floating on the pond's surface.

Franklin couldn't see the oil itself. The photos below show a pond surface like the one he watched: on the left, water rippled by wind; on the right, part of the surface after oil has spread over it.

Franklin wrote: "... the oil, though not more than a teaspoonful, produced an instant calm over a space several yards square, which spread amazingly, and extending itself gradually till it reached the leeside, making all that quarter of the pond, perhaps half an acre, as smooth as a looking-glass." Half an acre is a square about $$45\;\mathrm{m}$$ on a side — a bit bigger than an Olympic-sized swimming pool. A teaspoon of oil has a volume of about $$V \approx 5\;\mathrm{cm}^3.$$

__(a)__ Franklin could not see the oil directly. How did he know where the oil patch was and how big it had grown?

__(b)__ Like a lump of dough being rolled out, the oil covers more area by getting thinner. Model the patch as a flat layer with __uniform__ thickness $$h$$ and area $$A,$$ so its volume is $$V = Ah.$$ Estimate $$A$$ in $$\mathrm{cm}^2.$$ (Careful: $$1\;\mathrm{m}^2$$ is not $$100\;\mathrm{cm}^2.$$)

__(c)__ Estimate the thickness $$h$$ of Franklin's oil layer, in centimeters and in nanometers ($$1\;\mathrm{nm} = 10^{-7}\;\mathrm{cm}$$).

__(d)__ Franklin wondered why the oil stopped spreading instead of thinning out until it covered the whole pond (or, in the ocean, the whole ocean). What assumption about the oil layer lets the thickness from part (c) serve as an estimate of the size of a single oil molecule?

__(e)__ Olive oil is mostly __oleic acid__, a fat molecule whose structure is shown below: the gray balls are carbon atoms, the white are hydrogen, and the red are oxygen. The distance between adjacent carbon atoms is about $$0.15\;\mathrm{nm},$$ and the chain contains $$17$$ carbon-carbon bonds. About how long is an oleic acid molecule, and how does Franklin's 1774 estimate compare?

label: I2P08
name: The Terminal Velocity of a Sheet of Paper — A falling object speeds up until the air drag force on it…
desc: A falling object speeds up until the air drag force on it balances gravity; after that it falls at a steady speed called its __terminal velocity__. Balancing the drag force against gravity gives the formula $$|v_{\rm terminal}| = \sqrt{\dfrac{2mg}{C_D \rho A}},$$ where $$m$$ is…
statement:
A falling object speeds up until the air drag force on it balances gravity; after that it falls at a steady speed called its __terminal velocity__. Balancing the drag force against gravity gives the formula $$|v_{\rm terminal}| = \sqrt{\dfrac{2mg}{C_D \rho A}},$$ where $$m$$ is the object's mass, $$A$$ is its cross-sectional area, $$g$$ is the acceleration due to gravity, $$\rho$$ is the density of air, and $$C_D$$ is the drag coefficient, a number near $$1$$ for most blunt objects.

An earlier estimate found that a skydiver, with mass $$m \approx 80\;\mathrm{kg}$$ and cross-sectional area $$A \approx 0.5\;\mathrm{m}^2,$$ has a terminal velocity of about $$50\;\mathrm{m/s}.$$

Use that result to estimate the terminal velocity of a single sheet of notebook paper falling flat. A sheet of paper has mass $$m \approx 5\;\mathrm{g} = 5\times 10^{-3}\;\mathrm{kg}$$ and area $$8.5\;\mathrm{in} \times 11\;\mathrm{in} \approx 100\;\mathrm{in}^2 \approx 6\times 10^{-2}\;\mathrm{m}^2.$$

__(a)__ Which of the quantities $$m, g, C_D, \rho, A$$ in the terminal velocity formula are (approximately) the same for the paper as for the skydiver, and which are different? Use your answer to explain why, when comparing the two, $$|v_{\rm terminal}| \propto \sqrt{\dfrac{m}{A}}.$$

__(b)__ Approximately how many times bigger is the ratio $$\dfrac{m}{A}$$ for the skydiver than for the paper?

__(c)__ Use proportional reasoning — not a fresh calculation from the full formula — to estimate the paper's terminal velocity. Your answer only needs to be right __to order of magnitude__, that is, within a factor of $$10.$$ Why is this estimate much easier to test at home than the skydiver estimate?

label: I2P08
name: Did Thin Air Set the Long-Jump Record? — In 1968, Bob Beamon of the USA broke the world record in the long…
desc: In 1968, Bob Beamon of the USA broke the world record in the long jump while winning Olympic gold in Mexico City: he jumped $$8.90\;\mathrm{m},$$ beating Ralph Boston's previous record of $$8.35\;\mathrm{m}$$ by what sports fans considered a huge margin. Mexico City sits at high…
statement:
In 1968, Bob Beamon of the USA broke the world record in the long jump while winning Olympic gold in Mexico City: he jumped $$8.90\;\mathrm{m},$$ beating Ralph Boston's previous record of $$8.35\;\mathrm{m}$$ by what sports fans considered a huge margin. Mexico City sits at high altitude, where the air is thin, so Beamon felt less air drag while airborne than he would have at sea level. How much did the thin air help him — and would he still have broken the record at sea level?

While airborne, a long jumper is a __projectile__ — an object in motion pulled primarily by gravity. Air drag pushes backward on the jumper, shortening the jump, but only a little: a long jump modeled without air resistance looks pretty much like a real long jump, so we are estimating a fairly small effect. The drag force has magnitude $$|F_{\rm drag}| = \dfrac12 C_D \rho A v^2,$$ where $$C_D \approx 1$$ is the drag coefficient, $$A \approx 0.5\;\mathrm{m}^2$$ is the jumper's cross-sectional area, $$\rho$$ is the density of air, and $$v$$ is the jumper's speed. The air density is $$\rho \approx 1.2\;\mathrm{kg/m^3}$$ at sea level but only $$\rho \approx 1.0\;\mathrm{kg/m^3}$$ in Mexico City. Here is what an Olympic long jump looks like:

__(a)__ For a projectile in general, which conditions make air resistance __less__ important: high or low projectile mass? traveling a long or a short distance? high or low air density? Briefly explain each.

__(b)__ Elite long jumpers are very fast runners — some compete as sprinters too, and professional male sprinters run $$100\;\mathrm{m}$$ in about $$10\;\mathrm{s}.$$ Estimate Beamon's speed $$v$$ during the jump.

__(c)__ Estimate the drag force on Beamon while jumping in Mexico City. Carry the units through the calculation, and express the result in newtons ($$1\;\mathrm{N} = 1\;\mathrm{kg\,m/s^2}$$).

__(d)__ Without redoing the whole calculation, use the proportionality $$|F_{\rm drag}| \propto \rho$$ to find the drag force he would have felt at sea level, and then the extra force $$|\Delta F|$$ that the thin air spared him.

__(e)__ A force of size $$F$$ applied for a time $$t$$ to an object of mass $$m$$ pushes it a distance $$\ell = \dfrac12 \dfrac{F t^2}{m}.$$ Estimate the duration $$t$$ of Beamon's jump from his jump distance and his running speed, take his mass to be $$m \approx 70\;\mathrm{kg}$$ (a reasonable mass for an adult male athlete), and estimate how much extra jump distance the thin air gave Beamon.

__(f)__ Compare your answer to the $$0.55\;\mathrm{m}$$ by which Beamon beat the old record. Would he have broken the record at sea level anyway? Professional track and field measures jumps down to $$0.01\;\mathrm{m}$$ — at that level of precision, does air drag matter?

label: I2P08
name: Blades of Grass on a Baseball Field — How many blades of grass are contained in an American baseball field?…
desc: How many blades of grass are contained in an American baseball field? An estimate like this breaks into two pieces: the area of the field, and the number of blades of grass per unit area. __(a)__ A square about $$140\;\mathrm{m}$$ on a side has roughly the area of __two__…
statement:
How many blades of grass are contained in an American baseball field? An estimate like this breaks into two pieces: the area of the field, and the number of blades of grass per unit area.

__(a)__ A square about $$140\;\mathrm{m}$$ on a side has roughly the area of __two__ baseball fields. Use that fact to estimate the area of one baseball field in square meters. (Careful: cutting a square's side length in half cuts its area by a factor of four, not two.)

__(b)__ The photo below shows a baseball lying in grass. A baseball is about $$7\;\mathrm{cm}$$ in diameter, which gives the photo a natural __scale__. Use the photo to estimate the number of blades of grass per square meter of field. Watch the units: explain why the answer comes out in $$\mathrm{blades/m^2}$$ rather than $$\mathrm{blades^2/m^2}.$$

__(c)__ Combine parts (a) and (b) to estimate the total number of blades of grass on the field. Which part of the estimate carries the most uncertainty, and what real-world features of baseball parks keep this answer from ever being pinned down precisely?

name: Filling a School Bus from a Faucet — How long would a kitchen faucet have to run to fill an entire school bus…
desc: How long would a kitchen faucet have to run to fill an entire school bus with water? This estimate breaks into two pieces: the volume of a school bus, and the flow rate of a faucet. __(a)__ When estimating the volume of a complicated shape, it often works well to model it as a…
statement:
How long would a kitchen faucet have to run to fill an entire school bus with water? This estimate breaks into two pieces: the volume of a school bus, and the flow rate of a faucet.

__(a)__ When estimating the volume of a complicated shape, it often works well to model it as a rectangular prism (a box) with some length $$\ell,$$ width $$w,$$ and height $$h,$$ as in the sketch below. Most people can stand upright inside a school bus, but a very tall person might not; a bus is somewhat wider than it is tall; and walking down the aisle takes roughly ten big strides. Use observations like these to estimate the volume of a school bus in $$\mathrm{m}^3.$$

__(b)__ You probably don't have a faucet's flow rate memorized, but you have filled bottles from a tap: filling a $$1$$-liter bottle takes about $$10\;\mathrm{s}.$$ Find the faucet's flow rate in liters per second, then convert it to $$\mathrm{m^3/h}.$$ (Useful facts: $$1\;\mathrm{h} = 3600\;\mathrm{s}$$ and $$1\;\mathrm{m}^3 = 1000\;\mathrm{L}.$$)

__(c)__ Estimate how long the faucet must run to fill the bus. Give your answer in hours, and also translate it into everyday terms (days or weeks).

statement:
Part A. In our estimation class, we introduced the idea of __pressure__ as a crushing force per unit area, pushing in from all sides. In SI, pressure is measured in __pascal__, $$\mathrm{Pa}.$$ The pascal is defined so that $$1 \;\mathrm{Pa} = 1 \dfrac{\mathrm{N}}{\mathrm{m}^2}.$$

(Remember that $$\mathrm{N}$$ is the symbol for the __newton__, the SI unit for force.)

This problem is broken into several parts. By the end, we will try to get a better understanding of pressure in fluids like water and air and use this to investigate a question we asked earlier: "How high is the atmosphere?" Along the way, we'll build models and compare them to real data.

To begin, imagine a student has begun using this simulation to measure the pressure at different depths under the surface of water. Inside the simulation, they kept gravity at its default value of $$9.8 \;\mathrm{m/s^2}$$ and fluid density at its default of $$1000 \;\mathrm{kg/m^3}$$

In the simulation, you can use the pressure meter to find the pressure at any point in the water. You can also adjust the quantity of water and turn on both a ruler that can be dragged around and a grid to help with measurements. These features are illustrated below The meter measures the pressure at the depth indicated by the red arrowsthe left and right of the meter. (The bottom of the meter or the top of the meter would be a slightly different pressure because they're at different depths.)

**Finish the student's data table, keeping the same number of significant figures they used.**

Be careful with your measurements; zooming in can help.

Part D. The student had heard that in physics, water and air are both considered __fluids__. (Although air is a gas and water is a liquid, "fluid" can refer to either gases or liquids in physics.)

Having already modeled the pressure under water, the student "conjectured" means "guessed" that essentially the same model could work for the atmosphere. They wanted to use a modified version of their water pressure model to estimate the height of the atmosphere.

To model pressure in the atmosphere, the student kept nearly the same equation, but changed $$\rho_{\rm water}$$ to $$\rho_{\rm air}.$$

They also had changed the variable $$d$$ to $$-h.$$ This is because $$d$$ represented a __depth__, which increases as we go further down. The student was interested in the __height__, which increases as we go further up. The minus sign reflects how depth and height increase in opposite directions.

Use the message board to share your ideas and respond to your classmates' ideas.

Also, the problem is not with the simulation we used. The linear model from the simulation works very well on real data taken underwater, but not very well on real data from the atmosphere.

label: I2P09
name: Part A. If you look at the stars in the night sky, you may notice that they are different…
desc: Part A. If you look at the stars in the night sky, you may notice that they are different colors. In this multipart problem, we'll study why stars are different colors and how those colors can be modeled. We know from the previous class that the energy stars give off comes from…
statement:
Part A. If you look at the stars in the night sky, you may notice that they are different colors. In this multipart problem, we'll study why stars are different colors and how those colors can be modeled.

We know from the previous class that the energy stars give off comes from nuclear fusion in the star. Fusion reactions happen deep in the core of the star. We can't observe them directly, and the light given off by those reactions never reaches us because it all gets absorbed by the outer layers of the star.

The light we see from the star is the glowing of the outer layers of the star due to its temperature. This phenomenon is called __black-body radiation__ (even though stars are not black). Everything gives off black-body radiation. The colder something is, the longer the Light travels through space as a wave. The wavelength $$\lambda$$ of a wave is the distance between any two of its peaks of the blackbody radiation it gives off. We normally use $$\lambda,$$ lower case Greek lambda, as the variable for a wavelength.

Measuring the wavelength of light coming off an object lets us determine its temperature. Red light has the longest wavelength we can see, and red stars are the coolest stars we can see. White stars are hotter and blue stars are even hotter.

Imagine that, in an experiment on black-body radiation, a scientist collected the data on temperature and Black bodies give off light at many wavelengths simultaneously. Here, we're reporting the approximate wavelength where the object gives off the most light. wavelength of a hot glowing body.

\begin{tabular}{|r|r|} \text{temperature } $$(10^3 \;\mathrm{K})$$ & \text{peak wavelength} $$(10^2 \;\mathrm{nm})$$ \\ \hline $$1.0$$ & $$29$$ \\ $$2.0$$ & $$14$$ \\ $$3.0$$ & $$9.7$$ \\ $$4.0$$ & $$7.2$$ \\ $$5.0$$ & $$5.8$$ \\ $$6.0$$ & $$4.8$$ \\ $$7.0$$ & $$4.1$$ \\ $$8.0$$ & $$3.6$$ \end{tabular}

Which of the following is a good description of this data? Choose two total: one of (a) or (b) and one of (c) or (d).

Peak wavelength increases with temperature.

Peak wavelength decreases with temperature.

The relationship is approximately linear.

The relationship is not close to linear.

Part B. As we saw in part (A), the color of light can be described by its wavelength, but another description is via the light's __frequency__ $$f.$$

Frequency is the rate at which peaks of a wave pass a given point. In the above animation, we see an illustration of a wave moving, and a pendulum has been synced up to the wave. The pendulum oscillates $$25$$ full trips in $$60 \;\mathrm{s}.$$ That makes the frequency of both the pendulum and the wave $$\begin{aligned} f &= \dfrac{25}{60 \;\mathrm{s}} \\[6pt] &\approx 0.42 \;\mathrm{s}^{-1}. \end{aligned}$$

Frequency can be measured in the unit __hertz__, which has the symbol $$\mathrm{Hz}.$$ The definition is $$1 \;\mathrm{Hz} = 1 \;\mathrm{s}^{-1}.$$

The frequency of the wave in the GIF can be written $$f = 0.42 \;\mathrm{Hz}.$$

The frequency in hertz is the number of wave peaks that pass any given point in one second. Soon, we will use the frequency of light to take a second look at the blackbody radiation data, but first let's orient ourselves to the relationship between frequency and wavelength.

Imagine a wave that always has the same wavelength, but can travel either at high speed or at low speed. When would it have higher frequency?

Part F. The relationship between temperature and frequency of the peak wavelength of light coming off a star was discovered empirically by American astronomer Samuel Langley. Langley had no theory behind the relationship, though.

Using your data table from the previous problem, plot the frequency versus temperature of a star, with frequency on the vertical and temperature on the horizontal. Find a best fit line. This line has a slope, which Langley could have found. What is the slope of the line?

Part G. German physicist Max Planck built a theory of black body radiation and used it to help start the field of __quantum mechanics__.

Planck's theory predicted: $$f_{\rm peak} = 2.821 \dfrac{k_B T}{h}.$$

In this formula, $$f_{\rm peak}$$ is the peak frequency of radiation coming from a black body like a star or the one in the experiment we've been analyzing. $$k_B$$ is a constant from thermodynamics that allows scientists to convert from temperatures to energies. In Planck's time, it was known to be $$k_B \approx 1.38 \times 10^{-23} \;\mathrm{m^2 \cdot kg \cdot s^{-2} \cdot K^{-1}}.$$

Based on your analysis of the temperature and frequency data, what value does this experiment give for $$h?$$

label: I2P09
name: Lighting a Bulb: Closed Circuits — Physicists often want to know how one factor affects another: how do the…
desc: Physicists often want to know how one factor affects another: how do the materials chosen affect a structure's strength? How does a star's distance affect its brightness? How does a gas's temperature affect its volume? To practice answering questions like these with data and…
statement:
Physicists often want to know how one factor affects another: how do the materials chosen affect a structure's strength? How does a star's distance affect its brightness? How does a gas's temperature affect its volume? To practice answering questions like these with data and graphs, we start with electric circuits. You can experiment with the same circuit-building simulation we used at https://phet.colorado.edu/sims/html/circuit-construction-kit-dc-virtual-lab/latest/circuit-construction-kit-dc-virtual-lab_en.html — drag batteries, wires, and light bulbs from the supply area into the work area and connect them by pulling their ends toward each other.

A battery pushes electrons through a circuit. The strength of that push is the battery's __voltage__, for which we use the variable $$U.$$ Voltage is measured in __volts__ $$(\mathrm{V}).$$ An ordinary household battery supplies only about $$U = 1.5\;\mathrm{V}.$$

__(a)__ Four circuits are shown below, labeled (A) through (D). Which of them will light up the light bulb?

__(b)__ In a circuit that does work, describe the path the electrons follow, starting from the black end of the battery. Use your description to explain why the failing circuit(s) in part (a) fail.

__(c)__ In the simulation, it is possible to make a wire or bulb catch fire, like this:

Once you have a working circuit, what could you change to start a fire like this one?

label: I2P09
name: Designing the Current-versus-Voltage Experiment — A class ran a shared experiment in the circuit simulation…
desc: A class ran a shared experiment in the circuit simulation at https://phet.colorado.edu/sims/html/circuit-construction-kit-dc-virtual-lab/latest/circuit-construction-kit-dc-virtual-lab_en.html. Each student built the same simple circuit — one battery, wires, and the standard…
statement:
A class ran a shared experiment in the circuit simulation at https://phet.colorado.edu/sims/html/circuit-construction-kit-dc-virtual-lab/latest/circuit-construction-kit-dc-virtual-lab_en.html. Each student built the same simple circuit — one battery, wires, and the standard light bulb — and inserted an __ammeter__. An ammeter measures __electric current__: the rate at which electrons run through it. Current uses the variable $$I$$ and is measured in the SI unit the __ampere__ $$(\mathrm{A}),$$ often abbreviated "amps." Increasing the battery voltage $$U$$ makes the electrons move faster, so more electrons pass any point each second and $$I$$ increases. For an ammeter to work, the current must run through it, so the circuit has to be broken open and the ammeter inserted, like this (here it reads $$0.9\;\mathrm{A}$$):

Each student then set their battery's voltage to ten times their birth-month number (a student born in March, month $$3,$$ used $$30\;\mathrm{V}$$), measured the current, and recorded the pair $$(U, I).$$ Everyone was told to use the same type of light bulb, but students used whatever lengths of wire they liked.

__(a)__ In an experiment, the __independent variable__ is the one the experimenter directly changes; the __dependent variable__ is the one measured to see how it responds; and a __control variable__ is one deliberately kept the same in every trial. Classify each of these as independent, dependent, or control: the electric current, the battery voltage, the type of light bulb. When the class combines everyone's data into one plot, which variable should go on which axis?

__(b)__ Did the class treat the length of wire as a control variable? If wire length did affect the current, what would happen to the class's combined data? What is an uncontrolled variable like this called?

__(c)__ In 2012, the OPERA collaboration (a group of particle physicists studying very light subatomic particles called neutrinos) announced they had measured neutrinos moving faster than the speed of light — something physicists had thought impossible. What do you think happened next: did scientists try to find a mistake in the measurement, try to find a theoretical explanation, or simply accept the result? How does this story connect to part (b)?

label: I2P09
name: Conductance: The Slope of the Current Graph — In a simulated circuit experiment, each student in a class…
desc: In a simulated circuit experiment, each student in a class connected one battery to the same type of light bulb, set the battery's voltage $$U$$ to a multiple of $$10\;\mathrm{V}$$ between $$10\;\mathrm{V}$$ and $$120\;\mathrm{V},$$ and used an ammeter to measure the current…
statement:
In a simulated circuit experiment, each student in a class connected one battery to the same type of light bulb, set the battery's voltage $$U$$ to a multiple of $$10\;\mathrm{V}$$ between $$10\;\mathrm{V}$$ and $$120\;\mathrm{V},$$ and used an ammeter to measure the current $$I$$ through the bulb. When the class plotted everyone's data — current $$I$$ in amperes on the vertical axis, voltage $$U$$ in volts on the horizontal axis — the points fell on a straight line through the origin. For example, $$U = 120.0\;\mathrm{V}$$ produced $$I = 12.00\;\mathrm{A}.$$

__(a)__ The slope of a line is $$\dfrac{\text{rise}}{\text{run}}$$ between any two points on it. What units does the slope of this graph carry? Compute the slope using the points $$(0\;\mathrm{V}, 0\;\mathrm{A})$$ and $$(120.0\;\mathrm{V}, 12.00\;\mathrm{A}).$$

__(b)__ SI defines one ampere per volt as one __siemens__: $$1\;\dfrac{\mathrm{A}}{\mathrm{V}} = 1\;\mathrm{S}.$$ Is $$\mathrm{S}$$ a physical quantity or a unit? The physical quantity measured in siemens is called __conductance__, with symbol $$G.$$ What is the conductance of the class's light bulb?

__(c)__ In algebra, a line through the origin is $$y = mx.$$ Write the corresponding equation for the current $$I$$ through the bulb in terms of its conductance and the battery voltage. Why would it be wrong to write $$I = G \cdot \mathrm{V},$$ or to use $$\mathrm{S}$$ or $$\mathrm{A}$$ anywhere in the equation?

__(d)__ If we swapped in a bulb with a larger conductance, would the current at any fixed voltage increase or decrease? What would change about the graph?

label: I2P09
name: Plotting the Bouncing Basketball — A basketball is full of air, and air is affected by temperature, so the…
desc: A basketball is full of air, and air is affected by temperature, so the outcome of a basketball shot could depend on the temperature! Students investigated the effect of temperature on a basketball's "bounciness." They used an oven and a refrigerator to bring the ball (and the…
statement:
A basketball is full of air, and air is affected by temperature, so the outcome of a basketball shot could depend on the temperature! Students investigated the effect of temperature on a basketball's "bounciness." They used an oven and a refrigerator to bring the ball (and the air inside it) to a desired temperature, then quickly moved it to the same room-temperature room and dropped it from $$1\;\mathrm{m}$$ above the ground. A phone app used sound to measure the __bounce time__ — the duration of the ball's first bounce, which with some equipment is easier to measure than the bounce height. They repeated this for three bounces at each temperature and averaged the results: $$\begin{array}{|c|c|}\hline \text{Temperature, } T \; (^\circ\mathrm{C}) & \text{Average Bounce Time, } t \; (\mathrm{ms}) \\ \hline 10 & 315 \\ \hline 30 & 444 \\ \hline 50 & 563 \\ \hline 70 & 621 \\ \hline \end{array}$$

Important control variables included the drop height, the particular ball, the surface the ball lands on, the way the ball is released (no spin, no throwing), and the wind. Unlike the circuit data from the simulation, the pattern here is not obvious at a glance, so we build a plot. Get graph paper, a pencil, and a ruler.

__(a)__ Which variable should go on the horizontal axis, and why?

__(b)__ Suppose your graph paper is $$40$$ boxes wide and $$29$$ boxes tall. We want the temperature axis to start at $$-10^\circ\mathrm{C}$$ — below the lowest data point, so the plot can make predictions there — and reach at least $$70^\circ\mathrm{C}.$$ Choose a convenient temperature-per-box __scale__ for the horizontal axis. Then choose a starting value and a milliseconds-per-box scale for the vertical axis that covers all the data with room to spare on both ends.

__(c)__ Draw and label your axes, then plot a dot for each data point — a __scatterplot__. The data should look close to a line, but not exact. Draw a __best fit line__: a line that is as close to the points as possible, on average.

__(d)__ Use your best fit line to predict the bounce time when the temperature is $$0^\circ\mathrm{C}.$$ When a class did this exercise, predictions ranged from about $$240\;\mathrm{ms}$$ to $$290\;\mathrm{ms}.$$ Why didn't everyone get the same prediction?

label: I2P09
name: How Far Can You Trust a Best Fit Line? — Students measured how a basketball's __bounce time__ $$t$$ (the…
desc: Students measured how a basketball's __bounce time__ $$t$$ (the duration of its first bounce after being dropped from $$1\;\mathrm{m}$$) depends on its temperature $$T.$$ Their data, with each value an average of three drops, measured to the nearest $$1\;\mathrm{ms}$$…
statement:
Students measured how a basketball's __bounce time__ $$t$$ (the duration of its first bounce after being dropped from $$1\;\mathrm{m}$$) depends on its temperature $$T.$$ Their data, with each value an average of three drops, measured to the nearest $$1\;\mathrm{ms}$$: $$\begin{array}{|c|c|}\hline T \; (^\circ\mathrm{C}) & t \; (\mathrm{ms}) \\ \hline 10 & 315 \\ \hline 30 & 444 \\ \hline 50 & 563 \\ \hline 70 & 621 \\ \hline \end{array}$$ A hand-drawn best fit line predicts $$t \approx 273\;\mathrm{ms}$$ at $$T = 0^\circ\mathrm{C}.$$ There are also mathematical methods for fitting: __least squares linear regression__ uses a formula (built into most graphing calculators) to compute a slope and intercept from the data points. For this data, least squares gives a line passing through $$(0^\circ\mathrm{C}, 278.35\;\mathrm{ms}).$$ The data points lie as much as $$30\;\mathrm{ms}$$ away from the best fit line.

__(a)__ What do you think of predicting that an experiment at $$0^\circ\mathrm{C}$$ will measure exactly $$278.35\;\mathrm{ms}?$$ Comment on both the __precision__ (level of detail) of this prediction and its likely __accuracy__.

__(b)__ Recall the force of air drag: $$F \propto v^2.$$ There was a theoretical reason for this — multiplying an object's speed by $$\lambda$$ multiplies both the number of air molecules it strikes per second and the strength of each strike by $$\lambda,$$ so the force is multiplied by $$\lambda^2.$$ The basketball line, by contrast, is based only on data: we merely guessed that a straight line fits, with no theory behind it. A relationship like that is called an __empirical relationship__. If both models fit their data equally well, which would you trust more to make predictions, and why?

__(c)__ Would the linear model predict bounce time better at $$0^\circ\mathrm{C}$$ or at $$-100^\circ\mathrm{C}?$$ Estimate what the model predicts at $$-100^\circ\mathrm{C}$$ — what is truly ridiculous about that value?

__(d)__ Both $$0^\circ\mathrm{C}$$ and $$40^\circ\mathrm{C}$$ are just $$10^\circ\mathrm{C}$$ away from some point in the data set. Would you trust the model more at one of these temperatures than the other? Why?

__(e)__ Suggest some ways to work toward a better model of bounce time versus temperature.

label: I2P09
name: Error Bars on the Basketball Plot — Students measured a basketball's __bounce time__ $$t$$ (duration of the…
desc: Students measured a basketball's __bounce time__ $$t$$ (duration of the first bounce after a $$1\;\mathrm{m}$$ drop) at several ball temperatures $$T$$: $$\begin{array}{|c|c|}\hline T \; (^\circ\mathrm{C}) & t \; (\mathrm{ms}) \\ \hline 10 & 315 \\ \hline 30 & 444 \\ \hline 50 &…
statement:
Students measured a basketball's __bounce time__ $$t$$ (duration of the first bounce after a $$1\;\mathrm{m}$$ drop) at several ball temperatures $$T$$: $$\begin{array}{|c|c|}\hline T \; (^\circ\mathrm{C}) & t \; (\mathrm{ms}) \\ \hline 10 & 315 \\ \hline 30 & 444 \\ \hline 50 & 563 \\ \hline 70 & 621 \\ \hline \end{array}$$ They plotted the data and drew a best fit line. Analyzing the spread among repeated bounces at a single temperature, they estimated an uncertainty of $$\pm 20\;\mathrm{ms}$$ for every $$t$$ measurement; the uncertainty in temperature is $$\pm 0.5^\circ\mathrm{C}$$ because the digital thermometer reads out to the nearest $$1^\circ\mathrm{C}.$$

__(a)__ What can we add to a scatterplot to represent the uncertainty of each measurement? Add them to a plot of this data (they are the same size for every point). The result should look like this:

__(b)__ These additions should help us decide whether the linear model fits the data well. What exactly are we looking for on the plot when making that decision? Based on this plot, what is your verdict on the linear model in the range $$10^\circ\mathrm{C}$$ to $$70^\circ\mathrm{C}?$$

__(c)__ The __relative uncertainty__ of a measurement is $$\text{relative uncertainty} = \dfrac{\text{absolute uncertainty}}{\text{measurement}}.$$ Estimate the relative uncertainty in $$t$$ at $$T = 30^\circ\mathrm{C}.$$

__(d)__ Is that relative uncertainty "too big"? There is no fixed rule: cosmology routinely lives with large relative error, while LIGO's gravitational-wave distance measurements reach relative error near $$10^{-21}.$$ Think of astronomers Arthur Eddington and Frank Dyson, who measured the bending of starlight near the Sun during an eclipse to compare two competing predictions, Newton's and Einstein's. If Newton's and Einstein's predictions had been __further apart__, would Eddington and Dyson have been able to tolerate more measurement uncertainty, or less?

label: I2P09
name: From Data to Theory: Warm Balls and Deflategate — An experiment found an __empirical relationship__: the…
desc: An experiment found an __empirical relationship__: the warmer a basketball, the longer its bounce time (dropped from $$1\;\mathrm{m},$$ a ball at $$10^\circ\mathrm{C}$$ bounced for $$315\;\mathrm{ms}$$ while a ball at $$70^\circ\mathrm{C}$$ bounced for $$621\;\mathrm{ms}$$). An…
statement:
An experiment found an __empirical relationship__: the warmer a basketball, the longer its bounce time (dropped from $$1\;\mathrm{m},$$ a ball at $$10^\circ\mathrm{C}$$ bounced for $$315\;\mathrm{ms}$$ while a ball at $$70^\circ\mathrm{C}$$ bounced for $$621\;\mathrm{ms}$$). An empirical relationship becomes more trustworthy if we can tie it to theory. A basketball is full of air, and if you have ever tried to bounce a flat basketball, you know that high pressure means a bouncier ball. Here is a player shooting with a well-inflated ball:

and the same player shooting a somewhat flat ball, whose internal pressure is lower:

__(a)__ Using the idea that air is made of moving molecules, propose a hypothesis explaining __why__ heating the ball makes it bounce longer.

__(b)__ Is it fair to compare the results of two basketball games, one played in hot weather and one in cold? Do you think professional sports leagues regulate the pressure of their balls?

__(c)__ In 2014, the NFL (the American professional football league) suspected that star quarterback Tom Brady was asking for under-inflated footballs; officials measured some of his team's balls below the pressure limit set by the rules. Under-inflated balls are less bouncy and easier to catch — an advantage when throwing to a running teammate. The investigation found the footballs had been inflated in a warm locker room and then taken out to the cold field. What would happen to the pressure inside the balls then, even if no one let any air out?

__(d)__ Besides air molecules moving more slowly in the cold, what else could happen to the gas inside a football as the temperature drops? (Hint: think about any water vapor in there.)

__(e)__ Deciding whether the measured pressures indicated a __significant__ violation was complicated enough that the investigation hired a scientific consulting firm and a physics professor. What concept of data analysis becomes important in deciding whether measurements show a significant result?

label: I2P09
name: Reading the Atmosphere from a Graph — Since the late 1930s, the U.S. National Weather Service has measured…
desc: Since the late 1930s, the U.S. National Weather Service has measured the atmosphere with __radiosondes__ — small sensor packages carried up by weather balloons, recording temperature, height, and other data until the balloon bursts. Here is a radiosonde launch from 1936: Below…
statement:
Since the late 1930s, the U.S. National Weather Service has measured the atmosphere with __radiosondes__ — small sensor packages carried up by weather balloons, recording temperature, height, and other data until the balloon bursts. Here is a radiosonde launch from 1936:

Below is a scatterplot of temperature versus altitude from a radiosonde launched from the Oakland, California station in October 2020 (the full data set has over $$100$$ points; the plot shows its shape). The ground-level temperature that day was $$15^\circ\mathrm{C}.$$

__(a)__ Over roughly what range of altitudes does the data form a long, approximately straight line? Describe what the data does outside that range.

__(b)__ Two points roughly at either end of the straight portion are $$(1.0\;\mathrm{km}, 22^\circ\mathrm{C})$$ and $$(11\;\mathrm{km}, -50^\circ\mathrm{C}).$$ Find the approximate slope of the linear region and say in words what it means. Why are these two points convenient to use?

__(c)__ To finish a linear model $$T = (\text{intercept}) + (\text{slope}) \cdot h$$ for the straight region, we need the intercept on the vertical axis. Should we use $$15^\circ\mathrm{C},$$ the actual temperature at ground level? If not, what should we use instead? Write out the complete model, including the range of altitudes where it applies.

__(d)__ The slope of a temperature-versus-altitude graph is called the __lapse rate__, with symbol $$\Gamma$$ (capital Greek gamma). Using the theory of thermodynamics, scientists predict $$\Gamma = \dfrac{-g}{c_p} \approx -10^\circ\mathrm{C}/\mathrm{km},$$ where $$g \approx 10\;\mathrm{m/s^2}$$ is the acceleration due to gravity and $$c_p$$ is the __specific heat__ of air — a measure of how much heat must be added to air to raise its temperature by a given amount. Solve for $$c_p$$ and find its approximate value and units; then rewrite the units in terms of the __joule__, using $$1\;\mathrm{J} = 1\;\dfrac{\mathrm{kg \cdot m^2}}{\mathrm{s^2}},$$ and interpret what $$c_p$$ tells us.

__(e)__ The theoretical prediction $$\Gamma \approx -10^\circ\mathrm{C}/\mathrm{km}$$ holds for perfectly dry air, but it does not match the slope you measured in part (b) — a significant difference, indicating something is missing from the dry-air model. Real air contains water vapor, and as a patch of air rises, its temperature falls. What happens to some of that water vapor, and how does it explain the mismatch?

desc: When $$y = c \cdot x^a$$ we've said both $$``y$$ is proportional to $$x^a"$$ and $$``y$$ scales as $$x^a."$$ Relationships like this are also called __power laws__. One criterion you can use to decide whether something is a power law is to see what happens to $$y$$ when you…
statement:
When $$y = c \cdot x^a$$ we've said both $$``y$$ is proportional to $$x^a"$$ and $$``y$$ scales as $$x^a."$$

Relationships like this are also called __power laws__.

One criterion you can use to decide whether something is a power law is to see what happens to $$y$$ when you double $$x.$$

In a power law, doubling $$x$$ always multiplies $$y$$ by $$2^a.$$ For example, $$y = 3x^3$$ is a power law with $$a = 3.$$ If we choose $$x = 1,$$ then $$y = 3.$$ When we choose $$x = 2,$$ $$y = 24$$ which is $$2^3 = 8$$ times as much as when $$x = 1.$$ When we double $$x$$ again to $$4,$$ we again multiply $$y$$ by $$8,$$ getting $$192,$$ etc.

In a different power law with a different value of $$a,$$ doubling $$x$$ will multiply $$y$$ by some other value instead of $$8,$$ but it will always be the same value, no matter what initial $$x$$ we double.

Select the **two** equations below where the relationship between $$y$$ and $$x$$ is **not** a power law.

$$y = -3 x$$

$$y = \dfrac{1}{x}$$

$$y = 3x + 2$$

$$y = 2x^6$$

$$y = \sqrt{x}$$

$$y = 4^x$$

$$y = 2.4 x^{0.091}$$

statement:
Part A. The pendulum simulation we used in our class on uncertainty is available here

The simulation allows you to imagine you are on "Planet X," where gravitational acceleration is some unknown value we will call $$g_x.$$ In this multi-part problem, we will find $$g_x$$ by making measurements of the pendulum.

You'll need to know that __for small amplitudes__, $$T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{\ell}{g}},$$ where $$T$$ is the period of a pendulum and $$\ell$$ is its length.

It would be more accurate to say $$T \approx 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{\ell}{g}}$$ in Newton's model of mechanics, but you can treat it as an equality for the purposes of this problem; the approximation is close enough that any deviation from it doesn't matter, as long as you only let the pendulum undergo small swings.

You can measure the period of the pendulum using a stopwatch on the lower left.

You can also change the length of the pendulum using the slider bar in the upper right.

Fill out the data table below with the period $$T$$ of the pendulum for different lengths $$\ell.$$ You should be accurate to within $$0.03 \;\mathrm{s},$$ so take steps to reduce your random and systematic uncertainty.

You may want to write your values down somewhere, then fill in the data table. That will make it easier to re-enter the values if one of them is off on your first try.

In this problem, you are practicing the skill of making precision measurements. You will need to be within $$0.03 \;\mathrm{s}$$ of the correct answer for every box to be marked correct.

desc: For this experiment, you will need either a hollow ball (like a tennis ball) or a solid ball (like a marble). Build a ramp for your ball to roll down. You should be able to adjust the height of your ramp. For example, you could use a flat piece of cardboard as your ramp and…
statement:
For this experiment, you will need either a hollow ball (like a tennis ball) or a solid ball (like a marble).

Build a ramp for your ball to roll down. You should be able to adjust the height of your ramp. For example, you could use a flat piece of cardboard as your ramp and stack different numbers of books under one side to adjust the height.

Roll your ball down your ramp. Conduct several trials at each of several heights $$h$$, keeping the length $$\ell$$ of the ramp fixed. Using a stopwatch, time how long it takes your object to roll down your ramp for each height.

Newtonian mechanics predicts that the time to roll down the ramp will be \ for a solid ball and \ for a hollow ball. If you assume that same equation accurately models your experiment, what is your experimental value for $$g?$$ What is your uncertainty in $$g?$$

Make sure you include: **a)** A data table summarizing your results **b)** An appropriate plot and best-fit line used to estimate $$g$$ and its uncertainty **c)** An explanation of how you estimated the error in your result **d)** A discussion of how well your results match theory

To avoid your report being too long, you don't need to explain how you built your ramp; you may skip directly to your data table at the beginning of your writeup. You do need to identify whether you used a hollow or solid ball.

label: I2P10
name: The Cavendish Experiment: Measuring Big G — In the Cavendish experiment, a small sphere of mass $$m$$ hangs…
desc: In the Cavendish experiment, a small sphere of mass $$m$$ hangs from a delicately balanced rod, and a large sphere of mass $$M$$ is brought nearby. The apparatus measures the tiny gravitational force $$F$$ between the two spheres when their centers are a distance $$r$$ apart…
statement:
In the Cavendish experiment, a small sphere of mass $$m$$ hangs from a delicately balanced rod, and a large sphere of mass $$M$$ is brought nearby. The apparatus measures the tiny gravitational force $$F$$ between the two spheres when their centers are a distance $$r$$ apart.

Newton's model of gravity says the force between the spheres is $$F = \dfrac{GMm}{r^2},$$ where $$G$$ is a constant of nature called Newton's gravitational constant. Imagine we performed the Cavendish experiment with spheres of mass $$M = 158\;\mathrm{kg}$$ and $$m = 0.81\;\mathrm{kg}$$ and collected this data: $$\begin{array}{r | r} r \;\; (\mathrm{m}) & F \;\; (10^{-7}\;\mathrm{N}) \\ \hline 0.10 & 7.75 \\ 0.12 & 5.48 \\ 0.14 & 3.86 \\ 0.16 & 2.91 \\ 0.18 & 2.49 \\ 0.20 & 1.83 \\ 0.22 & 1.59 \\ 0.24 & 1.29 \\ 0.26 & 1.10 \\ 0.28 & 1.00 \end{array}$$

__(a)__ Ignoring everything in Newton's equation except the two variables of interest, write the relationship between $$F$$ and $$r$$ as a proportionality. (This kind of relationship has a famous name — what is it called?) Should a plot of $$F$$ versus $$r$$ rise or fall as $$r$$ increases?

__(b)__ Here is a plot of the data:

The points do fall as $$r$$ increases. Can you tell just by eyeballing this plot that the data __definitely__ follows $$F \propto r^{-2}$$ rather than, say, $$F \propto r^{-1}?$$ And why won't this plot let us determine $$G$$ using the data-analysis methods we know (finding best-fit lines and their slopes)?

__(c)__ We can fix the problem by __transforming__ the variable $$r$$: treat $$\dfrac{1}{r^2}$$ as a new variable, so the model $$F = GMm \cdot \dfrac{1}{r^2}$$ takes the linear form $$F = (\text{constant}) \cdot (\text{variable}).$$ Add an $$r^{-2}$$ column to the data table. (For example, the first entry, for $$r = 0.10\;\mathrm{m},$$ is $$100\;\mathrm{m^{-2}}.$$ Compute the rest, starting with $$r = 0.12\;\mathrm{m}.$$ Careful: as $$r$$ increases, should $$r^{-2}$$ increase or decrease?)

__(d)__ Plotting $$F$$ versus $$r^{-2}$$ is called __linearizing__ the data. Here is the linearized plot with a best-fit line:

The points now lie almost perfectly on a line. Is that evidence in favor of Newton's inverse-square model, evidence against it, or irrelevant to it? In terms of the variables appearing in $$F = \dfrac{GMm}{r^2},$$ what is the slope of this line?

__(e)__ Remembering that $$1\;\mathrm{N} = 1\;\mathrm{kg \cdot m \cdot s^{-2}},$$ what units does the slope of the linearized plot carry? (Hint: a slope is a $$\dfrac{\text{rise}}{\text{run}},$$ and the rise and run carry the units of the vertical and horizontal axes.)

__(f)__ A computer fit gives $$\text{slope} = 7.69 \times 10^{-9}$$ in the units you found in part (e). What value of $$G$$ does this experiment give? The accepted value is $$G \approx 6.67 \times 10^{-11}\;\mathrm{kg^{-1} \cdot m^3 \cdot s^{-2}}$$ — how does the experiment compare?

label: I2P10
name: A Perfect Line with the Wrong Answer — In a (simulated) Cavendish experiment, the gravitational force $$F$$…
desc: In a (simulated) Cavendish experiment, the gravitational force $$F$$ between a large sphere of mass $$M = 158\;\mathrm{kg}$$ and a small sphere of mass $$m = 0.81\;\mathrm{kg}$$ was measured at ten different separations $$r.$$ Newton's model predicts $$F = \dfrac{GMm}{r^2}.$$…
statement:
In a (simulated) Cavendish experiment, the gravitational force $$F$$ between a large sphere of mass $$M = 158\;\mathrm{kg}$$ and a small sphere of mass $$m = 0.81\;\mathrm{kg}$$ was measured at ten different separations $$r.$$ Newton's model predicts $$F = \dfrac{GMm}{r^2}.$$ When the data was linearized by plotting $$F$$ versus $$r^{-2},$$ the points fell almost perfectly on a straight line, and the slope of the best-fit line gave $$G = 6.00 \times 10^{-11}\;\mathrm{kg^{-1} \cdot m^3 \cdot s^{-2}}$$ — about $$10\%$$ below the accepted value of $$6.67 \times 10^{-11}\;\mathrm{kg^{-1} \cdot m^3 \cdot s^{-2}}.$$

__(a)__ Based on the nearly perfect straight line combined with the $$10\%$$ wrong answer, does this experiment suffer mostly from __random error__ or mostly from __systematic error__? What would the linearized plot look like if the error were mostly random?

__(b)__ Here is the experimental setup. Notice that there is a pair of spheres (one large, one small) on the left end of the rod and another pair on the right end.

Suppose a scientist analyzing the experiment calculated $$F$$ by considering only the attraction between __nearby__ spheres. Why would that produce a systematic error? Even after fixing this, can we ever guarantee that the systematic error in an experiment is zero?

__(c)__ Plotting $$F$$ versus $$r^{-2}$$ was not the only way to linearize this data. Suppose we insisted on keeping $$r$$ itself on the horizontal axis. What power of $$F$$ should we plot on the vertical axis to get a straight line? Name at least one more pair of transformed variables that would also linearize data obeying $$F \propto r^{-2}.$$

label: I2P10
name: Kepler's Third Law by Dimensional Analysis — Kepler's first law says that each planet moves around the sun…
desc: Kepler's first law says that each planet moves around the sun along an __ellipse__ — a stretched-out circle — with the sun off to one side at a point called a __focus__. While a circle's shape needs only one measurement (the radius), an ellipse needs two: the __semi-major axis__…
statement:
Kepler's first law says that each planet moves around the sun along an __ellipse__ — a stretched-out circle — with the sun off to one side at a point called a __focus__. While a circle's shape needs only one measurement (the radius), an ellipse needs two: the __semi-major axis__ length $$a$$ (half the long way across) and the __semi-minor axis__ length $$b$$ (half the short way across). Kepler studied each planet's __orbital period__ $$T$$ — the time to go once around its ellipse — as a function of its semi-major axis $$a.$$ Here is his data, with $$a$$ measured in astronomical units ($$1\;\mathrm{au}$$ is the semi-major axis of Earth's orbit, $$1\;\mathrm{au} = 1.496 \times 10^{11}\;\mathrm{m}$$): $$\begin{array}{l | r | r} \text{Planet} & a \;\;(\mathrm{au}) & T \;\;(\mathrm{days}) \\ \hline \text{Mercury} & 0.389 & 87.77 \\ \text{Venus} & 0.724 & 224.70 \\ \text{Earth} & 1 & 365.25 \\ \text{Mars} & 1.524 & 686.95 \\ \text{Jupiter} & 5.20 & 4332.62 \\ \text{Saturn} & 9.510 & 10759.2 \end{array}$$

__(a)__ Compare Earth and Saturn: $$a_{\rm Saturn} \approx 10\, a_{\rm Earth}.$$ If the plot of $$T$$ versus $$a$$ were a straight line through the origin, what would $$T_{\rm Saturn}$$ be? What is it actually, and what does that tell you about the shape of the plot?

__(b)__ A natural first guess is that the data is quadratic: $$T \stackrel{?}{=} c \cdot a^2.$$ If we test the guess by plotting $$T$$ versus $$a^2,$$ the resulting graph curves __downward__ (the original plot curved upward). What does that tell us about the quadratic hypothesis? Is guessing one relationship after another and hoping a plot comes out linear an efficient way to find the true power?

__(c)__ A better tool for finding proportionalities is __dimensional analysis__. Explain why it's dimensionally impossible to write an equation for $$T$$ using __only__ $$a$$ and no other quantities. (Use the dimension symbols $$\mathrm{T}$$ for time and $$\mathrm{L}$$ for length; note that the slanted $$T$$ is a variable, while upright $$\mathrm{T}$$ is a dimension.)

__(d)__ Since this is a problem about gravity, we include the gravitational constant $$G$$ and the sun's mass $$M_\odot$$: $$\begin{array}{c | c | c} \text{quantity} & \text{variable} & \text{dimension} \\ \hline \text{orbital period} & T & \mathrm{T} \\ \text{semi-major axis} & a & \mathrm{L} \\ \text{sun's mass} & M_\odot & \mathrm{M} \\ \text{gravitational constant} & G & \mathrm{M^{-1} \cdot L^3 \cdot T^{-2}} \end{array}$$ It turns out we should __not__ include the planet's own mass $$m.$$ Jupiter is more than $$5000$$ times as massive as Mercury — what feature of the data above shows that $$m$$ doesn't matter?

__(e)__ Use dimensional analysis to find the powers $$p, q, s$$ in $$T \propto G^{p} \cdot M_\odot^{q} \cdot a^{s}.$$ (Hint: only $$G$$ contains any time dimension, so start by matching the time dimensions; then patch up length using $$a$$ and mass using $$M_\odot.$$) Write the result in the form $$T = c \cdot (\text{something}).$$

__(f)__ According to your result, if the sun's mass were somehow increased (with $$a$$ unchanged), would $$T$$ increase or decrease? By what factor would you have to multiply $$M_\odot$$ to cut a planet's period in half?

label: I2P10
name: Choosing a Linearization and Weighing the Sun — Kepler's third law says a planet's orbital period $$T$$ and…
desc: Kepler's third law says a planet's orbital period $$T$$ and semi-major axis $$a$$ obey $$T \propto a^{3/2}.$$ Newton's theory of gravity goes further and predicts the constant: $$T = \dfrac{2\pi}{\sqrt{GM_\odot}} \cdot a^{3/2},$$ where $$G$$ is the gravitational constant and…
statement:
Kepler's third law says a planet's orbital period $$T$$ and semi-major axis $$a$$ obey $$T \propto a^{3/2}.$$ Newton's theory of gravity goes further and predicts the constant: $$T = \dfrac{2\pi}{\sqrt{GM_\odot}} \cdot a^{3/2},$$ where $$G$$ is the gravitational constant and $$M_\odot$$ is the mass of the sun. The data ($$1\;\mathrm{au} = 1.496 \times 10^{11}\;\mathrm{m},$$ $$1\;\mathrm{day} = 86{,}400\;\mathrm{s}$$): $$\begin{array}{l | r | r} \text{Planet} & a \;\;(\mathrm{au}) & T \;\;(\mathrm{days}) \\ \hline \text{Mercury} & 0.389 & 87.77 \\ \text{Venus} & 0.724 & 224.70 \\ \text{Earth} & 1 & 365.25 \\ \text{Mars} & 1.524 & 686.95 \\ \text{Jupiter} & 5.20 & 4332.62 \\ \text{Saturn} & 9.510 & 10759.2 \end{array}$$

__(a)__ Which of these plots should linearize the data (there may be more than one): $$T$$ versus $$a$$; $$T^{3/2}$$ versus $$a$$; $$T$$ versus $$a^{3/2}$$; $$T^{2/3}$$ versus $$a$$; $$T^2$$ versus $$a^3?$$

__(b)__ Notice that the data is bunched up toward small $$a$$ — there are more planets close to the sun than far away — and bunched-up data is hard to read. Among the correct choices $$T$$ versus $$a^{3/2},$$ $$T^{2/3}$$ versus $$a,$$ and $$T^2$$ versus $$a^3,$$ which produces the __least__ bunching of points along the horizontal axis? Then suggest a fourth linearization that spreads the points out even more evenly.

__(c)__ Suppose we only knew $$T \propto a^{3/2}$$ in the form $$T = c \cdot \sqrt{\dfrac{a^3}{GM_\odot}}$$ with $$c$$ unknown. Using the data table and the known value of $$G,$$ could we determine $$c?$$ Why or why not?

__(d)__ Here is the data plotted as $$T^{1/3}$$ versus $$a^{1/2},$$ with a best-fit line:

The slope of the best-fit line is $$\text{slope} = 7.15\;\dfrac{\mathrm{day}^{1/3}}{\mathrm{au}^{1/2}},$$ which converts to SI units as $$7.15\;\dfrac{\mathrm{day}^{1/3}}{\mathrm{au}^{1/2}} \cdot \left(\dfrac{86{,}400\;\mathrm{s}}{1\;\mathrm{day}}\right)^{1/3} \cdot \left(\dfrac{1\;\mathrm{au}}{1.496 \times 10^{11}\;\mathrm{m}}\right)^{1/2} \approx 8.17 \times 10^{-4}\;\dfrac{\mathrm{s}^{1/3}}{\mathrm{m}^{1/2}}.$$ Starting from Newton's equation $$T = \dfrac{2\pi}{\sqrt{GM_\odot}} \cdot a^{3/2},$$ find an expression for the slope of a $$T^{1/3}$$ versus $$a^{1/2}$$ plot in terms of $$2\pi,$$ $$G,$$ and $$M_\odot.$$

__(e)__ Set your slope expression equal to the measured SI slope and solve for $$M_\odot,$$ using $$G \approx 6.67 \times 10^{-11}\;\mathrm{kg^{-1} \cdot m^3 \cdot s^{-2}}.$$ The mass of Earth is about $$6 \times 10^{24}\;\mathrm{kg}$$ — roughly how many Earths is the sun worth?

label: I2P10
name: Galaxy Rotation Curves and the Dark Matter Mystery — For this problem, simplify planetary orbits to circles…
desc: For this problem, simplify planetary orbits to circles of radius $$r$$ traveled at constant speed $$v.$$ A planet's orbital period is then the distance around divided by the speed: $$T = \dfrac{2\pi r}{v}.$$ Newton's theory of gravity also predicts $$T = \dfrac{2\pi}{\sqrt{GM}}…
statement:
For this problem, simplify planetary orbits to circles of radius $$r$$ traveled at constant speed $$v.$$ A planet's orbital period is then the distance around divided by the speed: $$T = \dfrac{2\pi r}{v}.$$ Newton's theory of gravity also predicts $$T = \dfrac{2\pi}{\sqrt{GM}} \cdot r^{3/2},$$ where $$M$$ is the mass of the central body (for the solar system, the sun) and $$G$$ is the gravitational constant.

__(a)__ If all planets moved at the __same__ speed, what proportionality would relate $$T$$ and $$r?$$ Given that the true relationship is $$T \propto r^{3/2},$$ does Saturn move faster or slower along its orbit than Venus?

__(b)__ Set the two expressions for $$T$$ equal and solve for $$v.$$ What proportionality relates $$v$$ and $$r,$$ and what does a plot of $$v$$ versus $$r$$ look like for the planets?

__(c)__ Stars in a galaxy also orbit, pulled by gravity toward the galactic center. Here is the Andromeda galaxy, our nearest neighbor (also called M31):

Unlike the solar system, there is no single central "super-star." There __is__ a giant black hole at the center of most galaxies — about four million times the sun's mass in the Milky Way — but the whole galaxy is roughly a __trillion__ solar masses, so the black hole's contribution is small. By a result of Newton called the __shell theorem__ (exact for spheres, approximately right for galaxies), only the mass __closer to the center__ than a star's orbit affects the star's motion; the pull of mass farther out roughly cancels. So we can still use $$v = \sqrt{\dfrac{G \cdot M(r)}{r}},$$ where $$M(r)$$ is the total mass (stars, dust, everything) inside radius $$r.$$ Which star has the greatest mass causing its orbit: one near the center, one halfway out, or one near the edge of the galaxy?

__(d)__ Near the edge of a galaxy, the stars thin out, so moving farther out adds almost no new mass: $$M(r)$$ becomes roughly constant. What should a plot of $$v$$ versus $$r$$ — called the galaxy's __rotation curve__ — look like in that outer region?

__(e)__ Between 1968 and 1969, Vera Rubin and Kent Ford measured the speeds of hundreds of stars in Andromeda. Here is the rotation curve they found ($$r$$ is measured in arcminutes, an angle from the galaxy's center used as a stand-in for distance):

The vast majority of Andromeda's stars lie within about $$80$$ arcminutes of the center. Describe what the curve does between $$80$$ and $$140$$ arcminutes. Is that what your answer to part (d) predicted?

__(f)__ The most widely accepted explanation today is that galaxies contain a large amount of unseen mass extending well beyond the visible stars. How does that hypothesis explain the shape of the rotation curve, what is this unseen matter called, and roughly how much of it did Rubin calculate Andromeda needs compared to its ordinary matter?

label: I2P10
name: How Fast Do Water Waves Move? — Water waves do not all move at the same speed (unlike light waves in empty…
desc: Water waves do not all move at the same speed (unlike light waves in empty space). Water waves are __mechanical__: they can be understood with Newton's laws — forces acting on bits of water and accelerating them. (Temperature, a __thermodynamic__ property, doesn't noticeably…
statement:
Water waves do not all move at the same speed (unlike light waves in empty space). Water waves are __mechanical__: they can be understood with Newton's laws — forces acting on bits of water and accelerating them. (Temperature, a __thermodynamic__ property, doesn't noticeably affect them.) The most important feature of a wave for its speed is its __wavelength__ $$\lambda,$$ the distance from one crest to the next:

Wind, earthquakes, and boats can __create__ waves, but they don't keep waves moving or set their speed. Since different parts of a wave sit at different heights, there is vertical motion, and the force that drives traveling water waves is Earth's __gravity__. Our goal: a hypothesis for how wave speed $$v$$ depends on $$\lambda,$$ using dimensional analysis with the table $$\begin{array}{c | c | c} \text{quantity} & \text{variable} & \text{dimension} \\ \hline \text{wave speed} & v & \mathrm{L \cdot T^{-1}} \\ \text{wavelength} & \lambda & \mathrm{L} \\ \text{gravitational acceleration} & g & \mathrm{L \cdot T^{-2}} \\ \text{density of water} & \rho & \mathrm{M \cdot L^{-3}} \end{array}$$

__(a)__ One of the four quantities clearly cannot appear in a dimensionally valid equation for $$v.$$ Which one, and why?

__(b)__ Use dimensional analysis to find the powers in $$v = c \cdot \lambda^{p} g^{q}.$$ According to this hypothesis, what should a plot of $$v$$ versus $$\lambda$$ look like?

__(c)__ Here is a curve through real measurements of wave speed versus wavelength:

For which wavelengths does your hypothesis from part (b) look right, and for which does it clearly fail? If you linearized by plotting $$v$$ versus $$\sqrt{\lambda},$$ what would you expect to see? When a dimensional analysis fails like this, what is the most likely cause?

__(d)__ The missing ingredient at short wavelengths is __surface tension__: liquid molecules attract one another, and molecules at the surface get pulled back toward the liquid. Surface tension, written $$\gamma,$$ is a __force per unit length__. Starting from the dimensions of force, $$\left = \mathrm{M \cdot L \cdot T^{-2}},$$ find the dimensions of $$\gamma.$$ Then redo the dimensional analysis for short waves using $$\lambda,$$ $$\gamma,$$ and $$\rho$$ (no $$g$$): what is $$v$$ proportional to? Does it bend the right way to match the short-wavelength data?

__(e)__ A full Newtonian model including both forces gives $$v = \sqrt{\dfrac{g\lambda}{2\pi} + \dfrac{2\pi\gamma}{\rho\lambda}}.$$ Write the simpler approximate equations for $$v$$ when $$\lambda$$ is very large and when $$\lambda$$ is very small, and say which force dominates in each case. Then find the transition wavelength $$\lambda_{\rm transition}$$ — where neither force dominates — by setting the two terms under the square root equal.

__(f)__ The transition length is the __capillary length__ of water, about $$1\;\mathrm{cm}$$ — the same special length that sets the size of the largest water droplets and the widest straw that can hold water with your thumb over the top. Using $$\lambda_{\rm transition} \approx 1\;\mathrm{cm},$$ $$g \approx 10\;\mathrm{m/s^2},$$ and $$\rho \approx 10^3\;\mathrm{kg/m^3},$$ estimate the surface tension $$\gamma$$ of water. The accepted value is $$\gamma = 0.072\;\mathrm{kg/s^2}$$ — how does your estimate compare?

label: I2P11
name: In this problem, we'll analyze a thought experiment about buoyancy. Our goal is to…
desc: In this problem, we'll analyze a thought experiment about buoyancy. Our goal is to practice understanding the purpose and logical structure of thought experiments. Imagine an object on which the buoyant force goes at an angle away from the vertical, instead of vertically. Now…
statement:
In this problem, we'll analyze a thought experiment about buoyancy. Our goal is to practice understanding the purpose and logical structure of thought experiments.

Imagine an object on which the buoyant force goes at an angle away from the vertical, instead of vertically.

Now put this object on a horizontal circle track underwater. The track has no friction.

The track will prevent the object from moving up or down, but the horizontal part of the buoyant force will push the object around the track. The buoyant force is always present, so the object will move forever. In fact, we could hook it up to a generator and get infinite energy from it.

Which one statement below accurately summarizes this thought experiment?

The thought experiment's purpose is probably to show that buoyant forces usually **do** point at an angle, not vertically.

The purpose is probably to show that buoyant force **do not** point at an angle; they must be vertical.

The thought experiment is not useful because we can't really build a frictionless track, even though it doesn't break any laws of physics.

The thought experiment is a serious proposal for how to build a machine that will generate infinite free energy.

The thought experiment is probably supposed to happen in an environment with no gravity.

desc: Part A. Galileo's (fictional) rival, Professor Impetus the Impetuous, learned about Galileo's thought experiment on falling bodies. Remember that Galileo's thought experiment was designed to show a logical inconsistency in Aristotle's idea that more massive things fall to the…
statement:
Part A. Galileo's (fictional) rival, Professor Impetus the Impetuous, learned about Galileo's thought experiment on falling bodies. Remember that Galileo's thought experiment was designed to show a logical inconsistency in Aristotle's idea that more massive things fall to the ground more quickly when dropped and pulled by gravity.

Professor Impetus agrees with Galileo that Aristotle is wrong, but believes that Galileo is wrong, too! Her theory is that the acceleration of an object due to gravity depends on the average The density of an object is defined as its mass divided by its volume. of the object. The more dense the object, the greater its acceleration. In fact, objects of very low density may even have negative acceleration towards the ground, according to Impetus.

A third scientist, Dr. Vacuum, is trying to decide whose hypothesis fits in better with some observations they've made and some facts they know. That means Dr. Vacuum is trying to decide whether density affects gravitational acceleration or not. However, Dr. Vacuum doesn't fully understand the difference between thought experiments and the real world. Dr. Vacuum doesn't consider whether effects like air drag, or other non-gravity influences that are excluded in the thought experiments, are interfering with the observations.

Dr. Vacuum writes down a list of observations and facts. That list is shown below. Sort each item on the list by whether Dr. Vacuum thinks it agrees with Galileo's hypothesis, Professor Impetus's hypothesis, both, or neither.

**(a)** Take a piece of paper. Wad it up into a ball, but loosely. Drop it and see how long it takes to fall. Next, wad the same paper up more tightly, so it makes a smaller ball. Then drop it again. It will take less time to fall to the ground in the second case, when it's tightly wadded. Vacuum considers the paper ball more dense when wadded up. **(b)** Kepler's laws give a very accurate description of the motion of planets, despite Kepler not knowing the planets' densities. Kepler's laws can be derived mathematically from Newton's theory of gravity, and Newton's theory of gravity predicts that all objects will accelerate near the surface of Earth with the same acceleration. **(c)** A skydiver falls more quickly in a head first position than in a spreadeagle position, even though their density is the same in both positions. **(d)** Astronaut David Scott found that a hammer and feather take the same amount of time to fall from a given height when dropped on the moon, despite having different densities. **(e)** Some objects, like helium balloons, do not fall at all. They rise up through the air, despite not spending any energy to fly the way birds or airplanes do. This happens only with objects of very low density. **(f)** A helium balloon will not float on the moon. It will fall down in the same amount of time as a hammer or feather. **(g)** A small lead ball and a large lead ball, when dropped off a tower (as described in Galileo's thought experiment), really do hit the ground at almost exactly the same time. These balls have the same density.

Part B. In order to make quantitative predictions with their hypotheses, Galileo and Professor Impetus agree to write their hypotheses as equations.

In equations, Galileo believes $$a_{\rm gravity; \; Galileo} = g,$$ that the acceleration due to gravity of all objects near Earth's surface is the same and equal to some constant called $$g.$$

Professor Impetus believes $$a_{\rm gravity; \; Impetus} = c_g \cdot (\rho - \rho_0),$$ where $$\rho$$ is the density of an object and $$c_g$$ and $$\rho_0$$ are constants that are the same for all objects. $$c_g$$ takes the place of $$g$$ in Professor Impetus' hypothesis, but it is not an acceleration.

What are the dimensions of $$c_g?$$

mathjax: \[ \left = \mathrm{M}^{\blank} \cdot \mathrm{L}^{\blank} \cdot \mathrm{T}^{\blank} \]

allowed: -1.023456789

Part C. We know that Galileo's hypothesis on falling bodies is well-supported by real world evidence and logically consistent. On the other hand, Professor Impetus's idea that acceleration due to gravity depends on density disagrees with both experiment and mathematical theory, such as Newton's laws and Newton's theory of gravity.

Still, can a thought experiment alone show that Impetus' idea is logically inconsistent?

On the message board, participate in the conversation with the class on this topic. You might want to:

- Suggest a thought experiment that shows that Impetus's hypothesis is logically inconsistent or absurd - Explain why you think a thought experiment can't show Impetus's hypothesis is inconsistent, even if it is shown wrong by real world experiments - Respond to your classmates' thought experiments and arguments

label: I2P11
name: Alice is on a treadmill tilted on an incline. She is running hard and getting out of…
desc: Alice is on a treadmill tilted on an incline. She is running hard and getting out of breath when the Queen of Hearts (QoH) comes by. Alice: I'm getting very tired! **Running is so much harder when the treadmill is on an incline** like this. QoH: But you aren't running at all!…
statement:
Alice is on a treadmill tilted on an incline. She is running hard and getting out of breath when the Queen of Hearts (QoH) comes by.

Alice: I'm getting very tired! **Running is so much harder when the treadmill is on an incline** like this.

QoH: But you aren't running at all! You haven't moved one whit. Off with your head!

Alice: I beg your pardon but I believe your majesty is using the wrong reference frame. Viewed from the right reference frame, we see that running on an inclined treadmill is just as difficult as running up a hill of the same slope.

QoH: Little girl, you speak such nonsense! If you run up a real hill, you will get to a higher elevation above the surface of Earth. We can calculate how much energy that takes with the formula $$U = mgh$$ for gravitational potential energy. **But your elevation hasn't changed significantly**, so you haven't increased your potential energy. You are lying that it's hard work. Guards, seize her!

Alice: I'm sorry, I don't know that formula or what gravitational potential energy is! We didn't get to that in my physics class yet, but I don't think I can run without going anywhere much longer.

Who is right and who is wrong? Choose two: one of (a) or (b) and one of (c) or (d).

Evaluate both bolded statements - Alice's claim that the incline makes running more difficult and the Queen's claim that Alice isn't gaining any elevation.

We will learn more about gravitational potential energy next week. You don't need to evaluate everything each person says. Just evaluate whether each bolded statement is correct in itself, regardless of whether the rest of what that person says is accurate.

Alice is right about how hard it is to run on an inclined treadmill, the QoH is wrong.

Alice is wrong about how hard it is to run on an inclined treadmill, the QoH is right.

The QoH is right about the change in Alice's elevation.

The QoH is wrong about the change in Alice's elevation.

desc: Dorothy and the Scarecrow are arguing about whether throwing a ball perfectly horizontally will make it take longer to hit the ground. They imagine two balls, one dropped and the other thrown horizontally at the same moment. The horizontal speed of the thrown ball is $$v.$$ They…
statement:
Dorothy and the Scarecrow are arguing about whether throwing a ball perfectly horizontally will make it take longer to hit the ground. They imagine two balls, one dropped and the other thrown horizontally at the same moment. The horizontal speed of the thrown ball is $$v.$$

They want to ignore small effects like air resistance or the curvature of Earth.

It is difficult to throw a ball perfectly horizontally, so instead of a real experiment, you suggest Dorothy and the Scarecrow perform a thought experiment to settle their argument. In the thought experiment, you suggest they switch to a new reference frame.

Which of the following statements are correct? You may choose more than one.

Your thought experiments should find that the thrown ball takes longer to hit the ground.

Your thought experiments should find that the thrown ball hits the ground before the dropped one.

Your thought experiments should find that the balls hit the ground simultaneously.

Switching reference frames to a frame traveling to the right at speed $$v$$ is a productive thought experiment.

Switching reference frames to a frame traveling to the right at speed $$v/2$$ is a productive thought experiment.

Switching reference frames to a frame traveling downward at speed $$v$$ is a productive thought experiment.

label: I2P11
name: A gas like air is made of many molecules moving around randomly. At any given time, some…
desc: A gas like air is made of many molecules moving around randomly. At any given time, some molecules move more slowly and others move more quickly. The speed the molecules move is related to the temperature of the gas. The hotter a gas, the faster the molecules move on average…
statement:
A gas like air is made of many molecules moving around randomly. At any given time, some molecules move more slowly and others move more quickly. The speed the molecules move is related to the temperature of the gas. The hotter a gas, the faster the molecules move on average. There will still be some slow-moving molecules in a hot gas and some fast-moving molecules in a cold gas, but taken as a whole, faster speeds means hotter.

The __second law of thermodynamics__ says that heat always moves from hotter places to colder places as long as there is no energy being used to transfer the heat.

For example, suppose we have a box with a wall in the middle. There is some warm gas on the left of the wall and cool gas on the right. Then according to the second law of thermodynamics, heat can only move from left to right unless there is outside energy used to move it the opposite way. Not even a little heat is allowed to go the opposite direction.

In 1867, Scottish physicist James Clerk Maxwell invented a thought experiment that cast doubt on the second law of thermodynamics.

In this thought experiment, there is a box with warm gas on one side (side B) and cool gas on the other side (side A). There is a barrier in the middle of the box keeping the gasses separate. The box and barrier don't allow any heat to pass through them. The laws of physics say that in this situation, the two sides' temperatures would not change over time.

Next, Maxwell imagined a creature that could see gas molecules. Maxwell imagined the creature installing a trap door in the wall between the warm and cool gas. The creature could open or close the door whenever it wants without spending any energy because the door had zero friction. The creature watched the air molecules on side A, the cool side. It waited until, by chance, a particularly fast-moving air molecule from the cool gas was approaching the trap door. The creature opened the door to let only that air molecule pass, then closed the door again.

Then the creature watched the gas on the side B, the warm side. It waited until a particularly slow-moving air molecule from the warm gas was about to hit the trap door. It again opened the door and let the molecule through to the cool side.

Maxwell imagined the creature repeating this over and over. Eventually, a lot of fast-moving molecules would have moved from the cold air to the warm air, and a lot of slow-moving molecules would haved moved from the warm air to the cool air. This would raise the average speed of molecules in the warm air and lower the average speed of molecules in the cold air. As a result, the warm air would get warmer and the cold air would get colder, even though the creature hadn't used up any energy.

If such a creature could exist within the laws of physics, it would violate the second law of thermodynamics.

Scientists were confused by this thought experiment for a long time. They still believed that the second law of thermodynamics was correct, but the thought experiment seemed to show it was not correct. Many people proposed resolutions to the paradox of Maxwell's thought experiment.

Which one of the following, if it were correct, would be a valid resolution to the puzzle of Maxwell's thought experiment?

No such creature has evolved on Earth.

Scientists tried to build a version of Maxwell's thought experiment, but it was too hard to measure the speeds of the molecules with current technology.

According to the law of quantum mechanics, if the creature did exist, the act of measuring the speeds of the molecules would have to use energy, and that energy would be enough to move the heat from cool to warm air via conventional means (like using electricity to remove heat from an already-cool refrigerator)

Although the creature could move heat from cool to warm air without using energy, it could only do it for a little while. Eventually it would run out of molecules to trade back and forth and have to stop.

Real doors usually have a little bit of friction in them, so the creature's door isn't realistic.
