label: I2P11
name: Galileo's Rolling Ball — A __thought experiment__ is an experiment carried out only in our imaginations. We…
desc: A __thought experiment__ is an experiment carried out only in our imaginations. We never have to actually build it for it to be useful — thought experiments can go places real experiments cannot. One of the most famous is due to Galileo, who asked us to imagine releasing a ball…
statement:
A __thought experiment__ is an experiment carried out only in our imaginations. We never have to actually build it for it to be useful — thought experiments can go places real experiments cannot. One of the most famous is due to Galileo, who asked us to imagine releasing a ball near the top of a two-sided ramp:

__(a)__ The ball rolls down the left side, across the bottom, and up the right side. The ramp shown above is symmetric. How high on the right side could the ball rise before turning around?

__(b)__ Next, imagine the asymmetric ramp below, whose right-hand side is less steep than the left. How far should the ball rise this time? There are several plausible candidates: maybe the ball rolls the same __distance along the ramp__ on each side, or covers the same __horizontal distance__, or rises to the same __height__ it started from. The thought experiment alone doesn't settle which candidate is right. What might Galileo have done to find out?

__(c)__ Galileo did a real experiment — here is a modern version, a ball rolling on a curved track:

To a good approximation, the ball rises to the same height it was released from. In the real experiment, though, the ball rose to a slightly __lower__ height each time it rolled back and forth. What physical interactions cause this height loss? ("It loses energy" or "it loses momentum" only describes what happened — name the interactions responsible.)

__(d)__ The better we engineer the ramp, the closer the ball rises to its original height, so in the thought experiment we may imagine perfect engineering: no air drag and no rolling resistance, so the ball always rises __exactly__ to its release height. Now suppose we make the right-hand side of the ramp shallower and shallower. What does the ball's journey look like? Finally — the last step of the thought experiment — make the right-hand side perfectly flat and horizontal, as below. What does the ball do?

__(e)__ What was Galileo's main point — what big idea about motion was the whole thought experiment built to teach? What is the idea called today, and what competing belief, inherited from the ancient Greek philosopher Aristotle, was Galileo fighting against?

label: I2P11
name: Towing a Spaceship — __Newton's first law of motion__ says that a moving object continues moving in a…
desc: __Newton's first law of motion__ says that a moving object continues moving in a straight line at constant speed forever unless some influence (a push or pull, such as friction or drag) changes its motion. Also recall the difference between two words: __speed__ is how fast…
statement:
__Newton's first law of motion__ says that a moving object continues moving in a straight line at constant speed forever unless some influence (a push or pull, such as friction or drag) changes its motion. Also recall the difference between two words: __speed__ is how fast something moves, while __velocity__ includes the direction of motion as well. You are piloting a space tugboat in deep space, far from any planet, towing a heavy spaceship behind you on a long cable. There is no air and no friction out here.

__(a)__ You and the spaceship are both coasting along in a straight line at constant velocity. Does the cable need to be taut — that is, does the tug need to be pulling on the ship? Explain your reasoning using Newton's first law.

__(b)__ In which of these situations does the tug need to pull on the spaceship: speeding the ship up, slowing the ship down, or taking the ship in a circle at constant speed? Explain each case. (Careful with the last one — think about the difference between speed and velocity.)

__(c)__ To build intuition for the circular case, think about a real-world experience: whirling a ball on a string around your head, shown from overhead below. You don't touch the ball directly; any force on the ball comes from the string. In what direction does the string pull the ball?

__(d)__ Using your answer to (c): once the spaceship is up to speed, in which direction should the tug pull the cable to take the ship around a circle at constant speed — in the direction the ship is moving, or some other direction?

label: I2P11
name: Why Doesn't the Moon Fall Down? — Here are the Earth and moon to scale, in a photo taken by NASA's OSIRIS-REx…
desc: Here are the Earth and moon to scale, in a photo taken by NASA's OSIRIS-REx spacecraft in 2017: The moon has stayed up there for billions of years. Why doesn't Earth's gravity pull it down? Consider four candidate explanations. __(1)__ Earth's gravity doesn't reach as far as the…
statement:
Here are the Earth and moon to scale, in a photo taken by NASA's OSIRIS-REx spacecraft in 2017:

The moon has stayed up there for billions of years. Why doesn't Earth's gravity pull it down? Consider four candidate explanations. __(1)__ Earth's gravity doesn't reach as far as the moon. __(2)__ The moon is too big to be pulled in by gravity. __(3)__ Earth's gravity does pull on the moon, but it's so weak out there that it doesn't make any real difference. __(4)__ Somehow, the moon's sideways motion keeps it up. Some facts you can use: Newton's model of gravity says two bodies of masses $$M$$ and $$m$$ separated by a distance $$r$$ attract with force $$F = \dfrac{GMm}{r^2},$$ so the gravitational acceleration toward Earth obeys the inverse square law $$g \propto \dfrac{1}{r^2}.$$ At Earth's surface, $$g_{\rm surface} \approx 10\;\mathrm{m/s^2}.$$ The distance from Earth to the moon is $$r_{\rm moon} = 3.6 \times 10^8\;\mathrm{m},$$ and the radius of the Earth is $$R_\oplus \approx 6.4 \times 10^6\;\mathrm{m}.$$

__(a)__ What does Newton's formula say about explanation (1)?

__(b)__ We'd like to find $$g_{\rm moon},$$ the acceleration of the moon due to Earth's gravity. Can we just use $$g_{\rm surface} \approx 10\;\mathrm{m/s^2}$$ for the moon? Why or why not?

__(c)__ We'll compare the moon to an apple falling from a tree. In the inverse square law, the distance $$r_{\rm apple}$$ is measured from the apple to what, exactly? (Be specific — what part of the Earth?) What is the value of $$r_{\rm apple}?$$

__(d)__ Compute the ratio $$\dfrac{r_{\rm moon}}{r_{\rm apple}},$$ then use the inverse square law to find how many times weaker Earth's gravity is at the moon than at the apple, and find $$g_{\rm moon}.$$ (Careful: the __square__ in the inverse square law means a straightforward ratio of distances will not work.)

__(e)__ Your answer to (d) is a tiny acceleration. Is it small enough to rescue explanation (3) — that gravity at the moon is too weak to matter? Useful fact: a calculation (which you are not asked to do) shows that if the moon started from rest at its current distance and accelerated toward Earth under this gravity, it would crash into Earth in only about five days.

__(f)__ Galileo established that everything at the same distance from Earth falls with the same acceleration, no matter how massive it is. What does that say about explanation (2)? Which explanation is left standing?

label: I2P11
name: Newton's Cannon — Why does sideways motion keep the moon from falling to Earth? Isaac Newton answered this…
desc: Why does sideways motion keep the moon from falling to Earth? Isaac Newton answered this with a famous thought experiment. Start small: stand at the top of a tall tower and drop a ball; it falls straight down. Now instead __throw__ the ball horizontally. __(a)__ Neglecting air…
statement:
Why does sideways motion keep the moon from falling to Earth? Isaac Newton answered this with a famous thought experiment. Start small: stand at the top of a tall tower and drop a ball; it falls straight down. Now instead __throw__ the ball horizontally.

__(a)__ Neglecting air resistance, which of the candidate paths in the figure below does the thrown ball follow? Explain what is wrong with each of the other two. (The arrow shows the direction of the throw.)

__(b)__ What changes if you throw the ball harder?

__(c)__ Next, Newton imagined the tower sitting on the entire Earth, and imagined throwing the ball faster and faster — far faster than any person could throw. You can try this yourself in a simulation at https://glowscript.org/#/user/mark.d.eichenlaub/folder/My_Programs/program/newtontower — give the ball a small sideways push, then a bigger one, then a bigger one, increasing gradually. What eventually happens once the push is fast enough, even though Earth's gravity never stops pulling the ball down? Newton drew the picture below to illustrate the idea, imagining a cannon on a mountaintop so his readers could visualize launching the ball __very__ fast:

__(d)__ The speed needed is about $$8000\;\mathrm{m/s}$$ — faster than any real cannonball (fortunately, Newton's cannon was imaginary), but a powerful rocket can reach it. Roughly speaking, a rocket's flight to orbit has two steps: shooting straight up to get out of Earth's atmosphere, and then turning sideways and accelerating to about $$8\;\mathrm{km/s}.$$ Which step do you expect takes much more fuel, and why? (What would happen if the rocket only did the first step?)

__(e)__ The moon orbits Earth, but it travels much more slowly than $$8\;\mathrm{km/s}.$$ Why can the moon get away with a slower orbital speed?

label: I2P11
name: Galileo's Ship — Imagine you are in a windowless room inside a boat. The boat might be stopped in the…
desc: Imagine you are in a windowless room inside a boat. The boat might be stopped in the water, or it might be sailing smoothly at constant velocity. Your challenge: figure out whether the boat is moving, using only experiments performed __inside the room__. (No peeking at the…
statement:
Imagine you are in a windowless room inside a boat. The boat might be stopped in the water, or it might be sailing smoothly at constant velocity. Your challenge: figure out whether the boat is moving, using only experiments performed __inside the room__. (No peeking at the water, no GPS, no asking anyone outside — those all get information from outside the room.) This is another of Galileo's famous thought experiments, and unlike a real boat, the thought-experiment boat sails perfectly smoothly, with no waves rocking it.

__(a)__ First idea: walk around the room, carefully trying to feel the boat's motion. Assuming the boat is moving, which would feel easier — walking in the same direction the boat is moving, or walking in the opposite direction? Draw on your real-life experience riding in boats, planes, and trains.

__(b)__ Second idea: throw something. A professional baseball pitcher can throw a baseball at about $$100\;\mathrm{mph}.$$ Suppose the pitcher throws inside an airplane flying smoothly at $$600\;\mathrm{mph}$$ (with plenty of room to wind up). What is the fastest speed the pitcher's baseball moves: $$100\;\mathrm{mph},$$ $$700\;\mathrm{mph},$$ or is this somehow a trick question?

__(c)__ The resolution of (b) uses the idea of a __reference frame__: a point of view from which we measure motion. We often specify a reference frame by saying what we measure speeds "relative to." Restate your answer to (b) by giving the ball's top speed relative to the airplane and relative to the ground. How fast is the ball "really" moving?

__(d)__ Back in the boat: does throwing a baseball back and forth let you find out whether the boat is moving? What about juggling, or jumping to see which direction you jump farther in? What conclusion did Galileo draw from this thought experiment?

label: I2P11
name: What's Really Moving? The Train in Hugo — Have you ever sat in a train at a station and briefly wondered why…
desc: Have you ever sat in a train at a station and briefly wondered why the entire station started drifting backwards — before realizing that it was really your train starting to move forward? We usually treat the Earth as stationary, but sometimes your brain briefly assumes the…
statement:
Have you ever sat in a train at a station and briefly wondered why the entire station started drifting backwards — before realizing that it was really your train starting to move forward? We usually treat the Earth as stationary, but sometimes your brain briefly assumes the __train__ is stationary instead, and concludes that the trees and buildings are moving. The 2011 film __Hugo__ used exactly this trick. Here is a shot from the movie:

__(a)__ Watching the shot, which objects appear to be moving: the inspector (in blue), the train, the station platform, or the man with the briefcase?

Here is how the scene was actually filmed:

__(b)__ The studio's train couldn't roll along its tracks. Instead, the film crew pulled the entire station platform to the left while the train stayed put. Knowing this, which objects were __really__ moving? Is that even a well-posed question?

__(c)__ Galileo designed his reference-frame thought experiments with a purpose: he wanted to convince people of something about the Earth itself. What was his claim, and how does the ship thought experiment (no experiment inside a windowless room can detect smooth constant-velocity motion) support it?

__(d)__ The general principle is now called the __principle of relativity__: all constant-velocity reference frames are the same from the point of view of physics, so from inside a closed room you can never tell whether the room is moving at constant velocity. Which famous physicist later used this principle as one of the two assumptions of a celebrated theory, and what is the theory called?

label: I2P11
name: The Cannon on the Rolling Cart — A cart on wheels carries a little spring-loaded cannon that shoots a ball…
desc: A cart on wheels carries a little spring-loaded cannon that shoots a ball straight up. Since the ball goes straight up, it comes straight back down and lands in the cannon again. Here is the cart standing still: Now suppose the cart is rolling to the right at a constant speed…
statement:
A cart on wheels carries a little spring-loaded cannon that shoots a ball straight up. Since the ball goes straight up, it comes straight back down and lands in the cannon again. Here is the cart standing still:

Now suppose the cart is rolling to the right at a constant speed $$v$$ when the cannon fires:

__(a)__ Where does the ball land: behind the cannon, right back in the cannon, or in front of the cannon? Before settling the question, state one plausible-sounding argument for "behind" and one for "right back in the cannon."

__(b)__ The __principle of relativity__ says that all constant-velocity reference frames are physically equivalent: from inside a closed room, you cannot tell whether the room is moving at constant velocity. To apply it, imagine the rolling cart inside a windowless room on a ship. In the reference frame of the ship's room, the cart rolls to the right at speed $$v.$$ Meanwhile, suppose the ship is sailing to the __left__ at that same speed $$v$$ relative to the water. In the water's reference frame, what is the motion of the cart? Use this to settle part (a).

__(c)__ Another way to see the answer is the movie-camera trick (used in the film __Hugo__, where the crew moved the station platform instead of the train): film the rolling cart with a camera that moves right along with it. Viewed through that camera, the cart is stationary, the ball goes straight up and down, and the ground slides backwards:

And it really works — here is a real demonstration:

Whenever we go from a thought experiment to the real world, complications appear that the thought experiment left out. Give two physical effects that could make a real ball miss the real cart.

__(d)__ Galileo's ship argument requires the ship to move at truly constant velocity — you can distinctly feel acceleration (think of being pressed back into your seat as a car speeds up). Is a ship sailing the ocean at constant speed on a constant heading truly moving at constant velocity? (Hint: think about the shape and the motion of the Earth.) What is the resulting effect called, and does it invalidate the principle of relativity?

Part A. We've previously discussed several of Galileo's experiments and thought experiments, and in this problem we'll introduce one more.

In __Dialogues Concerning Two New Sciences__, Galileo described an experiment with a pendulum. The pendulum is attached to a ceiling at point $$A.$$ Galileo released the pendulum from point $$C,$$ as shown below.

After being released, the pendulum swung along the dotted arc in the picture above. It went through point $$B$$ and then on to point $$D$$ before turning around and returning towards point $$C.$$

Select the **two** statements which accurately describe the relationship between points $$C$$ and $$D.$$ You should choose one of (a) through (c) and one of (d) through (f).

In an ideal pendulum, they are exactly the same height.

In an ideal pendulum, $$D$$ is higher than $$C.$$

In an ideal pendulum, $$C$$ is higher than $$D.$$

In the real world, they are exactly the same height.

In the real world, $$D$$ is at least slightly higher than $$C.$$

In the real world, $$C$$ is at least slightly higher than $$D.$$

statement:
In our lesson on analyzing linear data, we discussed __current__, which is a flow of electrical charge. The symbol for current is $$I.$$

A current of $$I$$ flowing along a wire means that the amount of electrical charge that flows out the end of the wire in a time $$\Delta t$$ is $$I \cdot \Delta t.$$ The same amount of charge has to enter the beginning of the wire in that time.

Imagine current $$I_0$$ flowing from left to right in a wire. The wire enters a box, and two wires come out of the box, carrying currents $$I_1$$ and $$I_2.$$

Which **two** of the following statements can we justify using charge conservation?

If we know two currents, we can calculate the third.

If we know all three currents, we know how quickly the total charge in the box is changing.

$$I_1 = I_2$$

$$I_0$$ is the largest current

If the charge in the box is not changing, then $$I_0 = I_1 + I_2.$$

The area below the building has been secured specifically for your experiment; no people are nearby to get hit in the head by falling rocks, and the relevant safety authorities have approved your project. You also have adult supervision while on the building.

You take your first rock and throw it perfectly horizontally off the building.

Next, you throw your second rock straight upward from just past the edge of the building.

Finally, you throw the third rock straight downward off the building.

You throw all three rocks with the same initial speed and from the same initial height. None hit the building or any other obstacles; they all continue their trajectories until they hit the ground. The ground is level. You can assume that air resistance and other forces besides gravity are negligible.

Which rock hits the ground with the greatest speed?

name: Part A. In this problem, we'll use a thought experiment involving changing reference…
desc: Part A. In this problem, we'll use a thought experiment involving changing reference frames to get an alternative perspective on the kinetic energy formula. The goal of this problem is to demonstrate where the kinetic energy formula comes from, so you do not need to use the…
statement:
Part A. In this problem, we'll use a thought experiment involving changing reference frames to get an alternative perspective on the kinetic energy formula. The goal of this problem is to demonstrate where the kinetic energy formula comes from, so you do not need to use the kinetic energy formula to find the answers to the questions in this problem. Instead, by the time we're done all the parts, you should be able to explain why the kinetic energy formula works the way it does.

Imagine two boxes, $$A$$ and $$B,$$ of equal mass. At time $$t_1$$ the boxes are held stationary with a compressed spring between them. The spring stores some potential energy, which we call $$S.$$

The boxes are released and the spring pushes them apart so that all the potential energy in the spring is converted to kinetic energy in the boxes. At this point, the boxes move in opposite directions, each at speed $$v.$$ We can call this time $$t_2.$$

Once the spring has been released, it can be ignored. It has no mass.

At time $$t_2,$$ what is the kinetic energy of the box $$A$$ in terms of $$S?$$

Part B. Let's adopt a reference frame in which the right hand box $$B$$ is stationary at time $$t_2.$$ We will call this frame 2. (The original reference frame, in which both boxes have the same speed at time $$t_2,$$ is frame 1.)

What is the speed of the box $$A$$ at time $$t_2$$ in frame 2?

Part C. In frame 1, the total energy of the boxes and spring is $$S.$$ What is the total energy of the boxes and spring in frame 2 in terms of $$S?$$

Part D. At time $$t_2,$$ how many times as much kinetic energy does box $$A$$ have in frame 2 as it has in frame 1?

Part E. Doubling the speed of a box multiplies its kinetic energy by four, which is what happens when $$K \propto v^2$$

Doubling the kinetic energy of a box multiplies its speed by four, which is what happens when $$v \propto K^2$$

Spring energy is $$S$$

The coefficient in the kinetic energy formula must be $$\dfrac12$$

name: Two Caps in a Two-Diameter Tube — A horizontal tube is completely full of water. The left half of the tube is…
desc: A horizontal tube is completely full of water. The left half of the tube is wide and the right half is narrow. Two caps, $$A$$ and $$B,$$ fit snugly in the tube and can slide left or right, but no water can leak past a cap. The water fills all the space between the caps. __(a)__…
statement:
A horizontal tube is completely full of water. The left half of the tube is wide and the right half is narrow. Two caps, $$A$$ and $$B,$$ fit snugly in the tube and can slide left or right, but no water can leak past a cap. The water fills all the space between the caps.

__(a)__ Cap $$A$$ is pushed a distance $$a$$ to the right. What does cap $$B$$ do — move right, move left, or stay still? Explain your answer by thinking about the water between the caps. (It may help to imagine a line dividing the wide section from the narrow section.)

__(b)__ There is some quantity whose change has the same magnitude on the left side as on the right side — but it is not the distance the caps move. What is that quantity? When a quantity does not change over time, we say it is __conserved__; what conservation law are we assuming about the water? (Volume can be measured in liters: if $$1\;\mathrm{L}$$ of water leaves the left side, $$1\;\mathrm{L}$$ of water must be added to the right side.)

__(c)__ When a circular cap of radius $$R$$ slides a distance $$\Delta x,$$ it sweeps out a cylinder of volume $$\Delta V = \left(\pi R^2\right)\cdot\Delta x.$$ Suppose the radius of the wide section is $$R_A = 1\;\mathrm{m},$$ the radius of the narrow section is $$R_B = 0.5\;\mathrm{m},$$ and cap $$A$$ moves $$a = 1\;\mathrm{cm}$$ to the right. How far does cap $$B$$ move? (Careful: the answer is not $$2\;\mathrm{cm}.$$ Think of the tube as a three-dimensional object.)

__(d)__ Now remove the caps and let water flow steadily through the tube from left to right. Does the water move faster in the wide section, faster in the narrow section, or at the same speed everywhere? (Hint: imagine inserting imaginary caps that ride along with the water.) If $$R_A/R_B = 3,$$ what is the ratio of speeds $$v_B/v_A?$$

label: I2P12
name: Pulleys, Levers, and Conservation of String — A __pulley__ is a wheel that a rope can run over, like the one…
desc: A __pulley__ is a wheel that a rope can run over, like the one in the photo below. Pulleys can be used to lift things. The simplest pulley setup, called an __Atwood machine__, is shown below: two boxes connected by a single rope that runs over the pulley from one box to the…
statement:
A __pulley__ is a wheel that a rope can run over, like the one in the photo below. Pulleys can be used to lift things.

The simplest pulley setup, called an __Atwood machine__, is shown below: two boxes connected by a single rope that runs over the pulley from one box to the other.

__(a)__ In the Atwood machine, box $$A$$ falls $$1\;\mathrm{cm}$$ down. What happens to box $$B?$$ The amount of string on the left of the pulley changes, and so does the amount on the right — what about the string __is__ conserved?

__(b)__ Now consider the trickier setup below. The upper pulley is fixed in place; the lower pulley can move up and down. One string is attached to the ceiling, runs down around the movable pulley (segments $$s_1$$ and $$s_2$$), up over the fixed pulley, and down to box $$A$$ (segment $$s_3$$). Box $$B$$ hangs from the movable pulley by segment $$s_4,$$ and segment $$s_5$$ attaches the fixed pulley to the ceiling. If box $$A$$ falls, which direction does box $$B$$ move?

__(c)__ Box $$A$$ falls by a distance $$a.$$ For each segment $$s_1$$ through $$s_5,$$ say whether it gets longer, gets shorter, or stays the same length. Then: suppose someone claims that $$s_1$$ and $$s_2$$ each get shorter by the full amount $$a.$$ What problem would that create? Finally, how far does box $$B$$ actually rise?

__(d)__ A lever is another system where one part moves down while another moves up. The dot on the left side of the lever below is a distance $$a$$ from the fulcrum, and the right end is a distance $$b$$ from the fulcrum. If the left dot falls by $$1\;\mathrm{cm},$$ how far does the right end rise? (Hint: draw the lever tilted and look for similar triangles.)

label: I2P12
name: Exact and Inexact Conservation Laws — A __conservation law__ is a rule that a certain quantity does not…
desc: A __conservation law__ is a rule that a certain quantity does not change over time. Some conservation laws hold only approximately, while others — as far as we know — are exact. __(a)__ If you pull on a string in real life (without breaking it), does the length of the string…
statement:
A __conservation law__ is a rule that a certain quantity does not change over time. Some conservation laws hold only approximately, while others — as far as we know — are exact.

__(a)__ If you pull on a string in real life (without breaking it), does the length of the string increase, decrease, or stay exactly the same? Is conservation of string length an exact law?

__(b)__ You start with $$2\;\mathrm{gal}$$ of water in a $$5\;\mathrm{gal}$$ bucket, plus a completely full $$3\;\mathrm{gal}$$ bucket, as shown below. You pour the $$3\;\mathrm{gal}$$ bucket into the $$5\;\mathrm{gal}$$ bucket. Afterward, the $$5\;\mathrm{gal}$$ bucket does not contain exactly $$5\;\mathrm{gal}$$ of water. Here are six possible reasons: (1) some water gets spilled on the ground; (2) a little water is left behind in the $$3\;\mathrm{gal}$$ bucket; (3) the pressure of the water compresses it a little bit; (4) some water evaporates away; (5) some water vapor condenses out of the air into the bucket; (6) the initial volumes were not exactly $$2\;\mathrm{gal}$$ and $$3\;\mathrm{gal}.$$ Which of these reasons are genuine examples of the __failure__ of conservation of volume, and which are not? Explain each.

__(c)__ How big is the compression effect from reason (3)? In a bucket of water $$20\;\mathrm{cm}$$ deep, by roughly what fraction is the water at the bottom compressed by the pressure of the water above it? What does this tell you about how good the approximation of volume conservation is for everyday purposes?

__(d)__ Name two conservation laws that, in our best models of physics, are believed to be __exact__.

label: I2P12
name: A Ball on Galileo's Ramps — A ball is released from rest part-way up the steep left side of the asymmetric…
desc: A ball is released from rest part-way up the steep left side of the asymmetric ramp shown below. It rolls down the left slope, across the flat bottom, and up the shallower right slope until it momentarily stops and turns around. __Gravitational potential energy__ ($$U_g$$) is…
statement:
A ball is released from rest part-way up the steep left side of the asymmetric ramp shown below. It rolls down the left slope, across the flat bottom, and up the shallower right slope until it momentarily stops and turns around.

__Gravitational potential energy__ ($$U_g$$) is the energy an object has due to its height. We are free to choose where $$U_g = 0;$$ here we choose the flat bottom of the ramp. __Kinetic energy__ ($$K$$) is the energy any moving object has. Total energy is __conserved__ — it never changes, although it can change from one form to another. We can track the ball's energy with a bar chart in which each square represents a fixed amount of energy. At the moment of release, the chart looks like this (the chart has a third, unlabeled column that we will need later):

__(a)__ At the moment of release, why is all of the ball's energy in the $$U_g$$ column and none in the $$K$$ column?

__(b)__ A moment later, the ball is part-way down the slope and still speeding up. Which types of energy does it have now? Is its total energy more than, less than, or the same as at release? Describe what happens on the bar chart, as in the animation below.

__(c)__ Suppose you dragged squares from the $$U_g$$ column to the $$K$$ column at exactly the rate the ball really converts energy as it rolls down. Should your pace stay steady, get faster as the ball gets lower, or get slower? Why?

__(d)__ When the ball reaches the flat portion at the bottom of the ramp, what does its energy bar chart look like?

__(e)__ The ball then rises up the right slope until it momentarily stops. Use energy conservation to explain why, in the ideal case, the ball must rise to __exactly__ the same height it was released from — regardless of the slope of the right side. (The animation below shows the full energy story for one trip.)

__(f)__ In the real world, the ball rises a little lower with each pass and eventually stops rolling altogether, because of air drag and rolling resistance — together called __resistive forces__. Does this mean energy conservation fails when there are resistive forces? Where does the energy go? What does the bar chart look like after the ball has sat on the track for a very long time?

__(g)__ The three ramps below all have the same height but different slopes; ramp $$A$$ is steepest and ramp $$C$$ is shallowest. A ball is released from rest at the top of each ramp and rolls to the bottom, with no thermal energy losses. For which ramp is the ball moving fastest when it reaches the bottom?

__(h)__ For which ramp does the ball reach the bottom in the least time?

label: I2P12
name: Balanced Pulleys and Mechanical Advantage — An __Atwood machine__ is a pulley with a single rope running over…
desc: An __Atwood machine__ is a pulley with a single rope running over it and a box hanging from each end, as shown below. Consider an ideal Atwood machine: there is no friction, and the string and pulley are massless — only the boxes, with masses $$m_A$$ and $$m_B,$$ have mass. When…
statement:
An __Atwood machine__ is a pulley with a single rope running over it and a box hanging from each end, as shown below. Consider an ideal Atwood machine: there is no friction, and the string and pulley are massless — only the boxes, with masses $$m_A$$ and $$m_B,$$ have mass. When a box of mass $$m$$ changes its height by $$\Delta h,$$ its gravitational potential energy changes by $$\Delta U_g = mg\,\Delta h.$$ Total energy — kinetic plus potential — is conserved.

__(a)__ Suppose $$m_B > m_A$$ and the boxes are released from rest, so box $$B$$ accelerates downward and box $$A$$ accelerates upward. Both boxes gain kinetic energy. Given that total energy is conserved, what must happen to the __total__ gravitational potential energy? Box $$A$$ is rising and gaining gravitational potential energy — how can the total still go the way you said?

__(b)__ Now suppose $$m_A = m_B.$$ Imagine box $$A$$ rises a little while box $$B$$ falls the same distance. What happens to the total gravitational potential energy? Would the boxes, released from rest, accelerate? Does it matter whether the two boxes start at the same height? If someone gives the balanced system a push, what does it do afterward?

__(c)__ State the general rules these examples illustrate: when a stationary, unbalanced system is released, does it move toward higher or lower potential energy, and why? And what condition makes a system __balanced__, so it will not start accelerating?

__(d)__ Now consider the two-pulley system below: the upper pulley is fixed, the lower pulley can move up and down, and conservation of string length means that when box $$A$$ falls a distance $$a,$$ box $$B$$ rises only $$a/2.$$ Suppose $$m_A = m_B = 20\;\mathrm{kg}.$$ Which way does box $$A$$ accelerate — or is the system balanced?

__(e)__ With $$m_A = 20\;\mathrm{kg},$$ what must $$m_B$$ be to balance this pulley system?

__(f)__ You want to use this pulley system to lift a heavy piano. Should the piano take the place of box $$A$$ or box $$B,$$ and why? If you then want to lift the piano $$1\;\mathrm{m}$$ into the air, how far must you pull the end of the rope you are holding?

label: I2P12
name: The Hydraulic Press — A __hydraulic press__ consists of two vertical cylindrical tubes filled with water and…
desc: A __hydraulic press__ consists of two vertical cylindrical tubes filled with water and connected by a horizontal tube at the bottom, as shown below. The left cylinder is wider, with diameter $$D_A;$$ the right cylinder is narrower, with diameter $$D_B.$$ A platform floats on top…
statement:
A __hydraulic press__ consists of two vertical cylindrical tubes filled with water and connected by a horizontal tube at the bottom, as shown below. The left cylinder is wider, with diameter $$D_A;$$ the right cylinder is narrower, with diameter $$D_B.$$ A platform floats on top of the water in each tube so that no water can escape, and a ball sits on each platform: mass $$m_A$$ on the left and $$m_B$$ on the right. If the press is unbalanced, one ball falls, pushes water through the bottom tube to the other side, and makes the other ball rise. Recall that when a piston of cross-section area $$\pi R^2$$ moves a distance $$\Delta x,$$ it displaces a volume $$\Delta V = (\pi R^2)\,\Delta x,$$ and the total volume of water is conserved. Also recall $$\Delta U_g = mg\,\Delta h,$$ and that a system is balanced when a small motion would not change its total potential energy. (To avoid worrying about the potential energy of the water itself, imagine the balls only move short distances.)

__(a)__ If the hydraulic press is unbalanced and the balls move, which ball moves through the larger distance, $$A$$ or $$B?$$ Why? (This is the same argument as for a horizontal tube with two caps — the bends in the pipe change nothing.)

__(b)__ Suppose $$m_A = m_B.$$ Which way will ball $$A$$ accelerate: up, down, or neither?

__(c)__ Let $$m_B = 20\;\mathrm{kg},$$ $$D_B = 0.1\;\mathrm{m},$$ and $$D_A = 1\;\mathrm{m}.$$ What must $$m_A$$ be to balance the hydraulic press? (Hint: by what factor does ball $$B$$ move farther than ball $$A?$$ Then argue as you would for a pulley with mechanical advantage.)

__(d)__ Hydraulic presses can generate enormous forces, but what is the downside, in terms of the amount of motion you get on side $$A?$$

label: I2P12
name: The Seesaw and the Law of the Lever — In the animation below, an $$80\;\mathrm{kg}$$ adult balances a…
desc: In the animation below, an $$80\;\mathrm{kg}$$ adult balances a $$20\;\mathrm{kg}$$ child on a seesaw. The child sits four times as far from the fulcrum (the pivot) as the adult. Recall two facts: when an object of mass $$m$$ changes its height by $$\Delta h,$$ its gravitational…
statement:
In the animation below, an $$80\;\mathrm{kg}$$ adult balances a $$20\;\mathrm{kg}$$ child on a seesaw. The child sits four times as far from the fulcrum (the pivot) as the adult.

Recall two facts: when an object of mass $$m$$ changes its height by $$\Delta h,$$ its gravitational potential energy changes by $$\Delta U_g = mg\,\Delta h;$$ and a system is balanced when a small motion would not change its total potential energy. Call the child person $$1,$$ sitting a distance $$x_1$$ from the fulcrum, and the adult person $$2,$$ at distance $$x_2.$$

__(a)__ In words, using energy: how can a light child balance a heavy adult? (Imagine the seesaw tilting a little toward the adult, and compare the two changes in height.)

__(b)__ For the seesaw to be balanced, what must be the relationship between $$\Delta U_{g;1}$$ and $$\Delta U_{g;2}$$ when the seesaw tilts slightly? (Careful: they are not equal — if they were, tilting could raise the total potential energy.) Write the relationship as an equation, then substitute $$\Delta U_g = mg\,\Delta h$$ on both sides and simplify what you can.

__(c)__ The figure below shows the seesaw tilted slightly from horizontal. Use similar triangles to relate each person's height change $$\Delta h$$ to their distance $$x$$ from the fulcrum, keeping track of the fact that when one side goes up, the other goes down.

__(d)__ Combine your equations from parts (b) and (c) to eliminate the $$\Delta h$$ variables, and simplify. What famous equation do you get, and what is it called? Then summarize in a sentence or two __why__ that law is true, in terms of energy conservation.

label: I2P12
name: The Acceleration of a Block on a Frictionless Ramp — A frictionless ramp has length $$\ell$$ along its slope…
desc: A frictionless ramp has length $$\ell$$ along its slope, and one end is elevated to a height $$H.$$ A block is placed on the ramp and released from rest; with no friction, it slides (not rolls) down, getting faster the whole way. Your goal is to find the block's __acceleration__…
statement:
A frictionless ramp has length $$\ell$$ along its slope, and one end is elevated to a height $$H.$$ A block is placed on the ramp and released from rest; with no friction, it slides (not rolls) down, getting faster the whole way. Your goal is to find the block's __acceleration__ — the rate at which its speed changes.

Two energy formulas will help. Gravitational potential energy: $$U_g = mgh,$$ where $$m$$ is the mass, $$g$$ is the acceleration due to gravity, and $$h$$ is the height (we take $$h = 0$$ at the bottom of the ramp). Kinetic energy: $$K = \dfrac12 mv^2,$$ where $$v$$ is the speed. Total energy is conserved. Notice that neither formula contains the block's acceleration, so we will need a plan: (1) find the block's speed at the bottom using energy conservation; (2) find the time the trip takes using the ramp's length and the block's speed; (3) divide the speed gained by the time taken to get the acceleration; then test that the answer makes sense.

__(a)__ Let $$v_f$$ be the block's speed at the bottom of the ramp. The block starts with all gravitational potential energy and ends with all kinetic energy. Write the energy-conservation equation and solve it for $$v_f.$$ The mass should cancel — what does that tell you?

__(b)__ Let $$t_f$$ be the time the block takes to slide down. Someone proposes $$t_f = \dfrac{\ell}{v_f}.$$ What is wrong with that, and what is the correct expression for $$t_f$$ in terms of $$\ell,$$ $$g,$$ and $$H?$$

__(c)__ Acceleration is the speed gained per unit time. Combine your answers to (a) and (b) to find the block's acceleration $$a.$$ Simplify until no square roots remain.

__(d)__ Test your answer: check its dimensions, and check the special cases $$H = 0$$ and $$H = \ell.$$ What should the acceleration be in each special case, and does your formula agree?

label: I2P12
name: Charge Conservation and Two Metal Spheres — __Electric charge__ is a property of matter: electrons carry…
desc: __Electric charge__ is a property of matter: electrons carry negative charge and protons carry positive charge. Charge is measured in __coulombs__ ($$\mathrm{C}$$); a nanocoulomb ($$\mathrm{nC}$$) is a billionth of a coulomb. A __current__ is a flow of charge, and current is…
statement:
__Electric charge__ is a property of matter: electrons carry negative charge and protons carry positive charge. Charge is measured in __coulombs__ ($$\mathrm{C}$$); a nanocoulomb ($$\mathrm{nC}$$) is a billionth of a coulomb. A __current__ is a flow of charge, and current is defined to flow in the direction that positive charge moves (if electrons are moving, the current points opposite to the electrons). In physics, charge is __conserved__ — as far as we know, exactly.

Two metal spheres, each with radius $$r,$$ carry charges of $$4\;\mathrm{nC}$$ and $$-8\;\mathrm{nC}$$ respectively. They are connected with a wire, and current flows between the spheres until they have the same charge.

__(a)__ While the spheres equalize, which direction does the current flow through the wire — from the $$+4\;\mathrm{nC}$$ sphere toward the $$-8\;\mathrm{nC}$$ sphere, or the reverse?

__(b)__ Assuming no charge can leave the spheres or arrive from outside, which quantities does charge conservation say cannot change: the total charge on the two spheres, the average charge per sphere, the charge on the left sphere, the charge on the right sphere?

__(c)__ What is the final charge on each sphere?

__(d)__ Does charge conservation mean that, in real life, the spheres would keep their final charges forever? And here is a puzzle about the exactness of the law: we believe that before the Big Bang there was no charge at all, yet the Big Bang created all the charged matter in the universe. How could that happen without violating conservation of charge?
